Things are cleared up before the finis. The frontispiece shows Richard Hunt seated with a girl on a wayside bench.
34981-orthodox-daily-prayers:
Orthodox Daily Prayers is a prayer book issued by the seminary press named for Saint Tikhon. It was printed in 1982 with a bishop's blessing. Bishop Herman of Philadelphia gave that blessing, the front pages say. The contents list the prayers for a full day. Morning prayers open the book's working part. Commemoration of the living and the dead follows them. Prayers at the table and the order of compline come next. Prayers before sleep close the daily round.

Three canons and communion prayers fill the second half. An introduction explains the book's sources and purpose. The prayers come mainly through the Russian Church tradition. Other Orthodox traditions are very similar in this matter, it notes. Psalms of David stand among the gathered texts. So do the Lord's Prayer and prayers of desert fathers. The book teaches readers how to pray by giving models.
35203-in-the-van-or-the-builders:
Price-Brown, or Eric Bohn, wrote In The Van, or The Builders. McLeod and Allen issued it at Toronto in 1906. F H Brigden drew its pictures. A wolf's teeth clutch a young man's leg in front. That plate stands at page 116. Harold Manning's wedding opens the tale.

A little Abbey chapel hosts that November wedding. The minister's questions ring in clear, solemn tones. Will thou love her in sickness and health, he asks. Forsaking all others, keep thee only unto her, he adds. Harold answers I will. Ye builders, true on land and lake, a verse sings. Time has left you in its wake, it adds. Your stress must tell its story, it ends. Thank you very much, Harold exclaims in one plate. New home, sweetheart, another plate sighs late. A Canadian tale of builders opens in marriage and tests its vow in work and wilderness.
35221-the-nation-behind-prison-bars:
The Nation Behind Prison Bars, by George L Herr, was held under a 1913 copyright and printed at Louisville, Kentucky. Herr worked as a prison evangelist. A Bible line heads the book, on visiting those in prison. A photo shows Herr and his wife.

Herr gives the book to his wife, whose help made his work possible. He had written Light in Dark Places and You Are My Prisoner. His opening holds that the folk in prison in the United States could fill a good sized city. For the student of minds, he says, they form the most gripping of all objects. Tales and endorsements fill the book, from sad stories to a grand work highly commended. Church readers get prison work shown from inside the bars.
35393-the-revellers:
The Revellers is a novel by Louis Tracy, published in New York in 1917. Tracy was a prolific writer of adventure and mystery tales. The book opens with a stern reader droning through the eighteenth chapter of the second Book of Samuel, the lament for Absalom. The scene sets a tone of rigid piety against which the story's livelier characters will push.

Across twenty-one chapters the novel follows its cast through conflict, romance, and reversal toward a closing reckoning. Tracy writes in the brisk, dialogue-driven style that made his books popular on both sides of the Atlantic. The Revellers shows his craft in a domestic key rather than on the battlefield or the sea. It keeps the moral questions of its opening scene in view throughout.
35456-tales-by-polish-authors:
Tales by Polish Authors gathers stories by four writers in English dress. Else C M Benecke made the translation, and the Oxford edition is dated nineteen fifteen. Henryk Sienkiewicz heads the list of authors. Stefan Zeromski, Adam Szymanski, and Waclaw Sieroszewski stand with him. A translator's note at the front weighs their fame.

Of the four, only Sienkiewicz is well known in England, the note says. The others are widely read in Poland but new in English, it adds. Szymanski writes from his own banishment to Siberia, the note explains. Sieroszewski spent fifteen years there as a political exile. In that time he studied native tribes such as the Yakut and Tungus, the note says. A tale of Szymanski's Siberian sketches is called one of his most striking.
35457-more-tales-by-polish-authors:
More Tales by Polish Authors is a set of stories in English dress. Benecke and Busch translated them for Blackwell of Oxford in 1916. An earlier Tales by Polish Authors, by Benecke alone, fronts the volume. The Contemporary Review praised that first book as full of genius. A note thanks Szymanski and Zeromski for leave to print their stories.

Nevill Forbes, reader in Russian at Oxford, granted leave for others there. Retinger and Wolff also gave permission for the three remaining authors. Repszowa helped the translators much, the note adds in gratitude. Peasants, soldiers, and small towns of partitioned Poland fill the tales. English readers of 1916 met Polish fiction in the war's shadow.
35478-neighbours:
Robert Stead wrote a Canadian novel printed at Toronto in 1922. Stead had written The Cow Puncher, The Homesteaders, Dennison Grant, and The Empire Builders. My earliest recollection links back to a grey stone house by a road entering a little Ontario town, the narrator begins. Across the road was a mill pond, and across the pond an old fashioned woolen mill, the occasion and support of the town.

His father worked in the mill, as did most men and many women of the place. Work ran from seven in the morning until six at night, before the eight hour day won ground. A wooden water wheel sprayed a mist of jewels into the river on sunny days. Mill town childhood, work, and neighbours shape a plain prairie bound tale.
35481-cannibals-all-or-slaves-without-ma:
George Fitzhugh of Port Royal, in Caroline County, Virginia, wrote this defense of slavery and attack on free society. Morris published it at Richmond in 1857 under the title Cannibals All, or Slaves Without Masters. Its chapter headings announce the argument: the universal trade, labor and capital, and the exploitation of skill.

Fitzhugh contends that free labor leaves workers as slaves without masters, exposed to hunger and want, and he points to England's poor laws, distressed needle-women, and French laborers as his evidence. Later chapters treat negro slavery directly, argue that private property destroys liberty and equality, and hold that government rests on force rather than consent. The book closes with a warning to the North, and it stands as a leading statement of the pro-slavery case of its decade.
35500-nuts-and-nutcrackers:
Nuts and Nutcrackers, by Charles James Lever with drawings by Phiz, was published in London in 1857. The title page piles up mottoes from Shakespeare, The Beggar's Opera, and John Bunyan on hard texts as nuts to crack and eat. Lever, an Irish novelist, turns here to short, sharp social sketches.

The opening nut declares this the age of popular delusions, when each class tries to seem what it is not. Lever mocks those who think Tories consistent, Whigs honest, or Repealers respectable. Indian chiefs who visited Disraeli to see aristocratic life get a dry laugh. The pieces crack at politics, fashion, and self-deceit with a quick, biting wit.
35654-the-stars-in-the-pool-a-prose-poem:
The Stars in the Pool is a prose poem for lovers by Edna Kingsley Wallace. Dutton published the book at New York in 1920. Wallace had written Feelings and Things among earlier works. Side notes mark the scenes and persons of the tale as it unfolds.

The story opens in a white castle amid a forest of lights and shadows. There dwells good King Telwyn, lord of the forest realm, with Queen Ellaline. Their daughter Roseheart is praised as fair as the dawn. Her hair holds the red of tried gold, and her eyes match the eastern sky at twilight. One day a young godlike guest comes over the sea. He is Flame, son of Lokus, lord of an island of fire mountains. The tale moves in high, archaic music suited to its billing as a prose poem.
35807-non-combatants-and-others:
Non-Combatants and Others is a tale of the great war by Rose Macaulay. Her past tales are named on the title leaf. It was print in nineteen sixteen. The book is sworn to the kin of the hand and to more fight men. A verse by a bard of the age stands at its head. A quote on war stands past that verse.

Let the foul scene go on, the verse says. There is mirth in the wings of the stage. It is saw dust that they bleed, but a box of death is brought. Great dins rise up past them. The gods them selves must feel a smart of the eyes as the fumes swell up. The quote past it is more blunt. War is just the slay of things and the smash of things, it says.
35879-the-rotifers:
The Rotifers is a science fiction story by Robert Abernathy, with illustrations by Virgil Finlay noted in the hosted text. A teaser states its hook in one breath. Beneath stagnant water shadowed by lilies, a man found the fascinating world of the rotifers, but it was their world and they resented intrusion. Rotifers are tiny water animals seen under a microscope.

Henry Chatham kneels by his garden pond with a glass fish bowl in thin, nervous hands. He dips it into green scummed water and gathers trailing water weeds into it. Clipped stems and pond water carry a hidden kingdom home with him. Small life, watched too closely, turns hostile in Abernathy's tale.
35942-the-siege-of-the-seven-suitors:
Siege of the Seven Suitors is a comedy novel by Meredith Nicholson, published in 1910. Houghton Mifflin issued the book at Boston and New York in October of that year. Phillips and Birch illustrated the volume, and its frontispiece names a character called Hezekiah. Nicholson is billed as author of The House of a Thousand Candles on the title page.

 The letter of dedication plays on a state where tales brightened the hunter camp fire before the people learned ink. Marshall, it says, is himself the best of story tellers of that company. The siege of the title is a courtship: one young woman, seven suitors, and a house under comic assault by all of them. Nicholson writes in the light Indiana manner that made his romances the parlor favourites of the Middle West in those years.
35972-for-the-school-colours:
For the School Colours is a school story by Angela Brazil. Blackie of London published it, with pictures by Salmon. Brazil's many school tales are listed in front. The School in the South and Loyal to the School stand there. Avelyn enters in the first chapter. An invasion follows close behind. The frontispiece shows a girl gasping at a parcel.

What have they sent me, she cries in the caption. Brazil wrote of boarding schools for girls like her readers. Honour, games, and friendship rule her world. The school colours stand for loyalty to the house. Pranks and scrapes fill the terms between matches. Her books built the classic girls' school story. Generations read them under the bedclothes by torchlight.
36648-home-influence-a-tale-for-mothers-:
Home Influence, A Tale for Mothers and Daughters, is a novel by Grace Aguilar, issued in a new edition at New York in eighteen fifty six. Aguilar dedicates it to a dear friend, in a letter that opens the book. That letter calls the story a picture of a mother's solemn responsibilities. Her intense anxiety to fulfil them is its theme.

Simple as the narrative is, Aguilar writes, its sentiments go deep. The influence of home on a daughter's character is the lesson each scene serves. Aguilar, a Jewish writer beloved by Christian family readers, made domestic faith her ground. Mothers were urged to read it with their daughters, as the title directs.
36737-the-book-of-the-duke-of-true-lover:
The Book of the Duke of True Lovers is a medieval love story by Christine de Pisan. Alice Kemp-Welch translated it, for the first time, from the Middle French. Chatto and Windus published it in London in 1908. Laurence Binyon and Eric Maclagan turned its ballads into the original metres.

The volume belongs to a medieval library edited by Israel Gollancz. Only two manuscripts of the work were known to the translator. Both are early fifteenth-century French copies of the romance. One rests in the national library at Paris, the other in the British Museum. The Paris copy came from the famous collection of the Duke of Berry. Christine's own portrait, writing at her desk, ornaments the title page. The prose tale of a duke and his lady carries songs within its frame.
36837-the-lure-of-the-pen-a-book-for-wou:
Lure of the Pen is a book for would be authors by Flora Klickmann. Klickmann edited a girls' paper and women's magazine, her title page notes. The New York and London edition is dated nineteen twenty. Contents split into five parts. The first treats the manuscripts that fail, and why they fail.

A course in observation forms the second part. The help that books can give fills the third, with reading for data and for style. Points a writer ought to note fill the fourth, from practice before publication to local colour and atmosphere. Author, publisher, and public close the book in the fifth part. In the business of making literature, the text begins, the one thing in abundant supply is untrained mediocrity.
3690-floor-games-a-companion-volume-to-l:
Herbert George Wells writes a companion to his Little Wars, this time about games played on the floor with simple toys. The jolliest indoor games, Wells says, demand a floor covered with linoleum or cork carpet, where toy soldiers stand up and cities can rise. His list of toys runs to soldiers and civilians, bricks, boards and planks, clockwork railway stock and rails, tin ships, and Easter eggs.

Games include the Wonderful Islands, the building of cities, funiculars, marble towers, castles, and war games, though Wells allows very little of war itself. The book suits parents, teachers, and children who want inventive play from plain materials, and readers who enjoy Wells as a father writing about his sons' games.
37015-carolyn-of-the-corners:
Carolyn of the Corners is a children's novel by Ruth Belmore Endicott, printed at New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1918. It calls itself The Look Up Book. The pictures are by Edward Caswell. The book went through five printings before and just after publication. Thirty chapters tell the tale, from The Ray of Sunlight to The House of Bewilderment.

The first chapter opens at Joseph Stagg's hardware store in Sunrise Cove. She carries a satchel, and her name is Carolyn May. Chet Gormley tells the news and has ambitions of his own. The tale ends with the homing of Carolyn May. Endicott wrote a warm small town story of a child set down among strangers who become her own.
37019-the-girls-of-central-high-or-rival:
The Girls of Central High, or Rivals for All Honors is a tale for girls by Gertrude Morrison, out in nineteen fourteen. It is the first of a set of five books on the same school girls. The front list of that set names tales of a lake crew, of a ball game, of the stage, and of track and field. Drawn plates grace this book.

Parts run past school sports pro and con, false proof, a ghost house, and a boat race. Laura, the lead girl, works in her fathers gem shop on the last day of the week. Her father trusts her, not her brother, to dust the trays of rings. A plate shows her tip a full globe of fish onto a fire, a hint of the scrapes to come.
37089-the-locusts-years:
The Locusts' Years is a novel by Mary Helen Fee, the author of a work on the Philippines. It came out in Chicago in 1912 from A. C. McClurg and Company, with pictures by Charles Sarka. The book is given to the author's brother. The first chapter opens with a cold thought on men and the order of the world.

When a man can look on a victim of the social order with cool scorn and feel no stir, the tale says, he is one of two things. He has a coarse and cruel grain, or he is a man of high civil polish. Judge Alexander Barton, the figure in view, has no doubt which of the two he is. The woman who prompts the thought is not past thirty, and her worth and fine stamp are plain to any reader of faces.
37103-of-the-just-shaping-of-letters:
Of the Just Shaping of Letters, by Albrecht Dürer, appears here in English dress by Nichol. Nichol worked from the Latin text of the 1535 edition. The piece forms book three of Dürer's Applied Geometry. Dover issued this edition in New York. A letter to his patron Wilibald Pirckheimer opens the work. Dürer laments young painters who work with no training. Great artists laugh at their blind efforts, he says.

The root fault, for Dürer, is lack of geometry. No one can be a true artist without it, he argues. He sets down first steps with compass and rule for keen beginners. Letters are built on true measure, not on guess. The treatise shows a master joiner of art and maths at work.
37181-the-war-workers:
The War Workers is a novel of home front labour by Delafield, published in London in nineteen eighteen. Delafield warns that her Midland Supply Depot has no counterpart in real life. Its director, Miss Vivian, runs the depot from the town of Questerham. The tale opens at the hostel where her voluntary workers lodge together.

Half a dozen of her staff talk of nothing but shop and Miss Vivian. She is fearfully busy, hard to reach, and worn by late troop trains. Her secretary alone works in her room and guards her door from callers. The others lose whole mornings waiting to be sent for with their questions. Surgical supplies, telephones, and visiting officials crowd her working day to bursting. The talk shows both the strain and the spirit of the depot.
37208-the-wayfarers:
Mary Cutting wrote a novel of young folk and kin in a small town world. The book came out in New York in 1908. Drawings by Alice Stephens show key scenes from the tale. It opens on a ferry boat at the home rush hour.

The tale follows Theodosia, called Dosia, and those who love or vex her. Cousins, suitors, and friends cross her path in town and home. Small acts, looks, and talks build the bonds of the plot. Readers get a calm, close look at manners and hearts of that time.
373-lay-morals-and-other-papers:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers essays and papers in this posthumous volume, with a preface by his wife. The pieces range from youth, marriage, and books to travel and moral choice. Many were written in his roaming years, and the preface recalls island days when leprosy touched every port they knew.

Stevenson argues in a warm, personal voice, mixing jest with stern sense. He praises courage, plain speech, and the habit of facing life as it is. Readers who know his tales will find the same mind here, turned to thought rather than plot, and just as keen on style and truth.
37388-tobacco-leaves-being-a-book-of-fac:
W A Brennan of the John Crerar Library wrote a book of facts on tobacco for smokers. The Collegiate Press issued it in 1915, with first copies out that December. Brennan worked in medical studies, which shapes his plain, fact-based tone. A sketch of a Kentucky tobacco plant fronts the work.

Chapters trace the plant's past, growth, trade, and curing in full. More parts treat cigars, pipes, chewing leaf, and snuff with counts and grades. Nicotine and leaf makeup get close, clear study. Growers, sellers, and smokers of the time could learn how each form of leaf reached their hands.
37390-my-memoirs:
My Memoirs is the autobiography of Marguerite Steinheil, published in New York in 1912 with many illustrations, including letters and photographs. Steinheil was the Parisian hostess whose salon drew the powerful, and whose friendship with President Félix Faure ended in scandal when he died in her company in 1899. The memoir's centre is a darker affair: the 1908 murder of her husband and mother, for which she was tried.

The contents run from her childhood and marriage through the salon years, the Dreyfus affair and Fashoda, to the fatal night, the investigations, her arrest and 353 days in prison. Closing chapters give the trial itself, the speeches for prosecution and defence, and life after the verdict. The illustrations press her case in pictures: her cell at Saint-Lazare, the bed on which she was bound, and the desk from which money was stolen.
37463-the-builders:
The Builders is a tale by Ellen Glasgow, put out at New York in nineteen nineteen. Her past tales are list at the front of the print. The list of parts falls in two books. The first book bears the name of shows. The second bears the name of truths. That split is the key to the whole tale.

The first book names its folk in its heads. Caroline heads the run. The time, a great house, and Angelica come next. A first night, a maid named Letty, and the finds of Caroline fill the mid run. A man named Blackburn, the good works of Angelica, and a strange cult stand past them. The world's view of a sad match closes that book. The second book moves to a book room, to shifts of life, and to a choice.
37550-campaign-of-the-fourteenth-regimen:
Campaign of the Fourteenth Regiment, New Jersey Volunteers, by Sergeant J Newton Terrill of Company K, was printed at New Brunswick in 1884 in a second edition. Terrill fought with the regiment through the Civil War. His book gives a full history of its marches and battles.

The contents promise details of every event from the departure from New Jersey to the return home. Terrill took an active part in the Maryland campaign and the great fights of the Army of the Potomac. The Wilderness, Spottsylvania, Cold Harbor, and Petersburg stand in his list. The tale ends with the capture of Lee army and the fall of Richmond and Petersburg. The text opens with the dawn of war and men leaving plough and store for the flag. Veterans kin get a regimental record by a man who was there.
37573-pencil-sketches-or-outlines-of-cha:
Pencil Sketches, or Outlines of Character and Manners, is a story collection by Eliza Leslie. Hart of Philadelphia published this selection in 1852.

Leslie's advertisement says the original work had long been out of print. A new generation, she hopes, will find amusement and improvement in domestic pictures. Their mothers, she notes, recognised them as true. Other pieces include Uncle Philip, The Album, The Set of China, and Laura Lovel. A tale of a cent and a ladies' ball follow. The Officers recalls the last war with England, and Peter Jones is a sketch from life. The first story opens with a naval officer home from a Mediterranean cruise. Bromley Cheston spends a week with his married sister in New York.
3761-this-country-of-ours:
Henrietta Elizabeth Marshall tells the story of America as a chain of tales for young readers. The book moves from early settlements through the colonial years, with governors, founders, and ordinary folk taking turns at the center. One vivid scene shows Boston gone mad with joy as two ships bring orders to proclaim William and Mary, with bells, bonfires, and a great procession to the town hall.

Marshall writes in a plain storyteller's voice, favoring deeds and scenes over dates and debates. Sir Edmund Andros sent home a prisoner marks one turning point among many. The book suits families and young students who want a first narrative of the United States, told as history that reads like a storybook.
37613-search-light-letters:
Robert Grant wrote Search-Light Letters, published by Scribner's Sons in New York in 1899. The book gives advice in letter form to four kinds of reader. Each set of letters throws a search-light, as the title promises, on the conduct of life.

Four letters go to a young man or woman in search of the ideal. Four more address a modern woman with social ambitions. A young man wishing to be an American gets four, and a political optimist three. The first letter assumes its reader keeps other people's money apart from his own, never lies to escape blame, and fears no duty. Manners come in for sharp notice too, down to knives, elbows, and gossip. Grant writes with a judge's plainness about character in the Gilded Age.
37662-seed-thoughts-for-singers:
Frank Herbert Tubbs wrote Seed Thoughts for Singers, a small book put out in New York in 1897. Tubbs ran the New York Vocal Institute as its music chief. He says that busy minds grow dull and need a push from a book or a teacher. His short thoughts are meant to start fresh thought in the reader.

Tubbs holds that thought is the root of all acts, great and small. A planned act, he says, is stronger than one done by habit alone. He calls his notes seeds, since each one should grow more thoughts in good soil. The book is aimed at busy teachers and voice pupils. It asks for a short read, then thought, then work done with more care.
37812-gentlemen-rovers:
Gentlemen Rovers tells true tales of American adventurers abroad, written by Alexander Powell. Scribner published the book at New York in 1913, with pictures. Powell had written The Last Frontier. A poem by Kipling about a leaderless legion stands at the front as a kind of motto.

The nine tales open with an army for rent, riding on elephants in India. Americans fight Napoleon, capture an African kingdom, and defend a privateer in the old wars. One pirate turns patriot, and one filibuster makes himself a king. Cities are captured by contract in the final tale. Powell celebrates restless men who served causes not their own. The book is popular history told as adventure, with maps of empire in the background.
37981-may-flowers:
May Flowers is a book of stories by Louisa Alcott, author of Little Women and Little Men. Little, Brown published it at Boston with copyright in 1887. The title story opens with six Boston girls who form a club for mental improvement. As descendants of the Pilgrim Fathers, they call it the May Flower Club. They meet once a week to sew and read well-chosen books.

At the first meeting of the season, president Anna Winslow proposes a book about working women. It is very true and very sad, her mother said, but it might do them good. Ella Carver would rather not know about sad things she cannot mend. Anna answers that they might help if they really tried. The exchange sets Alcott's theme: comfortable girls learning to see poorer ones, in her gentlest didactic manner.
38028-the-world-masters:
World Masters is a novel of future war by George Griffith. John Long published it in London in the year 1903. Griffith also wrote The Angel of the Revolution and A Honeymoon in Space. A prologue called The Moment of Triumph opens the tale in Strassburg. Night lies on the street, broken by patrols and by sentry calls.

High above that street a man paces a vast attic with jerky strides. The room looks over the old Fisher's Gate of the famous city. The River Ill leaves Strassburg near that gate in the scene set. Fortifications ring the city in that tense, war shadowed opening. Griffith's readers got invasion dread and super weapons in his pages.
38191-the-boyhood-of-great-inventors:
A Fraser Robertson wrote The Boyhood of Great Inventors, published by John F Shaw and Company at London. The Eddystone Lighthouse fronts the book. Eight lives fill the contents. John Smeaton, who built that lighthouse, stands first. John Flaxman the sculptor and Sir Humphrey Davy follow. Sir Richard Arkwright and Josiah Wedgwood come next, the cotton spinner and the potter. George Stephenson carries the railway into the set.

Thomas Alva Edison and James Watt close the run, the newest and the oldest of the steam-and-light men. Robertson wrote the Early Years of Some Noble Lives on the same plan. His boyhoods were meant for the school prize shelf: a great man's start in life, told plainly. The publisher's list around the book is a library of such improving volumes, Ballantyne and Alger among them.
38248-pottery-for-artists-craftsmen-teac:
George J Cox wrote a pottery book for artists, craftsmen, and teachers. The Macmillan Company held the rights in 1914, from November of that year. Cox taught pottery and modeling at Teachers College of Columbia University. His own drawings show the tools, wheels, and ware throughout.

The potter should stand with the artist, not the chemist, Cox argues early. A little science, half grasped, hinders more than it helps, he warns. Clear steps and full pictures make up for costly gear in schools. Craft students gain a plain, loving guide to clay from wheel to kiln.
38263-wild-life-in-the-land-of-the-giant:
Wild Life in the Land of the Giants is an adventure tale of two brothers by Gordon Stables. Hodder and Stoughton published the book at London, in an edition dated 1888. The narrator tells the story in his own voice. The first book of the tale is named Our Home by the Sea.

The narrator opens with a joke about his own name. His full string of names is far too long for daily use, he says. It went to church only twice, at his baptism and his wedding. His brother's name is longer still, which the elder finds unfair. Both names were the gift of a maiden aunt, Serapheema. The tale promises wild life in a land of giants, told by one of the brothers. Sea side home scenes ground the start of the adventure.
386-virginibus-puerisque-and-other-paper:
Robert Louis Stevenson reflects on youth, love, and marriage in the title essay of this set, then turns to books, travel, and talk. He opens with Shakespeare's marrying men and asks why modern lovers fear vows that older folk took lightly. Later essays weigh idleness, talk, and the art of living well.

Stevenson writes with wit and a light, probing touch, never preaching at length. His sentences sparkle, yet his points bite: youth wastes time, love tests pride, and books shape conduct. The volume shows the essayist at his most personal, thinking aloud for readers who like a sharp mind at play.
38615-quantity-cookery-menu-planning-and:
Quantity Cookery, menu planning and cooking for large numbers, by Lenna Richards and Nola Treat of the University of Minnesota, was published in Boston in April 1922. Both authors taught institution management in the college of agriculture. Chapters cover menu rules for crowds, standards for judging meals, types of menus, and charts and lists to aid planning.

A long recipe part runs from page 73 to 191, followed by a table of weights and measures. Chapter one insists that well-balanced, apt menus are a must for any house that serves food. With the best goods and cooks, it says, a manager fails if menus lack care. The book serves schools, hospitals, and hotels that feed many at once.
38757-new-old-and-forgotten-remedies-pap:
New, Old and Forgotten Remedies is a gathering of medical papers by many writers, collected and edited by E P Anshutz. It was published at Philadelphia by Boericke and Tafel in 1900. The house was the great homeopathic publisher of America. Anshutz tells in his preface how the book was made. Gems had to be dug from dusty piles of old journals. Each find had to be weighed to earn its resurrection. Some papers, he owns, are of doubtful value, and a few may have no right in the book at all.

Each paper treats one remedy and its proofs in practice. The writers are doctors of the homeopathic school for the most part. Old provings and case tales are brought back to working use. The book serves the practitioner who holds that time has buried good tools. It is a storehouse of the school at its height.
38846-the-wreckers:
The Wreckers, a railroad novel by Francis Lynde, was published at New York by Scribner in 1920. A front plate by Arthur Becher goes with the book. Lynde dedicates the tale to a grave official of the Union Pacific system. That man, he says, might well have played the part of Jimmie Dodds in his younger days.

At Sand Creek Siding is the title of the first chapter shown. A voice in the front scene speaks of difficulties and responsibilities. There is another side to it, the speaker insists to a man named Graham. Lynde wrote western railroad tales of graft, wrecks, and honest men. The wreckers of his title work the finance and the track alike. His heroes fight with timetables, courts, and dynamite.
38889-literary-shrines-the-haunts-of-som:
Literary Shrines is a travel book by Theodore F. Wolfe on the homes of famed American authors. Lippincott published the work at Philadelphia in 1895, and this text is from the fifth edition. Wolfe dedicates the volume to his wife, his companion on trips to literary shrines in both worlds. A companion volume treats the haunts of British authors.

The contents begin with a pilgrimage to Concord, called a village of literary shrines. Chapters visit the homes of Thoreau, the Alcotts, and Emerson's circle. The Old Manse receives a full chapter, with its famed study and its guests. Wolfe writes in a warm, recalling style rather than a guidebook's dry manner. Pictures in photogravure show the Wayside at Concord and other houses. The book served readers who wished to walk the ground their authors had walked.
38929-quacks-and-grafters:
Quacks and Grafters is an expose of quack cures by a man who quit the trade. The author hides his name as a late bone healer in the by line. Its full title adds the aim to show why such frauds bloom in the age. The book came out at Cincinnati in the year nineteen hundred and eight.

The gift page sends the book to the great American crowd with warm trust. The front talk says the age swarms with cure schools as in one past age. New finds in blood and germ lore then left room for frauds to thrive. Cures, cash, and press puffs form the web the book tears at. Plain cures and firm laws are pled as the way out of the mess.
39014-outline-studies-in-the-old-testame:
Outline Studies in the Old Testament for Bible Teachers is a teacher-training manual by Jesse Hurlbut. Eaton and Mains published it in New York in 1905. Its preface tells how the book was made. The New York State Sunday School Association asked for a two-year course in the Bible, one year on the Old Testament and one on the New.

The plan takes the historical point of view. It presents the lands of the Bible and the Israelite people with their institutions of worship. Hurlbut built the outlines from his earlier normal lessons and studies. The book trained Sunday school teachers to teach the Old Testament in order, with geography beside the text.
39145-the-devourers:
The Devourers is a novel by A Vivanti Chartres, published in New York and London in nineteen ten. The author dedicates it to her wonderchild Vivien, to read when she has wonderchildren of her own. Book one opens with a baby that speaks its first want in stark words. I am hungry, the baby says, in a silent, shadowy room.

Hurrying footsteps, light arms, and a laughing soothing voice answer that cry. A cheek is laid against comfort in the next breath. Motherhood as a devouring force, of hunger, love, and self given away, is the theme that bold opening states. Vivanti writes mothers and daughters with a poet's heat.
3953-cinq-mars:
This edition collects all of Alfred de Vigny's Cinq Mars, with prefaces by Charles de Mazade and Gaston Boissier. The life of Vigny traces a reputation of extraordinary ups and downs. First lauded as precursor of French romantic poetry, then sunk in semi oblivion, he was recovered in the last years as a main illuminating force of the nineteenth century. He stands, the preface says, between Musset and Chenier, lyric and philosophic at once.

A tense passage shows the plot's heart, as the Cardinal's guards question Cinq Mars and allow him to advance only with De Thou. The Cardinal Duke says sharply that he has come too late to speak with the king. Then Louis the Thirteenth himself speaks, torn between irritation at his minister and knowledge that he owes him the day's success. Readers who want Cinq Mars whole will find conspiracy, friendship, and a king's divided mind.
39547-beaumaroy-home-from-the-wars:
Beaumaroy Home from the Wars, a novel by Anthony Hope, was first published in London in 1919. Eighteen chapters open with Doctor Mary's paying guest. Mary Arkroyd tells how her wedding plans broke two days before the rite. Her half-brother Gilly had been killed just three months before.

Her groom, Captain Cranster, is caught in a scandal that all had kept quiet. Settlements were signed and rooms at Bournemouth stood ready when the truth came out. Later chapters name a Captain Duggle, a stranger, and a car behind trees. A tower secret, gold, and a grave add weight. Hope blends drawing-room talk with mystery in the wake of war.
39641-georgina-s-service-stars:
Georgina Service Stars, by Annie Fellows Johnston, was printed in New York by the Britton Publishing Company under a 1918 copyright. Thelma Gooch drew the plates. Johnston wrote Georgina of the Rainbows and Two Little Knights of Kentucky. A Tennyson line heads the book, for the deed sake have I done the deed.

Johnston gives the book to those behind the service flags, whose part in the world struggle can never be chronicled. Their sacrifices are unnumbered, and their wounds are within. She praises the silent heroism which shoulders the double load and faces the loneliness undaunted. A plate line says that if anyone comes along, the heroine begins knitting. The tale opens to the sound of the town crier bell up a crooked harbor street. Girls of 1918 got a home front war story.
39810-a-prince-of-dreamers:
Flora Annie Steel wrote a historical novel printed in New York in 1909. Steel was known for On the Face of the Waters and A Sovereign Remedy. Verses from Abul Faiz, poet at the court of Akbar, and from Hafiz stand at the front. The book is given to the memory of a prince of dreamers and a king of kings.

The tale opens on a man in his forties with a fine face lined by thought. Dress, court, and custom in old India frame the story. Steel asks what a reader truly knows of a man from his outer show. Dreams, rule, faith, and the pull of the unseen shape the prince at the heart of the book.
39869-farming-with-dynamite-a-few-hints-:
Farming with Dynamite is a short booklet from the E I Du Pont de Nemours Powder Company of Wilmington, Delaware, with a copyright of nineteen ten. The firm was founded in eighteen oh two. The cover claims that dynamite saves money, time, and labour. It also claims that blasting removes stumps, boulders, and hard pan. New rich soil, more acres, easy ploughing, and bigger yields are promised.

The text first asks what dynamite is and meets a common fear. Many farmers, it says, think dynamite is too risky to handle. The firm holds that its Red Cross Dynamite is in fact safer than gunpowder with plain care. A free Handbook of Explosives for Farmers, Planters and Ranchers is offered to keen readers. The booklet is a sharp case of sales craft aimed at progressive farmers of the age.
399-cast-upon-the-breakers:
Horatio Alger Jr. tells of Rodney Ropes, a schoolboy left to a faithless guardian, in this rags-to-respect tale. Rodney learns his guardian has drained his funds, and he must leave school to earn his keep. Work, friendship, and pluck carry him through hard towns and harder masters.

Alger follows the familiar moral arc: honest toil beats sly schemes, and a true friend proves worth more than cash. David, a poor day scholar, opens the book as Rodney's first ally. The novel charms as a plain, hopeful tale for young readers, where grit and good conduct win out.
40023-monograms-ciphers:
Turbayne designed Monograms and Ciphers with his Carlton studio men. Jack at London and Edinburgh put out the plate book. Years of work designing letter devices fill it. Monograms, ciphers, and trade-marks are its trades in the introduction. Useful material on a workable scale is promised.

The plates form their own index by their arrangement, it says. Plate two holds combinations in A, and plate three follows. A device is looked for under its first letter in order. Two letters can be read in two ways within one device. Three different letters can be placed to read six ways, it counts. A full series runs to hundreds of devices. The letters O and Q can be made interchangeable in working. Most devices give but a single reading by that rule, it adds. Turbayne gives the engraver a dictionary of entwined letters.
40161-a-book-about-doctors:
A Book About Doctors is a gathering of medical anecdotes by John Cordy Jeaffreson, printed at New York in 1904. It stands as volume four of the Doctor's Recreation Series. Jeaffreson also wrote A Book About Lawyers and lives of Byron and Shelley. A front picture shows Professor Billroth's surgical clinic.

Twenty chapters run from sticks and wigs to quacks and fees. Early English physicians take their turn, among them Sir Thomas Browne and Sir Hans Sloane. Chapters treat bleeding, imagination as a remedy, and Mesmer. Jeaffreson says he picked the best medical tales from tradition and books, and set them out in a readable and attractive form.
40371-britain-in-the-middle-ages-a-histo:
Florence L Bowman, an Oxford modern history graduate, wrote a history of Britain in the middle ages for beginners. She lectured at Homerton College, Cambridge. The book was first issued in 1919, with a second edition in 1920. A picture shows the arming of a knight. Contents open before the coming of the Romans. The Romans and the Saxons follow in short chapters. The preface is dated from Homerton College in December 1918.

Cambridge University Press published the textbook across the empire. Bowman's beginners are school pupils meeting castles, barons, and parliaments. Short chapters and clear narrative suit the classroom. The book belongs to the post war rebuilding of school history. Putnam handled it in New York.
404-industrial-biography-iron-workers-an:
Samuel Smiles continues his Lives of the Engineers with this 1863 study of iron workers and tool makers. He traces iron from early smelters and smiths to the furnace masters who built modern British industry. Chapters follow the Forest of Dean, Sussex cannon works, and the shift from wood charcoal to pit coal.

Smiles profiles inventors and mechanics whose toil, thrift, and skill shaped trade and war. Dud Dudley, early coal smelters, and later engineers each get a clear, fact-filled life. The book praises useful work without show, and it still reads as a solid record of how iron made an age.
40412-through-the-year-with-famous-autho:
Through the Year with Famous Authors, by Mabel Patterson, was published in New York in 1925. Patterson sorts short quotes by the day of the year. Each quote comes with a brief life note on its author. January opens with Maria Edgeworth, born on the first of that month. Richard Henry Horne and Arthur Hugh Clough share that same birth day.

Readers move through the months meeting poets, novelists, and thinkers in date order. Notes give birth and death dates, chief works, and a few facts. The plan suits daily reading in small doses. It also serves as a handy first guide to many writers. Patterson aims to pair a thought for the day with a face and a life behind it.
40500-leatherface-a-tale-of-old-flanders:
Leatherface, a tale of old Flanders by Baroness Orczy, was copyrighted in 1916 and published in New York by George H Doran Company. Orczy also wrote The Scarlet Pimpernel. The tale is set in the Low Countries under Spanish rule. A prologue opens at Mons in September 1572.

In the prologue, Alva's camp lies south of the besieged city while the Prince of Orange waits to the north with a handful of unpaid, mutinous men. Three books carry the story through Brussels, Dendermonde, and Ghent. Chapter heads name the Blood Council, the subject race, and the ruling caste. Vengeance, reprisals, and a last stand drive the plot toward an hour of victory.
40513-danes-saxons-and-normans-or-storie:
Danes, Saxons, and Normans, or Stories of Our Ancestors, is a history by Edgar. Beeton of London brought the book out in the year 1863. Edgar had writ Boyhood of Great Men and Cavaliers and Roundheads before. His preface says he tells the Norman Conquest in popular form. Chief personages of that age stand forth in his picturesque account.

He opens with the Normans under Rolf forcing a settlement in France. That went on while Alfred the Great fought the Danes in England. Links between Rouen and Westminster grew from there on. William the Norman's invasion of England follows from those first ties. Hastings was no curtain-drop but the first scene of a new act. Quarrels in the Conqueror's own house fill the later story here. Son fought father and brother brother in that fierce succession war. Henry Plantagenet's peaceful crowning closes the long drama of houses.
40525-kathie-s-soldiers:
Kathie's Soldiers is a story by Amanda Douglas, printed at Boston, with copyright in 1899 and a first entry in 1871. Douglas wrote the Helen Grant books and the Little Red House books, and Kathie's Soldiers stands among her six Kathie stories. A picture at the front shows a girl wishing she could go out with the gifts.

The first chapter is called Enlisting in the Grand Army, and the tale belongs to the years when soldiers filled a girl's world. Kathie's kindness runs to gifts carried out to the men, and the home front work of women and children stands at its heart. Douglas writes warm, moral tales of family life, and this one ties a girl's duties to a nation's call.
40534-talks-about-flowers:
Talks About Flowers, by Wellcome of Yarmouth, Maine, was published for the author in 1881. The preface, dated June 9, 1881, says the flower sketches first appeared in the Boston Journal and the Portland Transcript. Nearly every page was rewritten as the sheets passed through the press. The talks mix the history and literature of flowers with description and the mode of culture. A talk to farmers' wives and a talk about the wild garden open the sequence.

Named talks follow for phlox, verbenas, petunias, pansies, asters, balsams, geraniums, and begonias. Gladiolus, pelargoniums, fuchsias, coleuses, primroses, carnations, and climbers each get their chapter. Roses are left out on purpose: the queen of flowers had a whole separate Essay on Roses from the same pen. The book aims at amateurs and is priced to reach the masses, as the preface puts it.
40677-lives-of-illustrious-shoemakers:
Lives of Illustrious Shoemakers collects the biographies of eminent men who rose from the cobbler's bench. Winks wrote the volume. Funk and Wagnalls published it in New York. A long preface argues the craft's romance. Shoemaking alone bears the honourable title of the Gentle Craft.

The preface traces the sentiment to old saints' tales. Crispin and Crispianus stand among the patron saints. Shoemakers were famous for intelligence and argument, Winks writes. Their prominence in politics and religion drew remark everywhere. A change in the trade gives the book its urgency. Machinery has revolutionised boot and shoe making. The old cobbler in his leather apron is vanishing. Lynn and Northampton lose their conspicuous figure to the factory.
40719-dodo-wonders:
Dodo Wonders is a novel by E F Benson, author of Queen Lucia and David Blaize. The New York edition was copyrighted in nineteen twenty one, after magazine publication. A list of the author's books stands at the front. Contents run to twelve chapters. Dodo on old age opens the list, then highness and cross currents. A Waterloo ball and Dodo's apprenticeship take the middle heads.

Chapter one finds Dodo deep in her own talk. Having just lit one cigarette, she lights another at it, the tale says. She contemplates the two with a dazed expression. Her friend Edith has just returned from a musical tour in Germany. There she conducted a dozen concerts of her own music with flaring success, the chapter adds.
40923-british-political-leaders:
Justin McCarthy sketched these British political leaders with their portraits. Fisher Unwin printed the book in London in 1903. A photo of Arthur Balfour fronts the volume as first subject. Contents run Balfour, Salisbury, Rosebery, and Chamberlain in first places.

Labouchere, Morley, Aberdeen, and Burns follow among the thirteen lives. Hicks-Beach, Redmond, Harcourt, Bryce, and Campbell-Bannerman close the list here. McCarthy first knew Balfour in his earliest Commons days, he writes. The Fourth party had just formed under Randolph Churchill then. McCarthy past books on modern England stand listed by his name in the front pages.
40972-mythical-monsters:
Mythical Monsters is a study of legendary beasts by Charles Gould, printed in London in 1886. Gould was a member of the Royal Society of Tasmania and had served as a geological surveyor there. His book holds ninety-three illustrations. The frontispiece shows the Fung Wang from a Chinese source.

Gould's preface spends care on method. For the sake of one system, he has reduced the romanised spellings of Chinese sounds to the plan in Williams's dictionary. That clue shows the range of his hunt: dragons and great birds of the East stand beside the monsters of the West. A man of science by trade, he gathers the reports, sorts the names, and asks what kernel of fact might sit inside the tales. The book is a Victorian field guide to the creatures of myth.
41029-the-moon-destroyers:
Monroe Ruch wrote this tale of the moon, quakes, and space travel to come. The tale ran in Wonder Stories Quarterly in winter 1932. A front note calls the moon part of earth own system. Its pull makes tides and may slow earth spin, it says.

Professor Erickson heads a world quake institute high in the Himalayas. He watches a needle trace its path on a slow drum with pale face. Storms roar round the lab, but a darker cause moves the stylus. The tale builds toward a dive past wrecked ships at a cliff base.
41036-brave-deeds-of-union-soldiers:
Brave Deeds of Union Soldiers is a book of Civil War stories by Samuel Scoville, published in Philadelphia in 1915 and dedicated to Theodore Roosevelt. Scoville praises Roosevelt as one who believes in peace with honour, never in peace at the price of righteousness. A frontispiece shows Sergeant Hunter charging the Confederates.

Sixteen chapters tell the deeds. The escape from Libby Prison comes early, then two against a city and a set of boy heroes. The charge of Zagonyi, the locomotive chase, and Sheridan's ride follow. The bloody angle and the heroes of Gettysburg stand at the centre. A lone scout, forgotten heroes, and the three hundred who saved an army fill the later pages. The boy-general and the medal-of-honour men close the book. Published fifty years after the war, it kept the Union's hero tales before a new generation of boys.
41274-a-new-catalogue-of-vulgar-errors:
Stephen Fovargue, a fellow of St John College, Cambridge, wrote A New Catalogue of Vulgar Errors, printed at Cambridge for the author in seventeen sixty seven. The price was half a crown. A Locke quote heads the book, on men who yield not to reason laid clear as daylight. A Horace line stands beside it. Sellers in London and Oxford stocked it.

To show the use of education, no method beats showing what dull mistakes men fall into for want of it, Fovargue says. The errors of men with no knowledge in the sciences are so numerous that a full list would need a complete system of natural philosophy, he grants. Such a work is needless in this era of the sciences, he adds. His sheets treat only a choice set of common errors. Curious readers get an early debunking book, brisk and learned.
41303-a-ladder-of-swords-a-tale-of-love-:
A Ladder of Swords is a tale of love, laughter and tears by Gilbert Parker, printed at New York and London by Harper and Brothers in 1904. The pictures are by the Kinneys. Its title comes from a woman's letter quoted at the front. But I have been climbing a ladder of swords these many years. The book is inscribed to the Countess of Darnley, the friend of Michel and Angèle.

The tale opens in the register of the Walloon church at Southampton. A second record tells of a wedding that August. Angèle Claude Aubert, daughter of a councillor of the Parliament of Rouen, was married to Michel de la Forêt, of a noble Flemish family. Parker builds his romance on those records: a tale of refugees and lovers in the spacious times of Elizabeth.
41400-miss-eden-s-letters:
Violet Dickinson, great-niece of the writer, edited these letters of Emily Eden, published by Macmillan at London in 1919 with portraits of Eden's circle. The introduction sketches Eden's great friends, among them Lady Theresa Lewis and Pamela, daughter of Lord Edward FitzGerald, the leader of the Irish rebellion of 1798 who died in Newgate Prison.

Pamela's correspondence with Eden ran thirty years. It tells of her marriage to Sir Guy Campbell in 1820, her eleven children, and her struggle to educate them on a dwindling income. Eden's own letters, the body of the book, began in 1814 and were written chiefly to her elder sister Eleanor at Eastcombe, near Greenwich. Fourteen chapters carry the letters from 1814 to 1863, and both friends died in 1869, Pamela aged seventy-three and Emily seventy-two.
41430-english-lakes-water-colours:
English Lakes Water Colours is a picture book of lake views by Heaton Cooper. The artist painted the lakes of the north west of England for this set. It stands in a run of town and shire books in the same soft mode. The book first came out in the fall of nineteen nineteen.

A dusk view of Grasmere lake heads the set of fine soft plates. Church, dove cot, stone steps, and broad lakes fill the list in turn. A famed house on Coniston lake earns its own plate in the set. Short text walks with each view to name its hills and tales. The book served as a gift of the lakes for those who roamed them.
41458-the-gay-triangle-the-romance-of-th:
William Le Queux opened a tale of air adventure on the Norfolk fens at night. A strange shape slides from a lonely shed beside the road. It is a car of odd design, wide and high, of shining metal, on frail bicycle wheels. No engine roar comes from it, though the air reeks of petrol.

The car halts where the road runs on a bank above flood level. Two figures in leather helmets climb out, a young man and a girl. In minutes the car has changed its shape. Long rods shoot from its sides, cloth unrolls between them, and the wings of a small monoplane stand out. A propeller folds out from a hidden door in front. The machine lifts without a sound into the mist. Rasputin's jewels give the first chapter its name.
41515-wheat-and-huckleberries-or-dr-nort:
Wheat and Huckleberries, or Dr Northmore's Daughters is a novel by Charlotte Vaile, published at Boston in 1899 with illustrations by Alice Barber Stevens. Vaile dedicates the story, in dear remembrance of an early home, to a friend. The chapters move between the farm, the old place, Aunt Katharine Saxon, huckleberrying and a prayer meeting.

The book opens at harvest. How the doctor came to own his farm was never clear to his neighbours. The mortgage ate his modest income, yet he prized the place above all he owned and dreamed of ending his days cultivating it. His daughters' interest is more practical: July, the threshing machine abroad, and the social season of a country doctor's family.
41602-outline-studies-in-the-new-testame:
Outline Studies in the New Testament is a teach guide by Jesse Hurlbut, out in nineteen six. New York and Cincinnati houses of church print share the book form. Its scheme splits the course in eighteen drills for class use. Land and folk of Palestine open the drills in the first ranks. The life of Christ fills drills three through ten of the set.

Years of prep, shade, fame, and strife split that life course in scheme. Cross day and the forty days past it close the Christ drills. Church growth in Judea and past it fills the late drill ranks. Paul prep and church spread to far folk close the set. Front words call the Bible the book that pays deep search most.
41825-the-road-builders:
Samuel Merwin wrote The Road-Builders, a novel of railway work first published in nineteen hundred and five. Part of the tale had run in The Saturday Evening Post as A Link in the Girdle. Pictures by F B Masters fill the book.

Young Van takes a job on a line being pushed through hard country. Chapters follow the money behind the road, life at Mr Carhart's camp, and a find at a water-hole. Shots are fired, a scouting party rides out, and a show-down comes. The goal is Red Hills, where a large station with a steel and glass shed is planned. Grit and teamwork drive the tale.
42090-flagg-s-the-far-west-1836-1837-par:
Thwaites edited this twenty seventh volume of the Early Western Travels series. Clark printed it at Cleveland in 1906 with notes, index. Part two of Flagg Far West, 1836 to 1837, opens it. De Smet letters and sketches, 1841 to 1842, close the volume.

Flagg tour beyond the mountains outlines western life and scenery there. Prairies, rivers, ancient mounds, and early French settlements fill his chapters. De Smet spent a year among Rocky Mountain Indian tribes then. Twelve letters of 1841 and a residence account of 1842 follow. An Indian symbolical catechism explanation closes the volume after the residence narrative ends there.
4218-sisters:
Ada Cambridge's novel Sisters follows a man who dreads a letter from his baby's caretaker, a lady of whom he stands in undignified dread. Mentioning the matter next day, he finds after breakfast a letter forwarded from Five Creeks, her handwriting paling his brown face.

His stout heart flutters at the sight, and he keeps the letter unopened for some time, afraid to know what he already guesses it contains. Cambridge writes Australian domestic life with warmth and humor. Readers who enjoy family novels of the colonies will find a charming, human story.
42441-the-coming-of-cassidy-and-the-othe:
The Coming of Cassidy — and the Others is a set of western stories by Clarence Mulford, author of Hopalong Cassidy and Bar-20 Days. McClurg of Chicago published it in 1913, with illustrations by Maynard Dixon, from magazine copyrights reaching back to 1908. The contents open with The Coming of Cassidy itself, then The Weasel and two Jimmy Price stories.

The Luck of Fools, Hopalong's Hop, Dealing the Odd, The Norther, The Drive, and The Hold-Up follow. Four Sammy stories close the book: Sammy Finds a Friend, Sammy Knows the Game, His Code, and Sammy Hunts a Job, then When Johnny Sloped. The frontispiece shows a rope suddenly yanking a man from the saddle. The first story opens with a trail boss shaking his fist after a departing puncher. A passage preserved in the copy gives the Bar-20 talk.
42518-talks-to-farmers:
Talks to Farmers, by the Reverend Charles H Spurgeon, was printed in New York by Funk and Wagnalls in 1889. Spurgeon was the famed London preacher. His talks take farm life as the text for short sermons to plain folk.

The list opens with The Sluggard Farm, from the Bible verse on the field of the slothful grown over with thorns. The broken fence, frost and thaw, and the corn of wheat dying to bear fruit follow. Later talks treat the ploughman, ploughing the rock, and the parable of the sower. Spring in the heart, farm laborers, and the sheep before the shearers fill the mid list. The joy of harvest, threshing, and wheat in the barn close the set. Church readers get Spurgeon warm voice in field dress.
42639-the-expositor-s-bible-the-book-of-:
The Expositor's Bible treats the Book of Numbers, in a series edited by Robertson Nicoll. The set was sold in a new and cheaper edition at fifty cents a volume. Its list of Old Testament volumes spans Genesis to the prophets. Dods wrote Genesis, Chadwick Exodus, and Kellogg Leviticus for the line. Watson wrote the Numbers volume, and Deuteronomy fell to Harper.

Blaikie took Joshua and both books of Samuel for the series. Farrar, Dean of Canterbury, wrote both books of Kings in the list. Maclaren's Psalms fill three volumes, and Isaiah takes two more. Watson also wrote Job and Judges with Ruth for the house. The Numbers volume reads the fourth book of Moses verse by verse in that company. It gives the census, the wanderings, and the laws in plain exposition for pulpit and home.
42691-the-joys-of-being-a-woman-and-othe:
The Joys of Being a Woman and Other Papers is a book of essays by Winifred Kirkland. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston and New York in 1918. A foreword treats the ego in the essay as its theme. The title essay opens the contents at page one. A Man in the House and Old-Clothes Sensations follow it. Luggage and the Lady and Detached Thoughts on Boarding come next. The Lady Alone at Night and In Sickness and In Health add domestic pieces.

Later essays treat an educational fantasy and the author's own clothes. The Tendency to Testify and Letters and Letter-Writers follow. The Tyranny of Talent and The Woman Who Writes turn literary. Picnic Pictures and The Farm Feminine take the essays outdoors. A Little Girl and Her Grandmother gives a family piece. Kirkland writes the familiar essay in a light, personal voice.
4274-wives-and-daughters:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Wives and Daughters carries the subtitle An Every-Day Story. It ran in the Cornhill Magazine from August 1864 to January 1866. It appeared in book form in 1866. Gaskell died suddenly in November 1865, having finished all but the last chapter.

The novel is in one sense unfinished, with the editor's notes on her intentions included at the end. The story centers on Molly Gibson, a doctor's daughter, and the families around her. They include the Hamleys, a new stepmother and stepsister, and suitors who complicate her life. Illustrated by George du Maurier, it is often called Gaskell's masterpiece.
42811-japanese-colour-prints-and-their-d:
Japanese Colour Prints and Their Designers is a lecture by Frederick William Gookin. Gookin spoke before the Japan Society of New York in April nineteen eleven. The Society issued the lecture in print in nineteen thirteen. A loan collection catalogue of prints is bound with the lecture text.

A Harunobu plate, Lovers Walking in Snow, fronts the pictured volume. Moronobu, Kiyomasu, Masanobu, and Toyonobu plates show the early masters first. Kiyonaga holiday groups, Sharaku actors, and an Utamaro woman follow in turn. Toyokuni bath house women, a Hokusai Fuji, and a Hiroshige pine view close it. Gookin calls the Ukiyo prints a plebeian art of unique standing.
42840-sisters:
Sisters is a girls' novel by Grace May North, published by the Saalfield Publishing Company of Akron and New York in 1928. A frontispiece shows a girl asked to stand before a long mirror. The contents promise a long, busy story in many short chapters.

Jenny is introduced early, and forlorn Etta follows close behind. A pitiful plight, friends in need, and a wanted waitress position drive the opening movement. Jenny's teacher, an adventure filled day, and an old friend's appearance widen the cast. Plots and plays, ferns and friends, and pride meeting pride fill the middle chapters. A rustic cabin and fun as farmers promise a country turn. Saalfield sold such wholesome series fiction to American girls by the shelf. North's novel mixes work, friendship, and family feeling in the approved manner of its house.
42889-the-influence-of-the-stars:
A handbook of old world lore by Rosa Baughan. Baughan also wrote on palmistry and handwriting. This fourth edition, revised and enlarged, appeared at London in 1904. Three parts divide the work. Part one treats astrology. Part two covers chiromancy, the reading of hands. Part three explains physiognomy. Added chapters read the moles of the body. Another chapter teaches the mystical wheel of Pythagoras. A facsimile woodcut of 1657 forms the frontispiece.

The astrology part teaches the art step by step. Readers learn the zodiac signs first. The natures and dignities of the seven planets follow. Twelve houses, fixed stars, and nativities complete the course. Aphorisms from Ptolemy close the section. Ten plates illustrate a system once used in earnest.
42979-pomo-bear-doctors:
Barrett wrote a study of bear doctors among the Pomo people of California. The paper came out from the University of California in 1917. It runs from page 443 to page 465 with one plate. It sits in a set on the lore and old life of native groups. Barrett worked in the field of man's past and folk ways.

Bear doctors were men held to take bear form and use bear power. Barrett sets out what the Pomo said of them and how they acted. He notes their role in fear, cure, and strife in the group. Readers get a close record of a belief now long past.
42989-the-plattner-story-and-others:
The Plattner Story and Others is a book of short stories by Wells. Methuen published it in London in 1897. Wells dedicated the book to his father. The contents list seventeen stories in all. The title story opens the volume. The Argonauts of the Air and The Late Mister Elvesham follow. In the Abyss, The Apple, and Under the Knife come next. The Red Room and The Cone are also in the list.

The opening story weighs a pretty question of evidence. Seven witnesses vouch for the tale of Gottfried Plattner. One undeniable fact stands on their side of the scale. That fact is the inversion of Plattner's anatomical structure. Against it stand prejudice, common sense, and the weight of opinion. The narrator calls it the most preposterous story ever told. The volume gathers Wells's early tales of science and strangeness.
432-the-ambassadors:
Henry James follows Lambert Strether, a middle-aged man from Woollett, Massachusetts, to Paris in this major novel. Sent to fetch home a young man lost to Paris charms, Strether instead falls under the city's spell. He urges his charge to live fully, then learns how much that advice costs.

James writes in long, probing sentences that track Strether's shifting mind. Paris salons, gardens, and river towns form the bright ground of his slow awakening. The novel stands as James's great study of American innocence abroad, and of a man who finds his life only as it slips past.
4325-the-new-book-of-martyrs:
Georges Duhamel, a French surgeon and writer, wrote this book of the First World War from the hospitals and wounded towns of France. Translated by Florence Simmonds, its chapters include Throughout Our Land, the story of Carre and Leronudeau, memories of the martyrs, the death of Mercier, Verdun, and nights in Artois.

Duhamel opens with the cry of wounded men echoing from disfigured regions to the mountains, the ocean, and the inland sea. Every French town, he writes, bears wounds and has taken up the duty of easing suffering. The book is a witness to war's human cost, told by a doctor who saw it daily.
43522-the-kaiser-s-memoirs:
The Kaiser's Memoirs, by Wilhelm the Second, the former emperor of Germany, gives his own account of his reign from 1888 to 1918. Thomas R Ybarra made the English version, published by Harper in New York and London in 1922.

The chapters take the chancellors in turn: Bismarck, Caprivi, Hohenlohe, Bülow, and Bethmann. Wilhelm opens by protesting that he revered and idolized Bismarck, the creator of the German Empire and the champion of his grandfather. Later chapters treat his helpers in the government, science and art, the church, and the army and navy. The outbreak of war, the Pope and peace, and the end of the war with his abdication follow. Two closing chapters argue the question of guilt and look at the revolution and Germany's future. A portrait of Wilhelm fronts the book.
43534-what-s-your-hurry-a-deck-full-of-j:
What Your Hurry is a joke book, A Deck Full of Jokers, by George Niblo. Street and Smith of New York issued it in the Humor Library in nineteen o four. The price was twenty five cents for Humor Library number five here. Niblo also wrote BGosh, Atchoo, and Step Lively in the same line.

Sit down, stop right where you are, the game is not over, it opens. The teller has a few aces up his sleeve yet, he boasts to readers. A newly converted man wants to imitate Elijah in a chariot of fire. His parson reckons he just wants to get acclimated before the journey end. Circumstantial evidence from a flock of low roosting fowls proves the point.
43544-the-philosophy-of-life-and-philoso:
The Philosophy of Life and Philosophy of Language is a set of talks by Frederick von Schlegel. Morrison made the English form of the work from the tongue of its birth. It was put out at New York in eighteen forty eight. The talks fall in two great heaps. The first heap bears the name of life. The next bears the name of tongue.

The first talks treat the soul in its kinds. The think soul as the core of man's grasp heads the run. The love soul as the core of the good life, and wed life with it, comes next. The share of the soul in lore, and the word of God made known, stand past them. The soul past the wild world, and the soul past God, fill the mid run.
43552-wanderings-in-patagonia-or-life-am:
A young English traveller wrote this account of life at the far south of America in the 1870s. Wanderings in Patagonia tells of ostrich hunters on the great dry plains. The ostrich of that land is the rhea, a swift, flightless bird hunted on horseback.

The book stands in the Wanderer's Library style of its day: cheap, bright tales of wild places. Patagonia then lay at the edge of the known map for most readers. Its hunters rode with bolas and dogs after rheas, guanacos, and pumas. Camp life, native folk, and the hardships of the pampas fill such a tale. Few parts of the earth have changed so little in print since, or drawn so many seekers of the wild.
43582-the-mystery-at-dark-cedars:
The Mystery at Dark Cedars is a tale of search for girls by Edith Lavell. It was put out in nineteen thirty five. It stands in a set named for its young sleuth. Two more tales of that set are named at the front. The book is sworn to the daughter of the hand, who loves tales of this kind.

The folk of the tale are list at the front. Mary Louise Gay is the girl sleuth of the set. Jane Patterson is her close friend. A lone maid keeps the house of the name. Maids and men of that house fill the rest of the roll. The parts run from the house of doubt to the theft. Doubt folk, a talk with a maid, and the stole wealth come next.
43604-wood-working-for-beginners-a-manua:
Charles Wheeler wrote this manual of wood-working for those new to the craft. Putnam printed it at New York and London in 1900, with more than seven hundred plates. A line from Carlyle heads the book: know what thou canst work at, and work at it like a Hercules.

A workshop for amateurs opens the set: tools, wood, and working drawings. Then come things to make: toys, houses for beasts, gear for sports, and furniture. House-building for beginners takes the third part, with simple summer cottages. Boat-building closes the book, with a few simple boats. Wheeler gave the work to the young founders of Totlet Town, whose play first stirred him to write it.
43634-by-ways-of-war-the-story-of-the-fi:
By-Ways of War: The Story of the Filibusters is a history by James Jeffrey Roche, printed at Boston by Small, Maynard and Company in 1901. The copyright dates are 1891 and 1901. A picture of William Walker fronts the book, and maps show Nicaragua and Central America at the time of the filibusters. A line from Joaquin Miller stands at its head, on the leaded dice of war.

The first chapter traces the word filibuster from the Norse adventurers and the buccaneers to Miranda and his expeditions against Spain. The third tells the Lopez expedition to Cuba and the execution of Lopez and Crittenden. The fourth follows the Count Raousset-Boulbon to Sonora and Guaymas, and to his death. The fifth chapter opens the tale of William Walker: boyhood and education, doctor, lawyer and journalist, then California and the Sonora expedition.
4368-flappers-and-philosophers:
F. Scott Fitzgerald collected these eight stories under the title Flappers and Philosophers, dedicating the book to Zelda. The contents include The Offshore Pirate, The Ice Palace, Head and Shoulders, The Cut-Glass Bowl, Bernice Bobs Her Hair, Benediction, Dalyrimple Goes Wrong, and The Four Fists.

The Offshore Pirate opens on a blue Florida sea, beneath a sky blue as children's irises, with golden disks skipping from wave to wave toward sunset. Fitzgerald's flappers, philosophers, and young men of the Jazz Age move through parties, colleges, and resorts. The collection shows his early gift for glamour, irony, and the ache beneath bright surfaces.
43716-the-adventurers:
The Adventurers, subtitled A Story of a Love-Chase, is a novel by Gustave Aimard. Ward and Lock published it in London in 1863. A preface explains that this volume and its sequel, The Pearl of the Andes, complete the most important series of Aimard's Tales of Indian Life and Adventure.

The publisher lists the shelf order of the nine volumes, from The Adventurers through The Trail-Hunter and The Tiger Slayer to The Red Track. Aimard follows Fenimore Cooper, the preface says, in carrying one hero through a range of volumes, each complete in itself. But Aimard's hero, Count Louis, was a real man: the Count de Raousset Boulbon, who tried to found an independent kingdom in Mexico. A second figure, Valentine Guillois, is the author himself in disguise, a reckless Parisian schooled by nature in the New World.
4400-hira-singh-when-india-came-to-fight:
Talbot Mundy wrote this First World War adventure in the voice of Hira Singh, telling how Indian soldiers came to fight in Flanders. Mundy dedicates the book to Elmer Davis, through whom he tracked down the hero of the adventures and found the true account better than the newspapers promised. The hero is Ranjoor Singh and his men.

Mundy notes that had the men been Muslims, their feat would have been wonderful enough, but as Sikhs they defied the very nth degree of odds under splendid leadership. The tale follows escape, endurance, and loyalty across enemy lines. It gives a rare Indian voice to the western front, in a story told as Hira Singh himself tells it.
44044-london-souvenirs:
London Souvenirs holds sketches of old London life by Charles Heckethorn. Past books by his hand treat hid groups of all ages and a famed square. The book came out in London in the year eighteen ninety nine. Its parts roam clubs, coffee houses, inns, and the great money mart.

Dice clubs and high play lead, then witty wives and old coffee rooms. Past law men, famed stage men, and odd clubs earn their parts in turn. Tales of the stock mart, lost streams, and law bars fill the wide set. A Bank founder and a great court house close the gay tour. Fond recall and tart tales tune the whole to a hearth read.
44304-the-deserter-and-other-stories-a-b:
The Deserter and Other Stories is a book of war tales by Harold Frederic, published at Boston in 1898. Its sub-title calls it a book of two wars. Merrill, Sandham, Gaul, and Barnes drew its illustrations. The title tale runs in seven chapters. Discoveries in the Barn opens it, on the coldest morning of the winter. The scene is the northern tablelands below the Adirondacks. Old men there recall when deer were driven to the clearings for food.

A sudden departure and a father and son carry the deserter's tale on. Other plates show a bounty jumper, a cry of whose blood is this, and two dozen pike heads clashing down as one. The two wars are the Civil War and the Revolution, Frederic's twin grounds. His tales mix guilt, kin, and battle in the hills of New York.
44413-the-sea-rovers:
The Sea Rovers is a sea craft book by Rufus Rockwell Wilson, out in nineteen oh six. A Dodge house of New York brought it out with cuts by May Fratz. Parts treat the sea trades one by one from a home shore start. Gloucester fish folk open the book with their port in full view. Two or three hundred schooners crowd that port on a still June morn.

Ocean flyer crews and war ship men fill the next two parts. Sea guards, coast police, and the sea pilot get parts in turn. Deep sea divers and light house keepers stand mid book in the scheme. Life save crews on shore watch and Arctic whale men close the set. The front plate shows a Gloucester fish man in his gear.
44484-with-the-dyaks-of-borneo-a-tale-of:
With the Dyaks of Borneo, a tale of the head hunters, by Captain F S Brereton, was printed in London, Glasgow, and Bombay by Blackie and Son, in a new edition. William Rainey drew the plates. Brereton had written Kidnapped by Moors, a Boy of the Dominion, and the Hero of Panama.

Chapters open with Tyler Richardson, eastward ho, and preparing for a journey. A traitor and a villain, escape from the schooner, and courage wins the day follow. Flight across the land, meeting the Dyaks, and on foot through the jungle pace the mid tale. The pirate stronghold, a midnight encounter, and captain of a fleet raise the stakes. The Rajah of Sarawak, off to the river Sabebus, and hemmed in drive the close. Boys of the day got Borneo peril at full gallop.
44496-spiders:
Spiders is a small science manual by Cecil Warburton of Christ's College, Cambridge. Warburton was zoologist to the Royal Agricultural Society when he wrote. The Cambridge University Press put the book out in the year 1912. It stands in the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature set. A photograph of the banana spider opens the book at full size.

Early chapters ask what a spider is and how its spinnerets work. The round snare gets a full chapter on lines, spirals, and sticky beads. Warburton then weighs the mental powers of spiders, sense by sense. Trap snares, ballooning young, and the fresh-water spider follow in turn. The spider in a cage and the making of its cocoon come later. Instinct, not thought, drives the spider's craft, he holds throughout.
44534-a-trip-to-mars:
A Trip to Mars is a boys' adventure novel by Fenton Ash, author of The Radium Seekers. Chambers published the book at London and Edinburgh in 1909, with six coloured pictures by Groome. A frontispiece shows the travellers greeted on the red planet. Ash explains his method in a preface addressed to young readers.

Ash says he tries to mix amusement with sound teaching. What looks like wild fancy, he claims, rests each time on some ground in science. He notes the hard choice among rival theories about Mars itself. The planet may have air like ours, thinner air, or none at all. He chose the ground that best served a believable tale. The preface thanks reviewers who praised his first book for boys.
45016-with-rod-and-line-in-colorado-wate:
With Rod and Line in Colorado Waters is a book of fishing sketches printed at Denver in 1884. Chain, Hardy and Company, booksellers and publishers, issued it. A Scots line heads the title page, asking who ever heard of a good angler being a bad man. The contents promise sport and talk in near equal shares.

Chapters bear names like Fisherman's Luck, Black Lake in 1878, and An Idle Morning at Grand Lake. Others treat mules, music, and troublesome weather. One tells of camping with ladies and the baby. The opening sketch looks back forty years, a big slice off a life. The book keeps the tone of men telling stories by a camp fire.
45177-americana-ebrietatis-the-favorite-:
Hewson L Peeke wrote on the favorite drinks of America's forefathers. Americana Ebrietatis was printed in New York in 1917, in just one hundred copies. Peeke culled some four hundred volumes for his facts, he states. The book is given to his father, a praying dry voter.

Chapters treat schools, bench and bar, church and clergy, and Washington's ties to liquor. Christenings, weddings, vendues, and taverns each show drink at the center. Whiskey served as money at the traffic's flood tide, one part notes. Temperance readers gain a lawyer-briefed history of drink and its slow fall.
45288-jack-and-the-bean-stalk-english-he:
