Jack and the Bean-Stalk, retold in English hexameters by Hallam Tennyson, came out from Macmillan in London in 1886. Randolph Caldecott supplied the illustrations. Tennyson recasts the nursery tale in the long rolling line of classical epic. The mock-heroic measure is the book's chief pleasure.

Jack is a poor widow's heir who lives like a drone in a beehive. He sells the last cow for a handful of beans. His mother throws them out of the window, and by morning a stalk taller than a California pine stands there. A fairy meets Jack at the top and tells him the Giant slew his father. The Giant's wife is basting a young elephant when Jack shrinks back in alarm. Poem and pictures together make a handsome Victorian toy book out of an old tale.
45465-the-sunlit-hours:
Sunlit Hours is a book of love poems by Emile Verhaeren in English. Murphy translated the Belgian poet's verses for John Lane of New York. Lane issued the volume in the year 1916 for English readers. Contents list the poems by their first lines in roman numerals. Poem one cries, O the splendour of this joy of ours.

What though we see it break before us into flowers follows second. A carven column whereon monsters cling stands as the third poem. The night unfolding banishes the day, and a gracious gift recalled, ensue. Come out into the garden fair invites the beloved in poem ten. Verhaeren sings married love in free, swelling lines of praise.
45547-hal-kenyon-disappears:
Hal Kenyon Disappears is a boys' adventure novel by Gordon Stuart. Reilly and Lee published it at Chicago in 1936. The contents list twenty four chapters of mountain adventure. Mummy Canon opens the tale, and Doctor Byrd is introduced. A Fall from the Air and The Wreck and the Aviator follow. Lost, a scream in the waterfall, and Hal's discovery raise the stakes. Hal a Prisoner and the mystery of the leather bag come next. Airship Plans and Building the Airship give the boys a machine.

Clearing Hal and the Boy Scouts of the Air end the list. Mountain Lion Bridge closes the contents. The story opens with thirty boys of Lakefarm School shouting a school yell. Their cheer rings through Mummy Canon at evening. Hiking, flying, and caves carry this school camp adventure.
45558-the-history-of-the-fifty-ninth-reg:
A full record tells the war road of the Fifty-ninth Illinois Volunteers. The book's own sub-title calls it a three years' march. The men fought through Missouri, Arkansas, and Mississippi. Tennessee and Kentucky close the list of their grounds. A front plate shows Post and the chief staff of the unit.

Towns, skirmish lines, and great fights fill the march tale. Falls in fight and odd tales met on the road are set down. The land they crossed is drawn as they saw it. Names and posts ground the tale in real men's lives. Vets and kin get a march they can trace day by day.
45601-the-four-corners:
The Four Corners, by Amy Blanchard, is a girls novel of a Virginia family. Jacobs issued it at Philadelphia and London with rights in 1906 for it. The Corner series name plays on the four girls and their corners at home. Their rambling old house stands at the foot of Virginia blue mountains.

Nancy Weston, called Nan, is eldest of the four lively Corners there. Cousin Phil teases her as Sharp Corner; Aunt Sarah calls her West Corner. Chapters open with a new song and a fairy godmother visit in turn. Nan secret, a mother secret, and housewifely cares fill the early tale. Imprisonment, the red cloth, trouble, sacrifices, and fire crowd the close.
45678-tales-of-the-covenanters:
Tales of the Covenanters, by Ellen Jane Guthrie, is a book of Scottish martyr tales. This eleventh edition came from Simpkin, Marshall in London in 1920, with Morison at Glasgow. Six tales stand in the contents.

They are A Tale of Bothwell Bridge, The Laird of Culzean, and Peden's Stone. The Murder of Inchdarnie, The Laird of Lag, and The Sutor's Seat complete the set. An introduction opens with a poem by Hemans on nameless martyrs. Kings have shrines and tombs in minsters, the poem says, and heroes their mounds by the sea. But no stone marks where the thousands rest who died for truth and freedom. Their graves are unknown to man, yet marked of God. The prose then turns to Scotland, a land of romance. Her mouldering ruins, it says, are linked with legends that deepen their hold.
45796-twenty-six-years-reminiscences-of-:
W A Adams looks back over twenty-six seasons of grouse shooting in Scotland, in a book drawn by C Whymper and issued from the Field office in London in 1889.

His chapters cover the seasons from 1863 to 1888, then turn to the working side of the moor: heather burning, draining, dogs, and disease. Adams writes as an old hand whose rheumatic muscles have ended his days with a gun, passing on what the years taught him. He recalls when railways ended at Inverness and the far north felt as unknown as Labrador, and when grouse were a sport for the few. The book is both memoir and manual, rich in the small facts of bags, weather, and moor craft.
45799-the-golden-book-of-the-dutch-navig:
The Golden Book of the Dutch Navigators is a history by Hendrik Willem van Loon. The Century Company published it in New York in 1916. Seventy reproductions of old prints illustrate the voyages. Van Loon dedicates the book to his sons, Hansje and Willem. He calls it, in his opening letter, a story of magnificent failures. The men who fitted out the expeditions died in the poorhouse.

Sailors on those voyages drowned, froze, or died of thirst. Bad supplies from lying contractors buried many under coconut trees. Others were speared by Pacific islanders. Van Loon praises their grace under whatever came. Keep on smiling is the lesson he presses on his boys. The history of Holland, his introduction argues, is the conquest of the sea. America conquered the West; the Dutch conquered the water.
45805-recently-recovered-lost-tudor-play:
John S Farmer edits seven early English plays once thought lost, in a facsimile issued at Guildford in 1966. The Early English Drama Society first published the set at London in 1907.

Mankind, from about 1475, leads the volume. Its players are Mercy, Mischief, New Guise, Nought, and Titivillus the devil. Mercy opens with a speech on man's dear-bought redemption. Nature, by Henry Medwall, follows. John Redford's Play of Wit and Science comes next. Respublica and the interludes of Wealth and Health fill the middle. Impatient Poverty and John the Evangelist close the plays. A note-book and word-list end the book. These rough, funny moralities show the English stage before the playhouses rose.
45819-cressy-poictiers:
Cressy and Poictiers, the story of the Black Prince Page, is a tale by J G Edgar. It stands in Everyman Library, shaped by Ernest Rhys, and was printed in London by Dent and in New York by Dutton. A first edition came in February 1906 and a reprint in April. A Sidney line heads the book.

In his opening Rhys tells that the book was first made forty or fifty years before. Its editor then had a clear plan of bringing English history into holiday range. Edgar was one of his chief writers and made some capital stories and histories. The tale follows the Black Prince wars in France through his page eyes. Cressy and Poictiers, the two great English wins, give the book its name. Young readers get the Hundred Years War as a holiday story.
45873-reptiles-and-birds-a-popular-accou:
Reptiles and Birds, a popular account of their various orders by Louis Figuier, was published by D Appleton and Company of New York in 1870. Parker Gillmore, who signed himself Ubique, edited and adapted the English version. Three hundred seven woodcuts by A Mesnel, A de Neuville, and E Riou illustrate the work. A picture of hawking in the middle ages stands at the front.

Gillmore's preface says he fitted the matter to the present state of general knowledge, for readers of all classes. The contents open with the amphibians: frogs, toads, and salamanders, their structure, habits, and changes of form. True snakes follow at length, burrowing, tree, water, and sea kinds, harmless and venomous. Boas and pythons end the snake chapter in the pages shown. The bird half of the book treats the orders of birds and their economy in the same full manner.
45929-horae-subsecivae-rab-and-his-frien:
Rab and His Friends, and Other Papers collects the essays of John Brown, the Edinburgh physician and writer, under his Latin title Horae Subsecivae, meaning spare hours. The Stokes Company of New York published this Artist's Edition in 1903, with new illustrations by Jessie Shepherd and William McCullough.

The preface opens with famous advice: squeeze out the whey. William Taylor of Norwich gave that pithy counsel to Southey, Brown recalls, when the poet sent him the manuscripts of his huge quartos. Brown jokes that his own title suffered in translation, Horo Subsecivo being exchanged for Spare Hours. The papers themselves, headed by the beloved tale of Rab the dog, mix medical observation, character sketches and humour. Brown's essays were among the most cherished short prose of Victorian Scotland.
4615-the-upton-letters:
Arthur Christopher Benson published The Upton Letters in 1905, after the letters were returned to him by the widow of the friend to whom they were written. That friend, sorting papers a few days before his wholly unexpected death, had held the bulky packet. He said the letters should be kept together, and that Benson ought to publish them some day. His sudden death gave that unconsidered wish a certain sanctity, and Benson obeyed it.

A few merely personal matters and casual details were left out, but the main substance stands, and the letters appear just as they were written. Benson admits their hurried faults, and hopes their spontaneity makes up for them. Readers get an intimate Edwardian correspondence, full of books, friendship, college life, and daily thought, best read as a portrait of a mind in letters rather than as a formal essay.
46252-the-highflyers:
Clarence Budington Kelland's The Highflyers, copyright 1919 by Harper and Brothers, was reprinted by Burt at New York. It opens on Fred la Mothe telling a barroom story, after Scotch, soda, and ice have loosened his tongue. His tale is of Potter Waite, who bet even money he could fly round Windmill Point Light and back without busting his neck. Fred bet a dinner for four at the Tuller that Waite would bust at least a leg. Fred paid: the machine bounded and twisted like a leaf in a gale, and Waite landed like a man stepping off a Pullman.

The frontispiece shows a girl in riding breeches and puttees, dressed for the adventure. Kelland, author of The Source and Sudden Jim, sets the talk among young men around the lakes country. Waite's daredevil flying and his way with taxi drivers mark him as the book's highflyer.
46588-jack-harkaway-in-new-york-or-the-a:
Bracebridge Hemyng wrote a Jack Harkaway story for Beadle's Half Dime Library, number 101, dated July 1, 1879 and sold for five cents. Hemyng signs himself Jack Harkaway as well as author. Contents open with a special meeting of the Travelers' Club. The duel on the sands and the assassin at work follow. Adèle and the voyage come next.

An abandoned ship and the mystery of the deserted vessel fill the middle. A lovers' quarrel and a race precede later chapters. Jack Harkaway began in English penny papers as a schoolboy hero. Beadle's editions carried him to American boys at five cents a number.
46698-some-noble-sisters:
Edmund Lee, who wrote on Dorothy Wordsworth, gathered these lives of famed sisters. Clarke printed Some Noble Sisters in London in 1892. A line from George Eliot heads it: were another childhood world my share, I would be born a little sister there.

Lee states his aim in the preface with plain care. He has drawn from many sources the records of some of the world's notable sisters. The set is not full, he owns, but meant to stir and to cheer. It is designed above all for young women. No such record stood ready before, he says, and the lack alone justifies so slight a work. Susanne Kossuth, sister of the Hungarian hero, stands among the lives told.
46869-the-royal-institution-its-founder-:
Bence Jones wrote The Royal Institution, its Founder and its First Professors. Longmans at London put out the book in 1871. Jones was honorary secretary of the institution he describes. His preface begins the history with the life of its founder. Count Rumford's career determined its original form, he holds.

Short accounts of the earliest professors follow the founder's life. The spirit shown in them has been the life of the place, he says. Garnett and Thomas Young had little influence there beside the founder. When Rumford and Banks had left, Davy became the main supporter. To Davy chiefly it owes the form it now retains, Jones writes. Faraday's name has blended with the institution for fifty years, he adds. Few know what Davy made it, and fewer what Rumford meant it to be. Jones gives the great lecture house its first history.
472-the-house-behind-the-cedars:
Charles Chesnutt sets this novel of race and passing in post-Civil War North Carolina. A stranger from South Carolina returns to Patesville, where a light-skinned sister and brother live behind cedars, passing as white. Love, a tournament, and a courtship test their secret, while an old judge and loyal friends watch.

Chesnutt writes with quiet irony about color lines drawn by law and custom. The house itself stands for a hidden past that will not stay hid. The novel stands as a pioneering American work on race, identity, and the price of crossing a line society drew in blood.
47258-american-inventions-and-inventors:
American Inventions and Inventors is a school history by the two Mowrys. William Mowry and Arthur May Mowry wrote it for Silver Burdett in nineteen hundred. The pair also wrote First Steps in the History of Our Country. Their United States history for schools sold at one dollar in cloth.

The book belongs to a list for the study of American history in schools. Great men and their deeds frame the series title for young readers. Inventions and their makers give pupils a proud, plain tale of progress. Townsend MacCoun historical geography and wall charts complete the publisher list. Coloured maps in those aids show the nation growth change by change.
47333-christmas-stories-from-french-and-:
Christmas Stories from French and Spanish Writers, gathered and translated by Antoinette Ogden, was published by A C McClurg and Company of Chicago in 1892. Fifteen tales fill the table of contents, each with its author's name. The French side gives Alphonse Daudet three places, and the Spanish side gives Benito Pérez Galdós two. The book brings two literatures to one fireside.

Daudet's Three Low Masses and his Christmas supper in the Marais lead the French tales, with Coppée's Louis d'Or beside them. From the Spanish come Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer's Maese Pérez the organist and Pedro de Alarcón's poet's Christmas Eve. The first tale, A Bird in the Snow by Armando Palacio Valdés, tells of a blind musician whose father played cornet in a military band. He never heard from his brother in America.
47420-unaddressed-letters:
Unaddressed Letters, edited by Frank Swettenham, is a book of letters written to no reader. Lane issued it at the Bodley Head, London and New York, in 1898. Swettenham had written Malay Sketches, in a second edition.

Thirty-seven letters run from a hill of solitude to a close in heaven. Worship, west and east, and a clever mongoose open the run. Love in fiction, the jingling coin, and a strange sunset follow. Letter-writing gets a letter, and so do funerals and decay. Daughters and despotism, a fiancé, and by the sea fill the middle. Tigers and crocodiles, a rose and a moth, and a love-philtre turn the tale eastward. The first letter climbs a path round the Hill of Solitude. From its bench the writer watches the sun sink into the sea by a river mouth.
47505-louis-pasteur-his-life-and-labours:
Louis Pasteur: His Life and Labours is a biography by Pasteur's son-in-law, translated from the French by Lady Claud Hamilton. Appleton of New York published it in 1886, with an introduction by John Tyndall. The preface describes the author without naming him: an intimate of the house, neither fellow-worker nor disciple, who lives in complete familiarity with the dear master. He has no other title, and is almost proud of having none.

He was a constant inmate of Pasteur's laboratory. He passed happy years near the great investigator who discovered a new world, the world of the infinitely little. The book follows Pasteur from his first studies on molecular dissymmetry to his latest work on hydrophobia, virulent diseases, and artificial cultures. A quotation preserved in the copy gives the book's purpose.
47859-petrarch-s-letters-to-classical-au:
Petrarch's Letters to Classical Authors presents the letters Petrarch wrote to writers of ancient Rome, in English. Mario Emilio Cosenza translated them from the Latin and supplied a commentary. Cosenza taught Latin at the College of the City of New York. The University of Chicago Press published the volume in nineteen ten.

Petrarch addressed these letters to long dead authors as if they were living friends. That bold device let him praise, blame, and question the models of his own writing. Cosenza's notes set out the sources and the points at issue in each letter. The edition keeps the old spelling of the Latin based texts in its notes. Footnotes run in one long series through the whole book for the reader.
47961-natural-wonders:
Natural Wonders, by Edwin Tenney Brewster, is a science book for children in the Children Library. Doubleday issued the Garden City edition in 1928 from a 1912 copyright. How the chicken gets inside the egg opens the contents as chapter one. Some other sorts of eggs and little fishes in the brook follow in the list.

Plant eggs, then what boys and girls are made of, fill the next heads. More about living bricks and how much of us is alive continue the plain talk. How we grow, grow up, and grow old make a run of three chapters. Why we grow at all and things that need no learning close the listed heads. Plain questions of young readers get plain answers in this nature primer.
47971-field-book-of-western-wild-flowers:
Margaret Armstrong wrote the Field Book of Western Wild Flowers, issued in New York and London in nineteen hundred fifteen. J J Thornber of the University of Arizona worked with her on the text. Armstrong drew the pictures from live plants herself. The book holds five hundred drawings in black and white.

Forty eight color plates add to the black drawings. The guide covers wild blooms west of the Rocky Mountains. States from Washington down to Arizona form the ground it treats. Armstrong tells how desert heat shapes odd blooms in Utah and Arizona. Snow line plants and sea cliff plants get space too. She bills it as the first such field book for the whole West.
47993-a-renaissance-courtesy-book-galate:
Galateo of Manners and Behaviours is an old court book by Giovanni Della Casa of Italy. This form came out in nineteen fourteen as part of a set of books of the wise age. A front talk by Spingarn leads the work. The text is the old English dress of the tract, with its long gift note to a great lord of the queens court.

That note tells how the man found the tract of grace by a skilled hand of Italy, drawn into scores of tongues. He sought to make it speak English for the gain of his own land. Grace and court craft grow as twins, he says, and part them and both die. A list of parts and a note on past prints close the book. Its rules teach the small acts of the table, of talk, and of dress.
48026-the-sir-roger-de-coverley-papers:
The Sir Roger de Coverley Papers, edited for schools by Winchester of Wesleyan University, prints Addison's famous essays with notes. The book belongs to the Gateway Series of English Texts, under the general editorship of Henry van Dyke. It sold at forty cents, like its shelf-mates in the series. A map of part of London, drawn from Rocque's map of 1741 to 1745, fronts the text.

Every fifth line of the text is numbered on the page. The notes at the back point to those numbers, page by page and line by line. Companion volumes in the series cover Burke, Franklin, Lamb, Macaulay, Milton and Scott. School prices run from thirty to fifty cents. The set put standard English prose into cheap, sturdy school hands.
48103-terry-s-texas-rangers:
Terry's Texas Rangers is a regimental history by Giles, a veteran of that command, printed in nineteen eleven. The Terry Rangers were a Texas cavalry regiment in the Confederate army. Sixteen chapters run from the regiment's raising to its last campaign of the war. Giles tells in his opening how the book came to be written at last.

The survivors long wanted both a history and a monument to their service. Money raised went to the monument, an equestrian statue at Austin, instead. The wish for a written record still lived on in sketches by many members. Comrade Combs asked Giles to write for the sake of children and grandchildren. Giles grants the data are now too thin for a complete history. He offers his best effort so the regiment's part is not lost.
48168-funny-stories-told-by-the-soldiers:
Carleton Case bound war jokes and pranks told by the men who won. The book's rights date to 1919 from a Chicago house. Its sub-title calls the men victors in their gay hours. Secretary Baker tells a good one to lead the whole set. A neat garb on a Yank is kept by hard work, Baker says in front.

Works is hard, but the fruit more than pays, he tells the crowd. A tale of a train, a loose coat, and a sergeant starts the fun. Button up that coat, cries Sergeant Jabez Winterbottom in wrath. A pipe in your mouth breaks rule too, a major snaps back at him. Rank on rank tops each tale in the chain of jokes. Camp wit fills it.
482-the-woodlanders:
Thomas Hardy sets this novel in the woods and orchards of Wessex, where timber and apple trees rule life. Grace Melbury, back from school, is torn between Giles Winterborne, a loyal woodsman, and Edred Fitzpiers, a charming doctor with a roving eye. Marty South, a girl who cuts her hair for love, watches their fates.

Hardy writes with somber, lyrical prose, letting the woods mirror human hopes. Class, marriage, and pride tangle the four lives toward a bleak end. The novel stands among Hardy's great tragedies of place, where nature endures and people, for all their longing, do not.
48503-birds-and-nature-vol-08-no-1-june-:
Birds and Nature, volume eight, number one, came out in June 1900 at Chicago. The monthly serial promised forty pictures made by colour photography in each set, and called itself a guide in the study of nature. William Kerr Higley served as editor, and two volumes came out each year.

The number mixes verse and short prose on birds, beasts, and the outdoor world. Pieces treat Wilson's thrush, the homing pigeon, water insects, insect music, and the place of the fish in nature. A wheat harvest piece and a note on cattle bring farm life in as well. The colour plates let town readers study wild things they might never see close at hand.
49018-the-witness-of-the-stars:
Bullinger wrote this reading of gospel truth in the star signs. He published the book himself in London in 1893. A psalm line, he telleth the number of the stars, fronts it. The first book, The Redeemer, opens with the sign Virgo.

Coma, Centaurus, and Bootes attend Virgo as lesser star groups here. Libra brings Crux the cross, the Victim, and the Crown. Scorpio, Sagittarius, and the dragon fill the first book end. The Redeemed and a third book follow the same sign plan. Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and Leo signs structure the third book of the star witness.
49077-the-art-of-horse-shoeing-a-manual-:
Art of Horse Shoeing is a manual for farriers by William Hunting, a veterinary surgeon. Hunting edited a veterinary record and inspected horses for two London districts. Nearly one hundred pictures go with the text. The London edition is dated eighteen ninety five. Contents run to chapters on the form and action of the foot first.

Preparation of the hoof for shoeing follows, with faults to be avoided. The form and making of shoes take a chapter, then the choice of a shoe for each kind of horse and work. Fitting and application come next, with hot and cold fitting and tips. A chapter on roughing treats frost nails and movable studs. The book is written for three classes of readers, Hunting says. Horse owners, farriers open to conviction, and veterinary students are all addressed.
4908-five-of-maxwell-s-papers:
Five papers by James Clerk Maxwell gather work on light, color, and vision, including a curious test with the eye itself. The sample paper follows a dark spot that moves with the eye across the blue part of the spectrum. It refuses to pass into other colors. Maxwell traces it to the yellow spot on the retina.

He shows how to observe the effect with blue and yellow glasses, or with slowly turning papers. A quirk of sight becomes measured science in his hands. The papers' subject and method mark their author throughout. Readers with a taste for physics get a window into how a great tester watched his own eyes at work.
49097-killing-for-sport-essays-by-variou:
Henry S Salt edited a set of essays against hunting and shooting for pleasure. G Bell and Sons issued the book at London in 1915 for the Humanitarian League. Bernard Shaw wrote the preface.

The League's note sets out its ground with care. Fair games like cricket, rowing, and football win its full support. Blood sports, which rest on the death or pain of feeling creatures, stand in another class. The League asks for laws only against the worst kinds, those using tame or caught animals. It points with pride to the end of the Royal Buckhounds. George Meredith's letter of praise is quoted. The essays press the case from many sides, moral, social, and humane.
4937-hudibras-in-three-parts-written-in-:
Samuel Butler's Hudibras, written in three parts during the late wars, is the great mock-heroic poem of the English Civil War era. Its Presbyterian knight and his squire ride through a world of sects, factions, and learned folly, arguing theology and politics in verse that never quite lets its heroes look heroic.

The edition adds notes keyed by letters in the text, a glossary for Latin phrases, and translations by the transcriber, who warns they may be inaccurate. Butler's satire targets Puritan cant and Royalist bluster alike. Readers get a comic epic that still explains, better than any history, how England laughed at its own revolution.
4947-sisters:
Cherry Strickland, just eighteen, comes home engaged after twenty-one minutes, and this novel follows what that May evening in California sets in motion. She shuts the Strickland house door behind her, breath rising in deep, ecstatic breaths, half afraid the joy inside her might escape into the moonlight.

Her farewell to Martin and her swift run up the path open a story of sisters, suitors, and family feeling, where an engagement is only the beginning of the complications. An author name is absent from the record. Readers get a warm domestic romance about young love tested by kin, pride, and the long business of growing up.
49644-motor-matt-s-quest-or-three-chums-:
Motor Matt's Quest, or three chums in strange waters, is a five cent weekly tale issued at New York on June 12, 1909. It is number sixteen of a motor stories line of thrilling adventure. A picture at the front shows a boy yelling for help as he leaps into water, while Motor Matt stands ready to hurl a harpoon.

The contents open in the depths, then out of the jaws of death. Sealed orders, an American consul, and Motor Matt's patience follow in turn. On the jump, a landing party, and a chum in trouble carry the middle chapters. Such weeklies were the pocket cinema of their day, sold at news stands to boys for a nickel. Matt and his chums, with their motor boat, meet each new peril at full throttle.
49683-cruikshank-s-water-colours:
George Cruikshank's water colours are gathered in this 1903 volume from Black of London. Joseph Grego wrote the introduction. The plates shown are the 27 water colour drawings for Oliver Twist. They were printed by the Carl Hentschel colourtype process.

Grego traces the artist's long fight for credit. Stage versions of his works borrowed his scenes freely. Moncrieff wrote Tom and Jerry from Cruikshank's plates, the tale goes. Halliday later built a play from the designs in the same way. Cruikshank found his own share in these works ignored. He answered with a public claim to part authorship. Oliver Twist stood at the center of the quarrel. The introduction presents a combative veteran, sure of his gifts and ready to fight.
5004-the-motor-boys-on-the-pacific-or-th:
Clarence Young's Motor Boys on the Pacific sends the boys west with Professor Uriah Snodgrass, through bad news, a desperate race, and strange conversations. A motor boat carries them into fog and onto rocks, horned toads furnish comic relief, and news of a brig, a man on the rocks, and Mr. Blowitz's wants drive the plot.

Derelict hunting gives the voyage its purpose: the boys seek wrecked and abandoned vessels along the Pacific coast. Young keeps the pace brisk and the machinery lovingly described. Readers get a boys' motor adventure of sea, fog, and salvage, where a boat's engine matters as much as any hero's courage.
50108-a-father-s-legacy-to-his-daughters:
Doctor Gregory of Edinburgh wrote these letters to his daughters, here in a new edition printed at London in 1808 with plates. A front plate on religion, drawn by T Stothard, dates to March 1, 1797. The preface says the letters came from a tender father in failing health, written for his daughters' teaching and not meant for the public.

In such home talk, the preface argues, no sacrifices are made to fashion or custom. A father's love and care speak plain. The editor, his son, offers the treatise on the strength of the kind welcome given his father's other works. Gregory's counsel covers religion, conduct, and the dangers that rise even from good gifts, in the manner of a careful eighteenth-century father.
50121-fifteen-new-ways-for-oysters:
Rorer wrote a small cook book of fifteen fresh ways to cook oysters. The book came out in Philadelphia, its rights claimed in 1894. Her great cook book runs near six score times five pages. That book is bound in wash cloth at one dollar and three quarters. Cans, hot day dishes, and home sweets fill her shelf list.

Six small books at a quarter each stand in that neat row. Tea pan use, old town rules, and quick soups are in the six. Each bears its own hue cloth with bright stamp work in front. Arnold and Company put the small set out for home cooks. Oyster fans get fifteen new turns on one rich sea food. Brief steps rule it.
50220-the-railway-library-1909-a-collect:
The Railway Library 1909 gathers noteworthy chapters, addresses, and papers on railways, mostly printed during that year. Slason Thompson, manager of the Bureau of Railway News and Statistics, compiled and edited it at Chicago. Its tables track passengers, millions, and proportions across the industry. Footnotes and wide tables split into parts fill many pages.

The papers take up the great railway question of the day, how far the state should rule the roads. Writing on British railways weighs wise regulation against national ownership of the lines. With harsh and heavy regulation, one paper argues, taking the roads into public hands becomes unavoidable. The volume served railway men, lawmakers, and students of transport. It preserves the facts and the arguments of American and British railroading in 1909, a year when regulation hung over every boardroom in the business.
50469-a-prayer-book-for-soldiers-and-sai:
Leaders of the Episcopal Church made this small prayer book for troops in 1941. The Church Pension Fund printed it in New York. It was sent as a gift to men in the Army and Navy. A note from the head bishop greets each reader.

Inside are orders of worship, prayers, psalms, and Bible reads. Hymns close the book for use in camp or at sea. The Lord Prayer and the old creed stand near the front. The book aimed to give calm, strength, and hope in hard war days. The Army and Navy Commission of the church stood behind the gift.
50510-the-boys-book-of-famous-rulers:
Lydia Hoyt Farmer wrote this book of great rulers for boys, and Crowell printed it at New York in 1886. Farmer, who wrote The Story of Science, gave the book to her own children. Charlemagne fronts the volume in a plate.

Her aim, she says, is to give the chief events of each life in short, clear tale form. The age and the ways of each land come with the life. Agamemnon opens the roll, then Cyrus and Alexander the Great. Caesar, Charlemagne, Alfred, and Richard the Lionheart follow. Robert Bruce, the Philips and Ferdinands of Spain, Gustavus, Louis, Peter, and Frederick march on. Napoleon closes the grand line.
50550-captain-william-kidd-and-others-of:
John Abbott wrote this life of Captain Kidd and his fellow sea robbers for Dodd, Mead of New York. The rights date to 1874, with a fresh claim in 1902 by Laura Abbott Buck. Abbott's preface calls the tale as wild and strange as any in the tongue.

Kidd, a New York merchant turned pirate, heads the cast. Bonnet, Barthelemy, and Lolonois do their fierce feats beside him. Mary Read, the guiltless woman pirate, and the fierce Anne Bonney share the stage. Sir Henry Morgan's vast career and the zeal of Montbar close the roll. Abbott, a famed teller of lives for the young, gives each rover his full, grim due.
50572-goethe-s-theory-of-colours:
Goethe Theory of Colours is the English form of the German poet and thinker work on color, turned by Charles Lock Eastlake and printed in London in 1840. Eastlake adds his own notes. The book sets Goethe view of color against the received theory of Newton.

Eastlake says English writers had dealt mostly with the prism part of the work, where Goethe most defied Newton. He chose to give the theory whole, so science readers could hear Goethe speak for himself. Goethe treats how colors rise from light and dark, and how the eye plays its own part. The book joins art, science, and verse in one mind. Readers meet a famed clash on how sight and light should be read.
5066-the-whole-family-a-novel-by-twelve-:
The Whole Family, a novel by twelve authors, begins with an engagement that everyone calls pleasant news, and a decision that the father should speak first. William Dean Howells writes the father, newly arrived in the neighborhood, who must address the suitor's father about the match.

Elizabeth Jordan writes the schoolgirl. Bangs writes the son-in-law. Henry James writes the married son. Elizabeth Stuart Phelps writes the married daughter. Edith Wyatt writes the mother. Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews writes the schoolboy. Alice Brown writes Peggy, and Henry Van Dyke writes the friend of the family. Each chapter gives one member's view. Readers get a collaborative experiment in point of view, where one family's engagement looks different from every chair at the table.
5069-the-doctor-s-dilemma-preface-on-doc:
George Bernard Shaw's Preface on Doctors, attached to The Doctor's Dilemma, argues that medicine pays mutilation better than cure. A man who corrects an ingrowing toenail receives a few shillings, Shaw complains. A man who cuts your inside out receives hundreds of guineas. The exception is surgery on a poor person for practice.

Scandalized voices insist the operations are necessary, Shaw concedes, and they may be. But making the doctor judge of that necessity is like making the hangman judge of hanging. The preface ranges over fees, surgery, and professional power with Shavian wit. Readers get Shaw's case against medical monopoly, as provocative now as when it first appeared.
5076-the-spoilers:
Rex Beach's Spoilers opens on an Alaskan harbor agleam with anchored ships' lights, beneath crenelated mountains black against the sky. Glenister drinks cool air tainted with sea scent. The blood of his boyhood leaps within him. He murmurs that this is his country after all, with a hunger for the North in his veins.

Dextry warns him not to expand too strong in one spot, lest mountain air make men drunk, and returns to his pipe's villainous fumes. The novel follows gold-rush claim jumping, love, and fighting in the far north. Readers get a vigorous Alaska adventure, where the country's beauty and its greed contend for the same men.
50826-the-moons-of-mars:
Dean Evans wrote The Moons of Mars, a short tale of a strange small boy. Galaxy magazine ran the story in its September issue of nineteen hundred fifty two. A grown man tells of the day he met the child. Butterflies and a tune start the odd account in the street.

The boy swings a great butterfly net and whistles as he walks. His tune is The Calm, from the William Tell Overture, of all things. His mother taught it to him, he says with a grave still face. Martian boys have no earlobes, and this child has none at all. His steps and notes pick up just where they broke off, exact as a clock. The man trails him home to a crumbling row of houses. What manner of child walks and whistles with machine true aim?
50971-the-problem-makers:
Problem Makers is a science fiction story by Robert Hoskins, from Galaxy Magazine of August 1963. Mack drew the pictures for this tale of professional troublemakers in space. A deck line jokes that their one mission in the galaxy was making more problems. Three moons hang clouded over a village as men slip in by night.

Double bitted axes come out of belts as hands feel for door hangings in blackness. Luke Royceton draws a deep breath and screams the banshee signal for attack. Cooking fire coals are kicked alight and grass torches thrust in for flame. Village raids as policy give the story its dark, clever premise to unfold.
51011-the-ghost-camp-or-the-avengers:
Rolf Boldrewood wrote tales of the wild bush in his flat, famed set. This book is The Ghost Camp, or The Avengers in full. His list names Robbery Under Arms and The Miner's Right. Those books stand at a set price in one dress in the ads. Macmillan of London put this set out for all readers.

Ghost camps and men bent on pay back give the tale its name. Gold fields, bush roads, and old wrongs set the stage for strife. Boldrewood knew that life from his own years in the bush. His men speak in the true twang of the camps he knew. Each tale in his set stands on its own for new fans. Salt, dust, and grit rule it.
51081-the-amateurs:
Alan Cogan wrote a tale that ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in July 1955, drawn by Diehl. The ultimate show demanded the ultimate in showmanship, the blurb says. Now if only Mr Sims could measure up. To Mr Sims, it seemed as though they had walked along a hundred corridors. He felt as though he were taking the last walk to the gallows.

When the director finally led him outside, Sims saw daylight again, to his surprise. They were in rich parkland at the rear of the palace, where coloured fountains shimmered in the sun. It's a very nice place, said Mr Sims, remembering he had not spoken for five minutes. I suppose it's all right, Arthur Hoode agreed, his thin nostrils twitching. A death show in a gilded palace gets a cold satire.
51199-teddy-bears:
Adah Sutton wrote this child tale of teddy bears come to life in play. Schaefer drew the pictures for the Saalfield book of 1907. Chapter one brings the bears in a crate from factory to store. They rode packed in tissue and excelsior, some head down all the way.

Deft hands unpack them, brush their coats, and set them right at last. Chapters add Sally, Bob, a farm trip, and Bedelia at play. A kitchen visit, a telephone trick, and a nursery ball follow. Twins run off, and Bedelia takes a sea voyage near the end.
51409-public-school-life-boys-parents-ma:
Alec Waugh wrote a plain study of life in the English public schools, and Collins of London copyrighted it in 1922. A long opening letter to Arnold Lunn, dated December 6, 1921, sets out his aim. Novels on schools, Waugh says, must bend the system to a story. His book, though told as a tale, has one object only, to lay that life bare.

The chapters follow a boy through the whole course. They treat the prep school, the new boy, the second year, and the middle years. Waugh weighs games and the hold of sport, and gives a full chapter to the true ethics of cribbing. Prefectship and the last term come near the end. He closes with the old boy turned master and parent, and with plans on the right age to leave.
51441-third-reader-the-alexandra-readers:
McIntyre, Dearness, and Saul made a third school book for Canada's young. The book came out in Toronto in 1908 at forty-five cents. Both school chiefs held posts at normal schools of their towns. Alberta and Saskatchewan schools cleared it for use by law. The Canadian flag fronts the book in a proud plate.

Canada, Maple Land leads the songs in the book's list. The Shoemaker and the Elves, by Grimm, starts the tales. Blewett's song of the gold sea and Prescott's Work stand in verse. Kriloff's fable of wealth and a beggar adds a sly note. Tennyson's Eagle and Richards's Gold Windows shine in it. Tales, songs, and short reads mix.
51508-the-chasers:
The Chasers, a science fiction tale by Daniel Galouye, ran in Galaxy magazine in February 1961. Harrington illustrated the story for the magazine in that issue. A head note asks whether one civilisation can fail to make sense at all. As dust drifts clear of the ship landing skids, two things grow plain.

They have missed the city, if city it is, by miles in the landing. Yet they have slammed down near one of the many rural estates of the planet. The landscape will crawl with Zaortian Fuzzy Tails for a long while to come. The creatures pour from hatches sprung open by the crunching impact of the ship. Kent Cassidy untangles himself from the control column as the tale gets moving.
51532-in-the-land-of-cave-and-cliff-dwel:
In the Land of Cave and Cliff Dwellers is a travel book by Lieutenant Frederick Schwatka, the Arctic explorer. The Cassell company held its copyright of 1895, and an educational publisher reissued it. The contents begin in northwestern Chihuahua, preparing for the expedition, on the road from Deming, New Mexico, to Casas Grandes. Mexican Mormon colonies and ruins along the way fill the second chapter.

Sonora follows, with Hermosillo and the beautiful harbour of Guaymas, and fishing and hunting there. Central Chihuahua leads west to the great mining belt. Then comes the heart of the book: the land of the living cave and cliff dwellers, the Tarahumari Indians. The road runs on mule back through the Sierra Madre. Schwatka warns that first chapters of expeditions are full of promises, of which not one tenth may be kept. His journey into Mexico's canyon country remains a vivid record.
516-the-silverado-squatters:
Robert Louis Stevenson recounts squatting in a deserted silver mine on Mount Saint Helena in this California memoir. With his wife and stepson, Stevenson camps in the hills above Napa, visiting Calistoga, a petrified forest, and wine country. A hunter's family, sea fogs, and a toll house fill the days.

Stevenson writes with light, keen prose, praising the mountain as the Mont Blanc of its range. Mine tales, toils, and pleasures mix with sharp sketches of neighbors. The book charms as a honeymoon idyll in rough country, where a sick writer found health and a fine tale.
5177-birds-and-poets-with-other-papers:
John Burroughs's Birds and Poets, volume three of his collected writings, joins outdoor sketches with literary essays. Its papers include Birds and Poets itself, a bird medley, April and spring poems. Studies of Emerson and of genius and beauty complete the set, all written with a naturalist's eye for birdsong and season.

Burroughs moves easily from watching a mockingbird to judging a poem. The book shows why he was America's best loved nature writer. Readers who enjoy nature essays will find close observation, gentle humour. The belief that poetry and bird life belong to the same attentive way of seeing the world runs through it.
51840-the-spoilers:
The Spoilers is Rex E Beach's novel of the Alaska gold rush, copyrighted in 1905 and published in New York in April 1906, with four illustrations by Clarence F Underwood. Beach dedicated the book to his mother. Glenister, its hero, stands on the dock at Unalaska in the opening pages, drinking in the harbor lights and the mountains while the blood of his boyhood leaps in him.

Behind him sleeps the old Russian town, and before him lies the Santa Maria, ready for her midnight sailing. A frenzied horde of gold-seekers crowds toward the new El Dorado. The chapter titles chart the fight to come: a stowaway, a killing, a mine jumped, sluice robbers, vigilantes, and dynamite. Beach wrote the claim-jumping wars of Nome into one of the best-selling adventure novels of its decade.
51868-the-troublemakers:
The Troublemakers, by George Smith, ran in Galaxy Magazine in April 1960, with drawings by Dick Francis. The headnote links genetics and a thing called Hansen's Folly: one is statistical and the other impossible. The tale opens in a room that breathes wealth and taste.

The room is just ten feet by fourteen, yet its gear is choice beyond price. A chair of blackwood from Tau Ceti Five must have cost a fortune to ship. The coffee table is of earthly mahogany, antique or heirloom and in either case priceless. Paul Hanford swirls brandy while his wife sits unhappily in the fine chair. Their daughter Gloria draws the visitor's eye against his will. The visitor parks his comparison microscope on the priceless table without a qualm.
51923-the-impudent-comedian-others:
Frank Frankfort Moore wrote The Impudent Comedian and Others, a set of tales issued in eighteen ninety-six. The lead tale opens at the London house of Nelly Gwyn, the famed stage player. Her mother calls loudly for her through the hall.

Nelly had been an orange seller at Drury Lane before her rise. Now footmen in the king's scarlet stand in her hall, and fat spaniels rise to greet her. She sings on the landing, in pure lightness of heart. Evelyn, the grave diarist, had called her impudent. Moore tells her story with warmth and period colour.
51942-the-three-godfathers:
The Three Godfathers is a west tale by Kyne, with prints by a named hand. It came out at New York in the mid war years, from a book house of a great sheet. A short talk at its head sets its joke and its heart.

What is a godfather, the young bad man asks there. You are a most dull lad, his hurt pal tells him. A god sire is a sort of spare dad, who vows to shun the fiend with all his works and pomp. The young man grins a wan grin. All I have to say, he says, is that we three are a fine bunch of god sires. The tale then starts with a day raid on a bank that did not come off.
51981-sandburrs:
Alfred Henry Lewis wrote Sandburrs, tales of sport and low life in New York. Frederick A Stokes Company issued this second edition in New York in eighteen hundred ninety eight. Horace Taylor and George B Luks drew its plates. Lewis, of Wolfville fame, gave the book to James Robert Keene.

Spot and Pincher, a dog fight tale, opens the set in a bar. Martin, an East Side bar keep, heads the dog fight crowd there. His bull terrier Spot weighs thirty three pounds of live steel. Spot fights McDermott’s Pincher that night for five hundred dollars. Martin warns his dog of Pincher’s trick of snapping at legs. The pit stands sixteen feet square in a Bleecker Street loft. Lights blaze over the board walls as the crowd packs in. Spot wags his stump as if he drank in each word of the plan.
5222-the-satyricon-volume-05-crotona-aff:
This fifth volume of Petronius's Satyricon, in W. C. Firebaugh's translation, covers affairs at Crotona from chapter one hundred and twenty-five onward. Eumolpus, flushed with success, boasts that no wish of his can be resisted and that his friends can shield any crime, while his companions grow fat on the city's good things.

The volume holds only the Crotona episodes, in which legacy hunting, flattery, and greed drive the comedy to its most cynical pitch. Readers following the novel in order will find here the Satyricon's late satire on wealth and inheritance, told with unflinching humour.
52435-with-ski-sledge-over-arctic-glacie:
With Ski and Sledge over Arctic Glaciers is a tale of polar travel by Sir Martin Conway, published in London by Dent in 1898. Photographs by Garwood illustrate the book. The scene is Spitsbergen, in the summer of 1897. Conway and Garwood landed at Advent Bay ten days out of London. Two men of Vesteraalen made up the party of four. The small steamer that was to meet them had not come in, beaten back by weather. They pitched their tents and waited, in camp with a Swedish botanist and a Norwegian sportsman.

The chapters trace the work that followed. Up the Nordenskiöld Glacier, by water to Kings Bay, and over the Osborne Glacier the party pushed. The Spitsbergen Dolomites and the ascent of Mount Hedgehog stand in the list. It is a record of the first ski crossings of that ice world.
52531-green-doors:
Ethel Cook Eliot's novel Green Doors was published by Little, Brown at Boston in February 1933 and reprinted three times by April. The book is dedicated to her father. It opens in the office of Doctor Lewis Pryne, a famous psychiatrist, where Dick Wilder has talked his way past the secretary, Miss Frazier, on a regulation appointment. Dick declines a weekend of golf at Meadowbrook and offers instead a lovely new patient on a silver platter, in private.

The patient in the waiting room is Neil McCloud, a sullen, gorgeous fellow who seems unhinged. Pryne says he is perfectly sane: he has lost the power of speech, though he hears every word. Eliot sets the case up through banter between old friends, with the secretary taking notes. The title's green doors belong to the consulting-room world Pryne rules, brisk and amused.
5259-hildegarde-s-neighbors:
Laura E. Richards's Hildegarde's Neighbors, a story for girls in the Hildegarde series, opens with an arrival. It moves through old friends and new, Pumpkin House, Hester's playroom, teas at Roseholme, and good green wood. Later chapters bring a night-piece, a sailing trip, peril by water, Roger the Codger, and a morning hour before goodbye.

Richards writes warm, cheerful stories of girls' friendships and neighbourhood life, with illustrations in the original. The book offers young readers a gentle adventure among new neighbours, where kindness, play, and small dangers shape a happy summer.
52660-the-seekers:
The Seekers is a book by Jessie E. Sampter, put out at New York in nineteen ten, with first words by Josiah Royce. Its own short bill calls it a work that won its aim. That aim was a test, in live form, of faith with no sect mark. It was a search in right and in fair form, with young folk in new ways, in hunt for the sense of all things. A list of small print slips stands near the front.

The body of the book is the tale of a band and its meets. The start, the roll of the band, and then meet by meet, first to last, fill the list of parts. Eight teen meets in all stand in that run, with a tail part past them.
52662-the-emily-emmins-papers:
Carolyn Wells wrote The Emily Emmins Papers, issued by Putnam's Sons at New York and London in 1907 with pictures by Josephine Meyer. The book is made as a set of papers by Emily herself, and it opens with a ticket to Europe. Emily begins by praising the aimless ramble through city streets, a joy she sets against the fixed goals of most walkers.

From New York the papers cross the Atlantic to England in May. Chapters cover Mayfair, a hostess at home, a round of churches, Piccadilly Circus, and a French week end to close. Emily writes as a near New Yorker from a small suburban town, sharp and pleased with what she sees. The tone stays light and social throughout.
52800-lowney-s-cook-book-illustrated-in-:
Lowney's Cook Book is a household cookbook prepared by Maria Willett Howard and published in Boston in 1908. The title page calls it a new guide for the housekeeper. It promises a full record of dishes for any well-to-do family, clear enough for the beginner and complete enough for ambitious providers. Colour illustrations show the dishes.

Howard was among the most experienced teachers of cooking in the country, the title page says. Part one treats the value of food to the body, methods of cooking, carving, marketing, and a butler's duties. Part two gives the receipts: first courses, soups, fish, meats, and vegetables. The book came from the Lowney chocolate company of Boston.
5282-the-tales-and-novels-v9-belphegor-a:
Jean de La Fontaine's Tales and Novels continue in this ninth volume, in English verse translation. Its contents are Belphegor, The Little Bell, and The Glutton. Belphegor opens the volume, addressed to Miss de Chammelay, in which La Fontaine places her name with pleasure at the head of his last effusions. A companion record in this library carries the same three tales.

Belphegor tells of a devil sent from hell to learn whether wives are truly the cause of men's damnation, a story La Fontaine handles with wit and irony. Readers get three tales in which devils, bells, and appetites provide the comedy, all in the light verse manner of La Fontaine's tales.
52820-thoughts-on-slavery-and-cheap-suga:
James Ewing Ritchie wrote Thoughts on Slavery and Cheap Sugar as an open letter. Aylott and Jones issued it in London at eightpence the copy. The letter speaks to members of the British and Foreign Anti-Slavery Society. Their full annual meeting had just passed when he wrote.

Free trade man George Thompson had won a vote at that meeting. His change passed against the will of the group’s own heads. The pledge bound the Society to weigh cheap slave grown sugar. Ritchie begs his friends to read in a spirit of care. The group, he warns, is losing the broad mind of the land. Tory statesmen now quote it to bless harsh rule and force. Truth alone, he holds, is stronger than the sword’s iron arm. A peace Society must not beg aid from guns, he argues.
52828-watermelon-pete-and-others:
Elizabeth Gordon wrote tales in verse and prose for small children, with pictures by Clara Powers Wilson. Rand McNally and Company held the rights in Chicago and New York in 1914. The book stands in the Elizabeth Gordon Children's Series with the Dolly and Molly books. A blue bird at the front claims to have told the tales.

Watermelon Pete leads, a boy whose mouth is shaped like a slice of ripe melon. Piggy's Thistle Whistle, Lady Bug Goes Shopping, and Little Brown Hen follow. A baby elephant in new clothes and a brown dog with a white cat add charm. Young readers get short rhymes and gentle fun.
52897-the-colonial-clippers:
Basil Lubbock wrote The Colonial Clippers, in a second edition of 1921. James Brown at Glasgow put out the book that year. Lubbock had written The China Clippers and other sea books. Illustrations and plans fill this history of the emigrant ships. A front plate shows an emigrant fleet in Hobson's Bay, Melbourne.

Kent, Lightning, White Star, and Malabar ride in that painted fleet. Lubbock gives the book to all who learnt the art of the sea aboard them. Part one treats the emigrant ships and the power of gold. Steerage conditions in 1844 and the discovery of gold in Australia follow. Melbourne and its shipping in 1851 and 1852 take a chapter. First gold cargoes home and the great rush of 1852 come next. Maury's improvements on the old route to the colonies stand there. Lubbock gives the clipper age its loving record.
529-knights-of-art-stories-of-the-italia:
Amy Steedman tells young readers the lives of Italian painters in this art history for children. Giotto, Fra Angelico, Masaccio, Botticelli, Leonardo, Raphael, Michelangelo, Titian, and Tintoretto each get a story, with dates and pictures in color. She opens with picture books themselves, asking how art began.

Steedman writes simply, linking each painter's life to a famed work a child can picture. Assyrian carvings, Egyptian walls, and Greek marble set the long road to Florence. The book serves as a friendly first guide to Renaissance art, where masters appear as knights of a shared craft.
52968-readings-from-modern-mexican-autho:
Frederick Starr made Readings from Modern Mexican Authors at Chicago in 1904, for the Open Court firm. The book is given to Victoriano Agueros, a friend and helper in Mexican letters. Its contents name close to thirty writers, from Noriega and Garcia Cubas to Gamboa and Rabasa. Starr came to Mexico in 1894 knowing chiefly its old ruins and its peoples. Even the names of its pure writers were unknown to him then.

His first guide was Icazbalceta, a strict historian of whom any land might be proud. Hours of spare reading on trips and at work led Starr to make this book. He hoped it would bring new readers to men they had never met in print. Each author gets a share in English dress. The book opens a door on a rich, near world of letters.
53126-specimens-of-british-trench-orders:
Specimens of British Trench Orders is an official United States War Department publication of 1917, issued through the Army War College in Washington. Marked confidential and for official use only, it is War Department Document number 590. An order of May 15, 1917, signed by the chief of staff, publishes the specimens for the information of all concerned. America had just entered the Great War and needed British trench practice fast.

The body prints Canadian Corps trench orders in numbered paragraphs. They cover duties, sentries, and the care of rifles, equipment, and ammunition. Stand to, bombs and grenades, machine guns, and firing at aeroplanes follow. Further paragraphs treat sanitation, work time-tables, log books, communications, and alertness. Rum, rations and cooking, sprayers against gas, and the rules for reliefs are all specified. One note sets sentry tours at two hours by night, four by day.
53178-stories-and-sketches-by-our-best-a:
Stories and Sketches, by Our Best Authors, is an anthology of American short fiction. Lee and Shepard published it in Boston in 1867. The title page promises the best authors of the day, and the contents list fifteen tales by a dozen hands.

Seeley Regester opens with The Skeleton at the Banquet. Fitz Hugh Ludlow contributes The Proper Use of Grandfathers, and Louise Chandler Moulton a tale called Huger's Intentions. There are two ghost stories of the New London turnpike, a night in the sewers, and pieces on coming from the front and on why a certain lady fainted. Two items are unsigned, their authors hidden behind rows of stars. The first tale sets a widowed doctor at Christmas: his wife dead, his practice slender, and no invitation to dinner, while slow days settle over him. The volume samples post-war American magazine fiction.
5319-pagan-papers:
Kenneth Grahame's Pagan Papers gathers essays on the romance of the road and the rail, loafing, cheap knowledge, the rural Pan, and smoking, among others. Its contents include Non Libri Sed Liberi, Marginalia, The Eternal Whither, Deus Terminus, An Autumn Encounter, The White Poppy. The Lost Centaur completes the list, opening with Pantagruel's voyage to an island whose roads literally go to places.

Grahame, later famous for The Wind in the Willows, writes here as a lover of the countryside and of books. The essays offer readers a gentle, whimsical celebration of walking, reading. The pagan spirit of nature runs through prose that is both learned and light.
53280-will-rossiter-s-original-talkalogu:
Will Rossiter gathered these stage monologues, called talkalogues, under his own copyright of 1903, and the Ogilvie Publishing Company of Rose Street, New York, issued them as the work of American jokers. The publisher's note, in verse, advises a blue reader to read the book through, pass it to a friend, and buy another copy for himself.

The contents mix full monologues with dialect pieces and rapid-fire jokes. Moran supplies the opening talkalogues, Joseph Horrigan adds more, and Harry Newton contributes The Man from Squashopolis, The Pacific Slope, and a fifteen-minute piece with a playwright. Love and Lager Beer, happenings in Kerosenelampville, some western stories, and a joke of Li Hung Chang round out the bill. The first speaker rushes in fresh from an automobile argument with his wife over which of them is the better chauffeur.
53464-old-europe-s-suicide-or-the-buildi:
Old Europes Suicide, or The Building of a Pyramid of Errors is a war past by a British chief of the Royal build corps. Christopher Birdwood Thomson served in the Boer War, in the Balkans, and at the French front. He was his lands chief voice at the top war board till the peace. He quit the host in nineteen nineteen with the rank on his book.

The book gives a count of set deeds in Europe from nineteen twelve to nineteen nineteen. A quote from a famed wise man of old heads it, on how the past shows great acts and skips small moves of men. Parts open on a great stream and on a town in the fall of nineteen twelve, past a fight and a tract of wild hills. The Balkan wars and their peace pact fill the first run.
53635-a-cyclop-dia-of-canadian-biography:
Hector Charlesworth edited a thick book of short lives of leading Canadians, issued at Toronto by the Hunter-Rose Company in 1919 as the third volume of a national set.

Its pages give brief accounts of leading persons of the day. They were marked out in the professions, the army, politics, trade, and industry of Canada. The index alone runs to hundreds of names, from Sir Herbert B Ames and Sir James Aikins to Richard Bedford Bennett, then a rising western lawyer. A portrait of Sir Robert Borden, the war-time prime minister, fronts the volume. Books of this kind were sold by subscription and shelved with pride. Today they serve as a first stop for tracing Canadian careers of that era. Dates and posts are included.
53647-texas-flowers-in-natural-colors:
Eula Whitehouse made a book of Texas flowers in natural colors, first printed at Dallas in 1936 and again in 1948. She drew the illustrations herself from Box 739 at Southern Methodist University. The Texas bluebonnet, the state flower, fronts the book. A poem by Gertrude Whitehouse sings of Texas wildflowers from the pine woods to the prairies and from the Panhandle to the sea.

Such magic tints, pale pinks and dainty blues, no artist's palette can match, the poem says. Contents give plant parts and names, plant distribution, descriptions of plants, finding lists, and an index. Reference books on Texas flowers are listed for deeper study. Field walkers get a color key to the state's marvelous carpetry of bloom.
53680-pre-cis-writing-for-beginners:
Precis Writing for Beginners is a school book on the art of the short sum. Guy Pocock, a teacher at a sea school, wrote it for the young. It teaches how to boil a long tale down to its pith. The sum must stay a tale, not a list of points, he holds.

The book is built of tasks, each a tale to be cut down. Speech told at one hand, a snake, and two young chiefs start the set. A black realm, a prof with apes, and an isle fill the next tasks. A witch trial of the old days and a miser stand in the midst. Child hands in the mills and a hut tax weigh grave themes. The rules come one by one as the tasks are worked through in turn.
53778-first-lessons-in-natural-philosoph:
Joseph Martindale, once head of Madison Grammar School in Philadelphia, wrote this first science book for the young. Eldredge printed First Lessons in Natural Philosophy at Philadelphia in 1881. A paddlewheel steamboat heads the plates.

Our wish, the preface says, is to give both pleasure and profit. The most fine and useful things are those we meet each day. But we must know them a little before they can please or serve us much. Plain truths of science can be learned young, it holds. No more than the common wit of boys and girls is needed to grasp them. Air, heat, water, and the lever pass in short talks, each tied to things at hand. A schoolbook of the plain, kind sort.
53859-with-the-british-legion-a-story-of:
G A Henty wrote With the British Legion, a story of the Carlist Wars, issued in London by Blackie and Son in nineteen three. Ten full page illustrations by Wal Paget fill the book. The doings of the British Legion under Sir de Lacy Evans in Spain are but little known, Henty says. The expedition was a failure, he grants.

That failure came from no want of heroic courage, he holds. It came from the most scandalous neglect and ill treatment by the Government of Queen Christina, he charges. Within six months nearly five thousand men, half the Legion, had died from want, privation, or fever, he records. The rest, ill fed and ill clothed, stayed worthy of the army best traditions, he says. Boys get a Spanish civil war adventure on a true frame.
54273-locked-doors:
Locked Doors is a detective story by Mary Roberts Rinehart, first published in 1914 and reprinted inside her Crime Book omnibus beside The After House and The Red Lamp. A nurse tells the story, and it opens with detective Mr Patton offering her a case that has already unnerved another nurse.

The French governess had gone, Patton explains, and the family wanted the children competently cared for. But the first nurse left after four days, looking back over her shoulder as she came in. She had no real reason she could name. Rinehart builds the mystery from that household's strange manner of living, sending her narrator in with a fresh mind and no facts, exactly as Patton intends.
54445-the-hospital-murders:
The Hospital Murders is a detective novel by Means Davis, printed at New York in 1934. It opens in the Medicine Clinic of the Elijah Wilson Hospital. The loud speaker pages Doctor Ethridge Sterling, Junior, through laboratories, kitchens, and corridors. Cub Sterling answers from Ward D and takes a call from Harold Barton.

Five minutes later Sterling leaves by the elevator, nods to two internes, and goes out into Beeker Street. The chapter titles promise an unconscious intruder, murder, and autopsy findings. Three dolls figure in the tale, one by one, beside a brave nurse and a new patient in bed eleven. A chapter called The Control and a last chapter in the cupola close the list. Davis sets a murder puzzle inside a great hospital. Its doctors, nurses, and orderlies all move within reach of the crime.
54736-bible-characters:
Bible Characters gathers sermons and writings on the men and women of Scripture, published in Chicago and entered for copyright in 1902. The famous preachers drawn on are Dwight Moody, De Witt Talmage, and Joseph Parker. Great poems in print supplement the sermons, and a Doré painting of the Expulsion from the Garden fronts the book.

An introduction by the Reverend Gillette states the aim. Devout readers regret that they cannot know Jesus, James, John, Martha, and Mary in person. The best aids must bridge the gap of generations. Through these preachers' studies, readers draw near to Elijah, Isaiah, Paul, and the rest. The volume is a popular devotional work of its day, built from the pulpit's character sketches.
54773-excursions-in-art-and-letters:
Excursions in Art and Letters gathers essays by William Wetmore Story. Houghton, Mifflin published the third edition in 1893. The copyright dates to 1891. Story was a sculptor and poet long resident in Rome. His other books include poems and a novel.

Five pieces fill the volume. The first treats Michelangelo at length. The second treats Phidias and the Elgin marbles. A third studies the art of casting in plaster among the ancients. A conversation with Marcus Aurelius follows. The last piece attacks distortions of the English stage in Macbeth. The Michelangelo essay opens in a grand style. The death of the pagan gods, Story writes, was the deathblow of pagan art.
54959-the-pearl-fishers:
H De Vere Stacpoole wrote The Pearl Fishers, issued in New York by John Lane Company in MCMXV. Stacpoole had earlier written The Presentation and The Blue Lagoon. Copyright rests in nineteen fifteen with Street and Smith and with John Lane. Chapter one is Alone. Chapter two is The Island. A South Seas pearl lagoon is the scene. Schumer is the heavy figure of the tale.

The Secret of the Lagoon, Schumer Story, and Dredging follow the landing. Risk of War and The Black Pearl bring the stakes up. The Last of the Wreck and A Week Work fill the middle. The Schooner, The Punishment, and The Power of Schumer deepen the grip. Mostly about Pearls, Plans, and Schumer Goes Away follow. The First of the Two Pearls begins the close. Sea readers get a lagoon adventure of greed and pearls.
54999-music-and-its-masters:
Music and Its Masters is a book on the great men of tone by Boise, with six prints of their faces. It came out at two great towns of the trade in the first years of the last age. Its rights were held the year past by its house.

A kin book is praised at its front: a work on the great band works and their sense, now in its third form. That work takes the chief band works of the great men, it says, and shows their marks with bits of the score. It shows the stamp of each man and the aim of his art. This book does the same for the men them selves: the bard of the ring, and his peers in tone.
55018-good-times-with-the-juniors:
Lilian Heath made a book of gay group fun for church youth clubs. The book's rights date to 1904 with a Boston and Chicago house. Its list runs in A to Z form by each treat's name. The Advertising Carnival stands near the back of that list. A Barrel Brigade and a Bird Social lead the B names.

Handkerchief drills and a bean stalk climb fill the gay set. Cinderella's guest night and a Jack Frost night stand in the row. Flower shows, ad nights, and good luck nights mix in the fun. First of April tricks and valentine makes add spice in turn. Youth heads get a full year of planned cheer in one book. Each treat bears its full steps.
55274-the-wind-jammers:
The Wind-Jammers is a set of sea tales by Jenkins Hains, with rights of eighteen ninety-four. Hains was known past three sea books of like name. Past fifteen tales fill the book, from the first mate of a war ship to a tale past a cape reef. A plate shows a ship at claw past a cape.

The first tale is told by a boy past sixteen set to work in a ship yard. His task was to bear drink to the men and to hand out bolts and pegs. So he came to know the men at work on the vast hull of a war ship and their ways. One day a loose butt flew from its hold and hurt a man so bad he was laid off. A new hand of past thirty years took his place, grave of mouth and strange of eye.
55570-postal-riders-and-raiders:
W H Gantz wrote Postal Riders and Raiders under a pen name. He called himself The Man On The Ladder. The Independent Postal League issued the book at Chicago in 1912. It sold for one dollar and fifty cents, prepaid. The league sat at 5037 Indiana Avenue. Gantz kept the copyright that year.

Are we fools, the title page asks in bold type. If not, why act foolishly, it presses. Rail, express, and post men treat the public as fools, he claims. The foreword builds on one plain bet about readers. Each reader can think, and has the habit of it, he says. A man who lets others think for him should stop here, he warns. A fiery brief against the mail order of his day, the book rallies small shippers to fight back.
55626-science-in-short-chapters:
W Mattieu Williams wrote Science in Short Chapters, issued in New York by John B Alden in eighteen eighty three. Williams held fellowships in the Royal Astronomical Society and the Chemical Society. He had earlier written The Fuel of the Sun and Through Norway with a Knapsack. A preface dated Willesden, September eighteen eighty two, explains the design. The pieces are reprints of scattered notes and essays.

Williams kept busy readers in view, he says, selecting subjects of interest to folk who prefer sober fact to sensational fiction. His highest aim was clearness and simplicity with some attempt at philosophy, he adds. Chapters treat the fuel of the sun, Dr Siemens theory of the sun, and another world down here. The origin of lunar volcanoes, sun spots and climates, and the radiometer follow. General readers get short, plain science essays.
55635-goose-quill-papers:
Louise Imogen Guiney published Goose-Quill Papers at Boston in 1885. Roberts Brothers issued the book of short essays. Guiney gave the volume to Oliver Wendell Holmes in homage. A piece on the good repute of the apple opens the contents. An open letter to the moon follows later. Notes made by Troilus, gently, sit mid-book.

Essays treat teaching one's grandmother how to suck eggs. Old haunts, free thoughts on books, and a November festival appear. Pieces on graveyards, garden folk, and the beauty of idleness close the list. The garret gets its own short essay at the end. The apple essay starts with Atalanta and the apple of discord. Bragi and Hercules enter within its first lines. Light, bookish essays like these show the familiar essay alive in 1880s America.
55784-two-strangers:
Two Strangers is a novel by Mrs Oliphant, printed at New York by Fenno and Company with copyright of 1895. The opening scene is a family conversation about a newcomer. Ralph asks his mother who this young widow is, that he hears so much about. He can understand Lucy's rapture over any stranger, but his mother's enthusiasm surprises him.

The mother defends herself with dry humour. Lucy will not let the phrase stand. The stranger is a darling, as nice as nice can be: pretty, good and clever. The widow's arrival in a quiet circle, and the curiosity she excites, set Oliphant's machinery in motion. Two strangers, in the title's sense, are meeting: the widow in this world, and the world itself to her.
5592-the-complete-short-works-of-georg-e:
Georg Ebers's Complete Short Works gathers five shorter pieces: In the Blue Pike, A Question, The Elixir, The Greylock, and The Nuts. The collection opens with In the Blue Pike. There a rough fellow's curse is understood only by a sickly girl and a red-haired woman leading him by a chain like a tame bear. Nuremberg magistrates had earlier had Cyriax's tongue cut out.

The set ranges from wandering singers and pilgrims to fairy tale and romance, showing Ebers beyond his long Egyptian and German novels. Readers get a varied sampler of his shorter fiction, from street crowds to enchanted lakes, in one volume.
5600-the-historical-romances-of-georg-eb:
This omnibus gathers Georg Ebers's historical romances in one great volume, from Uarda and An Egyptian Princess through The Sisters, Joshua, Cleopatra, and The Emperor to Homo Sum, Serapis, and Arachne. Later romances follow: The Bride of the Nile, A Thorny Path, In the Fire of the Forge, and Margery. Barbara Blomberg, A Word Only a Word, and The Burgomaster's Wife join them, with shorter works and the autobiography completing the set.

The collection opens with Uarda, dedicated in verse to a fostering hand that released Ebers from suffering's grasp. Readers get Ebers's whole fictional world in one place, from ancient Egypt and Rome to medieval Nuremberg and besieged Leyden. It suits anyone who wants the novelist entire.
56135-tobacco-growing-curing-manufacturi:
Tobacco: Growing, Curing, and Manufacturing, edited by Warnford Lock, is a handbook for planters in all parts of the world. Spon printed the book in London and New York in 1886. The preface calls tobacco one of the most paying crops of warm lands.

Lock notes that the crop is grown widely on the mainland of Europe and had even been urged for British farms. Yet no English book on the theme alone had come out for nearly thirty years. Inquiries from men keen to start a tobacco estate had piled up with no guide to send them to. French, German, Dutch, and other planters all had handbooks of their own. This volume fills the gap for British settlers, and a book list at the end surveys the field.
56161-the-three-furlongers:
The Three Furlongers, published in 1914, is Sheila Kaye-Smith's novel of Sparrow Hall, where Surrey, Kent and Sussex meet in the woods. In Britain the book appeared as Three Against the World. Twilight falls over fields in three counties as the tale opens. Janet Furlonger waits in the kitchen, tall and proud in her terrible old clothes.

The first book, Three Against the World, moves through Sparrow Hall, rain, thick woods and a sermon on forgiveness. The second, The World Against the Three, brings the letter that did not come and woods at night. Kaye-Smith, the Sussex novelist, binds her three young people to one house and one landscape, and tests their love against the world outside.
5631-patty-s-suitors:
Carolyn Wells wrote Patty's Suitors, illustrated by E. C. Caswell, as another book about Patty, following the Patty books and the Marjorie books. Contents run from a valentine party and a telephone call through the Hepworths at home. A perfectly good joke, three pictures, and Princess Poppycheek follow, then suitors, a house party, Eddie Bell, and quarantine.

Later chapters bring meeting it bravely, a surprise, Sister Bee, Kenneth, an invitation, Belle Harcourt, May Day, moonlight, and a ride home in the runabout. Wells writes schoolgirl society with humor. Young readers get a lively romance of parties, suitors, and friendship.
56346-a-book-of-american-explorers:
A Book of American Explorers is a set of the tales of the first find men of the main of the west. Its text was writ in a day when the spell of words was not yet set firm. That note stands in the host text past the front. Spell forms in the book are thus left as they stood in their day. Marks in the text point to the words of the men who made the host form.

The first words of the book set out its root. It has at all times seem to me, the hand says, that the tales of the first find men are of a rare kind. Those men came to the shores of the new main with no lore of what lay past them.
56437-rice-papers:
Norris wrote tales of China from three years of work in that land. His book, Rice Papers, came out in London in 1905. He gave it to the chief and staff of the ship Tamar. A Chinese saw heads it: train your sight and you shall eat well. Norris grants his tales are not true, nor built on fact.

They were made to pass long hours in a glad way, he says. If they give the reader half that joy, he is paid in full. Ports, mess decks, and shore leave fill the tales' world. Wit and salt air mark his short, light prose. Such books gave home folk a taste of the far east run. Each tale stands on its own.
56593-contemporary-composers:
Daniel Gregory Mason published Contemporary Composers with Macmillan in 1918, gathering essays on the leading composers of his day. Portraits of Strauss, Elgar, Debussy, and d'Indy illustrate the book.

An opening essay, Democracy and Music, asks how the great social changes of the nineteenth century bear on modern music. Mason notes that music passed from the patronage of nobles, who kept men like Haydn in service, into the hands of all the people. Chapters then take up Richard Strauss, Edward Elgar, Claude Debussy, and Vincent d'Indy in turn, and a last chapter treats music in America. Mason writes as a critic who wants readers to think, not merely to agree.
5662-the-potato-child-others:
