Mrs. Charles J. Woodbury wrote The Potato Child and Others, a small story collection opening with its title tale. Elsie, a tender-hearted little girl, lives a hard and solitary life. When Miss Amanda selects her from the girls at The Home, the motherly matron feels sorry, knowing a kind word goes a great way with Elsie. Miss Amanda, plainly, will speak few words, kind or unkind, yet The Home is more than full.

Other stories include A Story That Never Ends and A Nazareth Christmas. Readers get gentle, old-fashioned tales of children, homes, and kindness, told with sentiment and care.
56671-the-last-three-soldiers:
William Henry Shelton wrote The Last Three Soldiers, issued in New York by the Century Company in eighteen ninety seven. Shelton gave the story to his young friends Gussie and Genie Demarest. Twenty five chapters fill the book. A front plate shows Philip crying, There they are, by the end of the house. The plot is a Civil War what if tale.

Chapter one is Completing the Line, then The Old Man of the Mountain. A Day of Discoveries, The Cipher Code, and Messages of Dire Disasters follow. The three soldiers make a remarkable resolution that ends in a battle. The Plateau Receives a Name and The Prisoners fill the middle. A mishap proves not always a misfortune, and a cave of bats brings wonder. Boys get three lads holding a mountain post alone.
57002-the-challoners:
E F Benson wrote The Challoners, a novel published in nineteen hundred and four. Benson was known for Dodo, and the book reached a third edition. A line from Browning's Guardian Angel stands at its head.

The tale opens on a midsummer evening at a vicarage, as heat gives way to soft warmth. Helen Challoner half sits, half lies in a long chair by the croquet lawn. A breeze from the flower-beds ruffles her hair as she reads a red-covered book. She reads with deep, lost focus. Family life, love, and social pressure in a quiet English world shape the story Benson tells.
5707-the-boy-scout-aviators:
The Boy Scout Aviators follows Harry Fleming and Dick Mercer, two boys caught between nations and new flying machines. Harry is an American abroad. He tells Dick that since he cannot be at home, he would rather be where he is than anywhere else. Dick answers with good-humored English teasing about what it means to be American. From that friendly opening, the story moves toward aviation adventure.

Readers get early flying lore mixed with scout ideals: courage, loyalty, and quick thinking under pressure. The book belongs to a wave of boys' adventure fiction that treated airplanes as wonders still fresh enough to thrill. Young readers who enjoy vintage aviation tales will find brisk action and earnest heroes, with friendship carrying the story between flights.
5730-friends-and-helpers:
Sarah Eddy compiled Friends and Helpers in 1899 to teach children to treat living creatures with considerate kindness. Her preface states the aim plainly: children should appreciate the services of man's helpers in the animal world, a lesson she felt many homes left entirely untaught. The book runs in three parts, gathering stories, poems, and lessons about animals that work beside people.

Readers meet horses, dogs, and farm animals as partners rather than tools, with tales that praise patience and gentle handling. The tone is earnest and humane, typical of humane education in its era. Teachers and families will find a useful historical reader on kindness to animals, and children will enjoy stories that ask them to notice the creatures around them.
57427-the-sheep-stealers:
Violet Jacob wrote The Sheep-Stealers, for Heinemann at London in 1902. The first edition came in August, and a second impression in September. Jacob gives the book to her mother on the dedication page. Contents open with the two communities of her Welsh border ground. Rhys, the dipping-pool, and a place called the yew-stump follow.

A chapter called Rebecca nods to the toll-gate riots of Wales. A dead man and a live coward, and a trip to Abergavenny, come next. Master and man, two meetings, and forget-me-nots fill the middle. The Brecon coach, seven snow-men, and the uses of a cast shoe stand late. Walters goes to chapel in the later contents. A bad debt and the way of the transgressor close the list. Jacob gives border farms, chapel, and crime in one tale.
57478-index-for-works-of-arthur-colton-h:
David Widger compiled an Index for Works of Arthur Colton, with links to all chapters of his books. Eight works are listed at the front. The Belted Seas leads the set. The Debatable Land, Bennie Ben Cree, and Port Argent follow. The Delectable Mountains and Tioba close the main list.

Chapter lists for each book fill the index. The Belted Seas runs to fifteen chapters, many told as Captain Buckingham's tale. Heads name the Hebe Maitland, the Hotel Helen Mar, and the loss of the Anaconda. King Julius and the voyage of the Voodoo sit in the middle. The Cruise of the Violetta and Harps Hung Up in Babylon end the set. The index serves readers who move through Colton's books in digital form.
57616-the-secret-of-wyvern-towers:
T W Speight wrote The Secret of Wyvern Towers, run complete in The Argosy, volume twenty six, number one, December eighteen ninety seven. Frank A Munsey published the magazine. The tale bears copyright eighteen ninety seven. Fifteen chapters fill the number. Felix Drelincourt owns Wyvern Towers and Barras Wood. Chapter one is Very Strange Tidings.

Two persons proclaimed themselves guilty of a fearful crime, the head note says. On a sunny May morning about forty years ago, Drelincourt stepped into a glade of Barras Wood. He stood a little over six feet, the tale notes. A vagabond life stood in peril from the crime. An unexpected legacy blotted out an identity, the head note adds. Sir John Conducts the Inquiry and A Backward Glance follow. An Amazing Confession and Waiting for the Verdict deepen the mystery. Readers get a full sensation novel in one issue.
57738-memoirs-of-eighty-years:
Memoirs of Eighty Years, by Gordon Hake, is the life story of a physician. Bentley printed it in London in 1892, as publishers in ordinary to the Queen. A couplet heads the title page: men, could they shun death, would be their own posterity.

The contents read like a diary of the life. Birth and parentage open it, with schooling begun eighty-four years back and still, he jokes, incomplete. The obscure roots of the Hakes and Gordons come next. A sister, a brother, an aunt, and Yorkshire kin fill the family chapters. One uncle, William Clarke, governed two schools and placed Hake and a Pollock in them. School at Hertford, measles and scarlet fever, and a boy sent home to die fill one chapter. He lived, and ran back to mischief. Seaford holidays with cousins close the early chapters.
57939-the-fall-river-tragedy-a-history-o:
The Fall River Tragedy, by Edwin Porter, gives a history of the Borden murders. Buffinton published it at Fall River in 1893. Porter was police reporter of the Fall River Globe. The title page calls it a plain statement of the material facts. Original engravings fill the book. Contents run to thirty two chapters. The first treats the discovery of the murders. Police searches of the house and the Borden family follow. A funeral, a reward, and a sermon on the crime come in turn.

Later chapters track Lizzie Borden's arrest and her plea of not guilty. The preliminary hearing and the superior court trial are reported day by day. Judge Dewey's charge to the jury closes the list. A hitherto unpublished account of the Trickey-McHenry affair is promised on the title page.
57973-the-hurricane-hunters:
Hurricane Hunters is a book on storm flying by Ivan Ray Tannehill, published at New York in 1956. Dodd, Mead and Company issued the book, copyrighted in 1955 by its author. It is illustrated with photographs of the work it describes in the text. 

Tannehill dedicates the book to his daughter and son in law, Doris and Bill. His acknowledgment says the narrative itself names the many men who furnished information for it. They gave it in personal interviews, by correspondence, or in their official reports of flights. The subject is the flying of aircraft into hurricanes to measure them from inside the storm. By the 1950s those flights were a settled, dangerous duty of American weather services. Tannehill, a weather bureau man, wrote the first popular account of the hunters and their machines at the height of the postwar storm warning effort.
580-the-pickwick-papers:
Charles Dickens follows Samuel Pickwick and his club through England in this comic classic, his first novel. The Pickwickians travel by coach, attend card parties, shoot badly, fall in love, and land in the Fleet prison over a breach of promise suit. Sam Weller, Pickwick's sharp servant, steals scene after scene.

Dickens writes in rich, bustling prose, mixing farce, ghost tales, and courtroom satire. Eatanswill's election, Dingley Dell's Christmas, and the Fleet's grim humor mark the road. The book endures as a joyful portrait of old England, where a kind, foolish gentleman learns the world by blundering through it.
5803-not-that-it-matters:
Milne gathers light essays in Not That It Matters. They range from the pleasure of writing and Acacia Road to a library and a chase. Superstition, the charm of golf, goldfish, and Saturday to Monday follow. A household book, Milne suggests in a prefatory note, means a book everybody in the house can enjoy, and these pieces aim at that shared pleasure. The pond, a seventeen-year-old, and further domestic subjects follow.

Readers get Milne's gentle, witty prose on ordinary life, where a walk, a game, or a goldfish becomes a small essay. The tone is urbane without being distant, and the humor depends on observation rather than punch lines. Fans of Milne beyond his children's books will enjoy these pieces, and general readers will find a companionable volume for short, pleasant reading.
58104-observations-on-coroners:
William Hewitt, a surgeon of North Walsham, wrote a plea on the office of coroner, printed for him in Norwich in 1852. He addresses the book to the Home Secretary. His charge is that men take an office whose duties they are not fit to perform.

The cases he tells come from his own neighbourhood. His theme is the inquest, the jury's search into the cause of a fellow creature's death. Such a search, he holds, calls for medical knowledge at its head. A coroner without that training may miss the very facts the court exists to find. The book is a small, sharp call for reform in one corner of English law.
58111-the-structure-and-habits-of-spider:
The Structure and Habits of Spiders, by Emerton, was published in Boston in 1883, from an 1878 copyright. Emerton says his aim is a plain account of the best known habits of spiders, with as much anatomy and sorting as those habits need. Tales of deadly poison, vast size, and uncanny wisdom are left out as doubtful.

The spinning and flying parts rest chiefly on Blackwall and Menge, and the trap-door parts on Moggridge. Most figures are new, cut from Emerton's own drawings by photography. Chapter one covers feet, jaws, breathing holes, spinnerets, eyes, and poison glands. Later chapters treat eating, biting, webs, and families, in a calm, fact-first style.
58222-the-destinies-of-the-stars:
The Destinies of the Stars is a work on the fate of the universe by Svante Arrhenius, head of the Nobel Institute at Stockholm. He had won the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 1903. The book was turned from the Swedish by Fries, and issued by Putnam's Sons in 1918.

The translator's preface traces a widening path. Arrhenius began with the very small, in the study of salts and currents. In time his thought broadened to the very large. The whence and whither of the whole material universe became his ruling passion. The book sets out that large view for the lay reader. Stars are born, burn, and fade in its pages, and man's place among them is the close concern of the work.
58279-modern-french-masters:
Marie Van Vorst wrote essays on modern French masters of painting, printed in Paris and New York in 1904. Alexander Harrison wrote the preface. The essays first ran in the Pall Mall Magazine, and Van Vorst inscribes the book to her friend George Halkett in thanks for its hospitality. Her Paris address stands in the dedication.

Puvis de Chavannes leads, with his Rhone and Saone at Lyons and his Saint Genevieve series at the Pantheon. Cazin, Rodin, Besnard, and Steinlen follow with full plates. In the midst of a stormy period of political tumult, Puvis passed from his country's life into its history, she writes. The essays give English readers a warm, close view of French art at its height.
58280-fools-of-fortune-or-gambling-and-g:
Fools of Fortune, or Gambling and Gamblers, is an exposé by John Philip Quinn. Quinn writes as a man who gamed for twenty-five years himself. He tenders the book to atone for years of tricking his fellow men. The title page promises a history of the vice in both hemispheres. It also pledges a full baring of frauds used by sharp men.

Professional gamblers, confidence men, and bunko steerers stand named in that pledge. Quinn calls gambling the vice that has snared more men than drink. Its pull works in secret and strikes at a root in most breasts, he says. Homes wrecked and lives blighted fill his count of its harms. Front pieces praise the work from men of law and public life. The book warns the green hand while it names each cheat plainly.
5829-the-moneychangers:
Upton Sinclair opens The Moneychangers in a business call, as Lucy wants to visit Montague's office to talk business, but he spares her the trouble. Montague calls the next morning at her apartment before going downtown. Lucy shows him her papers there. They include her father's will, a list of his property, accounts, and the rent roll of her properties in New Orleans. Money, inheritance, and power frame the novel.

Readers follow Sinclair's exposé of finance, as personal fortunes meet Wall Street schemes and the men who move markets. The novel favors plot and argument over lyricism, letting documents and deals drive the drama. It suits readers of Sinclair's muckraking fiction, and anyone curious about how early twentieth-century novels indicted American money power.
58355-the-three-brothers:
Eden Phillpotts, author of Children of the Mist and The American Prisoner, wrote this Dartmoor novel. Macmillan published it at New York in January 1909, dedicated to his brother Herbert Macdonald Phillpotts as a tribute of great affection. Book one opens on the moor in a clear May noon.

From Great Trowlesworthy's crown of granite the world extends to the moor-edge and the horizons of the sea. Dartmoor soaks her fill of sunshine; the heather still wears its winter coat while spring gorse leaps like running flame, and crow-foot stars the water's brink. A road runs across the waste to where the bridge of Cadworthy saddles the Plym, below Wigford Down and the gorges of Dewerstone. Phillpotts notes the change in the granites where kaolin, or china clay, emerges from their perishing stone. On the tor above, a girl sings with the running water and the lark.
58417-the-battle-of-the-rivers:
Edmund Dane wrote The Battle of the Rivers, issued by Hodder and Stoughton in London, New York, and Toronto in MCMXIV. The book belongs to the Daily Telegraph War Books. A prefatory note states the scale of the campaign. Chapter one is The German Plans. The retreat from Mons is handled elsewhere in the series, Dane notes.

On a scale before unknown in Western Europe, the succession of events named the Battle of the Rivers shows strategy and tactics of absorbing interest, Dane says. Strange and daring episodes fill the drama, he adds. Events that might seem confused fit into a clear sequence of causes and consequences, he holds. The story treats the German drive and the stand on the Marne and Aisne. War readers get an early, clear account of the nineteen fourteen campaign in France.
58446-sons-and-daughters:
Mrs Oliphant's Sons and Daughters, a novel in its second edition from Blackwood at Edinburgh and London in 1891, opens in a Harley Street library. Burton offers his son Gervase a share in the business; Gervase declines, disliking the way it is worked and pleading his training. The father calls the prejudice ridiculous: he chose that training, the ideal English education of Eton and Oxford, sparing no expense, with a Highland moor taken for the shooting and travel abroad.

The two are all their family, the mother long dead, the father living for the boy and the business. Gervase has done everything expected, at school and college, without disappointing anyone. Oliphant sets the classic Victorian knot: a fortune built by trade, a gentleman made by education, and the son's refusal to join them. The library, book-lined and lived-in, frames the argument.
58450-george-edmund-street-unpublished-n:
Georgiana King edited notes and papers of architect George Edmund Street. The Hispanic Society of America issued the book in 1916. King thanks the architect son for loan of notebooks and drawings. She says they gave her a close sense of his temper and art.

Contents hold a life essay, then tours in central Italy in notes. Long parts treat French churches, from Tours to Le Puy. An appendix adds a stone note and north German churches. Plates show Zamora, Leon, Salamanca, and Cologne in fine, clear views for the reader.
5848-the-flyers:
The Flyers opens at the Faraway Club on a cold, thick drizzle of an early spring night, with a biting wind sending chills to the marrow. The weather keeps indoors the few hardy members who have haunted the clubhouse since the season opened a week before. Not more than a dozen loyal devotees of open-air sports lounge about the big clubhouse. Three or four figures gather as the story begins.

Readers enter a club tale of fellowship, sport, and the longing for fair weather and far places. The opening favors atmosphere over action, letting drizzle, wind, and club talk set the mood. The book suits readers who enjoy club stories and early twentieth-century tales of friendship, where the promise of adventure hangs just beyond a rainy window.
58511-the-romantic-composers:
The Romantic Composers is a work of music history by Daniel Gregory Mason, author of From Grieg to Brahms and Beethoven and His Forerunners. Macmillan first published it in 1906, and Mason revised the copyright in 1934. A youthful water colour of Robert Schumann fronts the book. Its motto is Schumann's own: consciously or unconsciously, he wrote, a new school is being founded on the basis of Beethoven and Schubert.

A passage preserved in the copy sets the period. Historians of music, Mason writes, speak of the first half or three-quarters of the nineteenth century as the Romantic Period. The romantic composers are those who follow Beethoven. They include Schubert, Schumann, Mendelssohn, Berlioz, Chopin, and Liszt, among some others. Mason expects the school Schumann foresaw to mark a special epoch in the history of art.
58798-the-gun-runners:
Ralph Williams weaves a time-travel crime tale in Worlds of If Science Fiction, December 1954. The headnote names George Dolan's four problems at once.

They are a time-translator, a girl named Moirta from out of this world, the gun runners, and his own life. The runners are professionals. Their plan is sound but for one minor detail. They pick the middle twentieth century as their source of supply. Its guns are well made and reliable. Its controls are still loose enough for quiet buying. In their own day, banned time travel draws severe punishment. The profits match the risks. The headnote asks what a man can do with a victory at the far end of a bridge 10,000 years long.
58831-cordova-a-city-of-the-moors:
Cordova: A City of the Moors is a travel and history volume by Calvert and Gallichan, published in London in 1907 in the Spanish Series with 160 illustrations. Calvert dedicates the book to the Duke of Sotomayor, in thanks for hospitality in Spain. The chapters move from the Moorish capture of the city through the Omeyyad dynasty to the building of the great mosque.

Later chapters walk the Court of Oranges, the mosque, the cathedral and the Moorish bridge. A closing chapter gathers illustrious natives of Cordova, and two appendices treat the mosque again in detail. The illustration list runs to views of the bridge, the market street, water-carriers, muleteers and the provincial museum, making the book as much a picture tour as a history.
58856-throne-makers:
Throne-Makers is a set of biographical essays by William Roscoe Thayer. Houghton, Mifflin published it in 1899. The title papers treat four makers of nations. They are Bismarck, Napoleon the Third, Kossuth, and Garibaldi. A second group offers shorter portraits.

The Bismarck essay opens with a broad claim. One by one the nations come to their own, Thayer writes. Our age has seen the elevation of Prussia. Bismarck's mission was to complete the work of Frederick and Stein. Thayer praises and blames the Prussian system in turn. It turns men into machines, he says. Its soldiers and clerks are thorough beyond compare. The portraits that follow treat Carlyle, Tintoret, and Giordano Bruno. Bryant closes the book.
58942-in-the-dozy-hours-and-other-papers:
Agnes Repplier wrote In the Dozy Hours and Other Papers, issued in Boston and New York by Houghton, Mifflin and Company in eighteen ninety four. Repplier had earlier written Books and Men, Points of View, and Essays in Idleness, each at a dollar twenty five. She gave the book to Annis Lee Wister. Twenty two papers fill the volume. In the Dozy Hours stands first. A Kitten stands second.

Papers treat At the Novelist Table, In Behalf of Parents, and a Latin titled piece. A Note on Mirrors, Gifts, and Humor, English and American, follow. The Discomforts of Luxury, Lectures, and Reviewers and Reviewed fill the middle. Pastels, Guests, Sympathy, and Opinions follow. The Children Age, A Forgotten Poet, and Dialogues close the set. Essay lovers get Repplier crisp, bookish wit at her best.
59302-pioneers:
Pioneers is a science fiction story by Basil Wells. It appeared in Worlds of If Science Fiction in June 1955. A head note frames its theme as the morality of deception. Deception can be good or bad depending on circumstances, it says. Dorav and Tzal had the right way of looking at it. The circumstances were undoubtedly prime, the note adds. The story opens as a month long hibernation ends. Dorav Brink wakes on rubber and plastic couches in a small room. A feeling of completeness and achievement sweeps over him.

He has escaped Earth's mechanized domes and their endless boredom. Here on Sulle the Second there would be adventure and work in plenty. A dozen couches fill the room, most of them occupied. His gaze searches the huddled figures for the girl Rea. Wells opens a colonizing tale of sleepers waking.
59310-history-of-the-post-office-packet-:
History of the Post Office Packet Service covers the years seventeen ninety three to eighteen fifteen. Arthur Norway compiled the history from records, chiefly official ones. Macmillan of London and New York issued the book in eighteen ninety five. A front view shows the Windsor Castle packet under Captain Rogers.

Norway thanks a Falmouth lady for leave to copy four pictures she holds. Two show the Duke of Marlborough in action with the Primrose ship. Others show the Windsor Castle and the Hinchinbrooke packets at sea. Burton of the Old Curiosity Shop at Falmouth also lent aid there. Readers get the story of mail packets in the French war years.
59375-the-ethicators:
The Ethicators is a tale of the far worlds by Willard Marsh, first put out in a sheet of such tales in the eighth month of nineteen fifty five. The head note of the tale sets its hook in a few lines. Its crew were used to slow forms of life, but this was the worst they had met. Still, it is the charge of a man of the cloth to bring light where there is none.

The crew come from the world of a star they do not call by the name men give it. They call it, straight, the Sun, as home is Earth to them. They are the top beast kind of their world, and they call their kind by the name of man. They roam the stars in search of souls to save.
59421-chushingura-or-the-treasury-of-loy:
Chushingura, or the treasury of loyal retainers, is a Japanese play by three named authors, in a translation by Jukichi Inouye. The third edition was issued at Tokyo in 1917, with illustrations. A large woodblock fold out by a famed print maker stands at the front. It shows the faithful ronin withdrawing to Takanawa, its caption given in Japanese.

In his preface the translator tells the book's own history. Seventeen years before, he had issued a version with three acts left out, to keep the thread of the story unbroken. That small edition soon sold out, and a publisher asked him to touch up the old work. Instead he made a new and complete translation of the play. The famous tale of loyal retainers thus reaches English readers whole.
59485-wintering-bees-in-cellars:
E F Phillips and George S Demuth wrote Wintering Bees in Cellars, Farmers Bulletin 1014 of the United States Department of Agriculture, issued in September 1918. Phillips was the bureau's bee expert and Demuth his aide. The Bureau of Entomology gave the work. A map shows where the method fits.

Cellar wintering works well when the cellar keeps bees calm, the text says. It fits lands where winter cold holds near twenty five degrees. The cellar roof must sit below the frost line. Walls must be shielded at all points. Heat in the hives should hold at least fifty two degrees. No damp should gather in the hives. Bees go in after a good flight in late November and come out when fresh pollen comes.
59516-the-scamperers:
The Scamperers is a science fiction story by Charles Stearns, taken from Worlds of If magazine for June 1956. Wellesley was ordered to check on deviants or mutants. The evidence was often subtle, and he knew he could not afford to take a chance. The Earthman came to Ophir in the season of aphelion, when the binary suns were cold serpent's eyes above the chill mists.

Ophir's fern forests, craggy young mountains, and silent oceans spread below. Its magnificent organ-pipe cities were legend only: giant towers of shell, hollow as the hopes they inspired in the first planeteers two hundred years before. Small, mindless crustaceans built them. Wellesley's own destination is a small, shabby corporate plantation called Aidennsport. A note preserved in the copy gives his ship's course. It described an elliptical orbit bringing it near Ophir once every seventh sidereal month.
59549-signs-wonders:
Signs and Wonders is a book of short pieces by Beresford. Putnam published the work at New York in 1921. Beresford dedicates the volume to Walter de la Mare, and a verse from de la Mare's poem Fog stands at the front. A list of the author's earlier books fills a full page.

A prologue in play form, The Appearance of Man, opens the book. Two men and a woman meet and trade small talk about Putney and family health. Behind them a nebula spins slowly across an endless backdrop. Prehistoric beasts wander through the talk as if nothing were odd. The pieces that follow mix tales and sketches with odd twists. Titles include The Cage, The Perfect Smile, The Miracle, and The Night of Creation.
59806-the-dragon-in-shallow-waters:
V Sackville-West wrote a novel in 1922, having already published Heritage. A Chinese proverb gives the book its title and its opening note: the dragon in shallow waters became the butt of shrimps. The story opens in a factory gallery five hundred feet long. Iron girders span the roof in gaunt lines.

A drone of machinery fills the air, softened by the floor below. Three chimneys outside pour out black plumes over flooded country. Men push hand trucks between great square vats, each as large as a room. They look like pygmies beside the plant. Sackville-West sets human lives against heavy industry from the first page.
59813-the-footpath-way-an-anthology-for-:
The Footpath Way is an anthology for walkers published in London in nineteen eleven. Sidgwick and Jackson issued it, with an introduction by Hilaire Belloc. The pages collect prose and verse about walking from writers across three centuries.

The contents run from Sidney Smith and William Hazlitt on going a journey to Thoreau's Walking and the Wild. Stevenson's Walking Tours and Whitman's Song of the Open Road also appear. Wordsworth, Dickens, Borrow, Scott, Walton, De Quincey, and John Burroughs fill out the list. The opening essay praises the mountain walk as an antidote to city poison. It argues that a walker alone with nature is in good company. The anthology helped fix walking in print as a deliberate, literary pastime.
59822-epidemics-resulting-from-wars:
Friedrich Prinzing wrote a study of epidemics resulting from wars, edited by Harald Westergaard of Copenhagen and printed at Oxford in 1916. The book belongs to a Carnegie Endowment series on the causes and results of war. An introductory note by John Bates Clark explains the program. A conference at Berne in August 1911 had planned the inquiry.

The division behind the series sought thorough, scientific study of warfare. Its reports would show the direct and indirect results of war in print. If the evils of war prove larger and its benefits smaller than commonly thought, the director argues, such studies should convince. Prinzing's volume supplies the medical side of that ledger.
59895-the-four-stragglers:
The Four Stragglers is a war adventure novel by Frank Packard, printed at Toronto in 1923. A prologue, The Four of Them, opens the tale. The crash of guns, a flare across the heavens: battle, dismay, death, and a night of chaos. Four men lie in a thicket, and one speaks of a bloody Hun prison.

Another answers that they are lost, and very tired. The books that follow carry the four onward. Book One, Shadow Varne, jumps three years later, to gold plate and a writing on the wall. Book Two, The Isle of Prey, brings a mad millionaire, a man in a mask, and a gutter-snipe. Book Three, The Penalty, turns on a bronze key and the time-lock of the sea. Packard, the railroad novelist, spins his yarn from a lost patrol to a treasure hunt without pausing for breath.
60129-a-visit-to-the-saro-and-shera-yo-g:
C G E Mannerheim published an account of a visit to two small tribes of the Nanshan mountains, printed at Helsingfors in 1911. During his Central Asia expedition of 1906 to 1908 he spent some days among the Sarö and Shera Yögurs. Together they are called Huang fan, the yellow barbarians, in Chinese usage. They live near Kanchow and Hsuchow.

Mannerheim offers extracts from his journal to spread light on these little known peoples. A parallel vocabulary of both tribes' words follows. He adds body measurements and photographs. Some pictures come from his expedition, others from an ethnographic collection he made. The pamphlet is field science in brief form.
60149-pride-and-his-prisoners:
A L O E wrote Pride and His Prisoners, issued at London, Edinburgh, and New York by Thomas Nelson and Sons. Thirty chapters carry the tale. A front print named A Terrible Danger shows page two hundred and thirty. Four pictures in all aid the text. The Haunted Dwelling opens the plot.

Resisted yet Returning and Snares come next in the chapter heads. A glance into the cottage and a visit to the hall follow. A brother's effort, a quarrel, and a fatal step build the middle. Conscience asleep and a magazine mark the turn. The ascent, in the clouds, and soaring above pride name the climb out. A broken chain, an awful crisis, and the spirit laid close the moral tale. Faith and pride clash in a home frame for young readers.
6015-captain-macklin-his-memoirs:
Richard Harding Davis gives his young soldier's memoirs, with the narrator admitting it may seem presumptuous for so young a man to write his life. Most men wait until they have achieved something or reached old age, but the soldier's trade is hazardous, and tomorrow may not come.

Macklin calls soldiering the noblest profession a man can follow, and his pages run from West Point through Sagua la Grande, moonlit camps, and barrack yards. Davis writes with a reporter's briskness and a soldier's pride. The memoir treats youth, duty, and danger as reasons to set the record down now.
60278-the-thirteen-travellers:
Hugh Walpole gathered twelve short tales as The Thirteen Travellers in nineteen twenty-one, giving the book to Joseph Hergesheimer. Walpole had written novels such as The Captives and Jeremy. A note states that no figure in the book is drawn from a living person.

Each tale takes one traveller, from Absalom Jay and Fanny Close to Mr Nix and Lizzie Rand. One tale is called Nobody, and the last is Bombastes Furioso. Jay, a cousin of John Beaminster, came to note in smart London circles in the eighteen nineties. Walpole sketches each life with speed, wit, and a keen eye for social rank.
60384-the-poors:
The Poors, a science fiction story by Harry Lorayne, ran in Worlds of If in October 1957. Its tag line warns that television can change a life more than one thinks. The world has waited months for the first personal visit from outer space. Sixty thousand people crowd the Earth Interspace Airport behind ropes and guards.

Mr Kramvit of Planet Six is the guest. Fourth Vice President Vincent J Carrowick has been picked as his guide. The people of Six speak English well, and their Vidcope cameras will stay on Kramvit through the whole visit, showing Earth life on all six planets at once. Kramvit plans to tour all fifty three states. The tale asks what a world makes of itself when it knows it is being watched.
604-gulliver-of-mars:
Edwin Arnold sends navy lieutenant Gulliver Jones to Mars in this early planetary romance, first titled Lieut. Gulliver Jones. Jones, dreaming of steak in a New York slum, is whisked to a Mars of canals, strange folk, and a pale princess he loves, wins, and loses. War, flight, and ruin follow his quest.

Arnold writes in earnest, romantic prose, with Mars as a mirror of earthly longing. The tale predates Burroughs's Barsoom yet shares its wonder. The book charms fans of early science fiction, where a plain lieutenant's love drives him across a world.
60513-rabbits-have-long-ears:
Lawrence F Willard wrote Rabbits Have Long Ears, a short tale first printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in August nineteen fifty eight. The head note says the tale came from that magazine. A computer classified a being as a rabbit, the blurb says, and Montresig was not one to argue, long ears or not. Commander Losure is a cautious captain. He orders his ship to rest on a moon out of sight of telescopes on a green planet below.

Losure crew is still demoralized from a brush with high intelligence slugs on the last planet. They lost three men in that scrap, one a highly valued anthropologist. Only two more such men lie in the freeze locker, the tale notes with grim humour. Montresig, the second officer, reports nothing new, with a belated military burp. A first contact tale with satire on rank and machines follows.
6072-the-boy-allies-with-uncle-sam-s-cru:
Ensign Robert L. Drake opens with Jack's adventure, as Frank Chadwick jumps from a chair in a front window and runs to the door of Lord Hastings's London home. A form swings from the sidewalk along the drive, and Frank flings the door open crying Jack, fearing something happened during two weeks of silence.

Jack laughs that he is perfectly whole, though he expected to be gone only a day or two. Frank replies they sail tomorrow night, likely for America, and Jack arrives just in time. The Boy Allies join Uncle Sam's cruisers for wartime service, where friendship and quick action carry the boys across the Atlantic.
60990-gem-stones-and-their-distinctive-c:
Herbert Smith of the British Museum wrote on gem stones and their distinctive characters in a book first printed at London in 1910 and reaching a third edition in 1919. Many diagrams and thirty two plates, three in colour, go with the text. Introduction opens the work, then the characters of gem stones: crystalline form, reflection, refraction, and dispersion.

Measurement of refractive indices, lustre and sheen, double refraction, and absorption effects follow. Colour and dichroism, specific gravity, hardness and cleavability, and electrical characters complete the tests. The technology of gem stones treats the unit of weight, fashioning, names of precious stones, manufactured stones, and imitation stones. Diamond leads the precious stones, then its occurrence and the historical diamonds. Corundum, sapphire and ruby, and beryl with emerald and aquamarine follow. Jewelers and collectors get a scientist's key to telling stones apart.
61055-the-valley-of-the-masters:
The Valley of the Masters is a tale by Charles Minor Blackford. The tale ran in Worlds of If magazine in September 1961. Henry's sin was curiosity and his crime witchcraft, the blurb says. His real offense was wanting his dying world to live on. Henry hides in underbrush to watch a group pass his path.

Twenty-five to thirty young folk walk slowly in ragged groups by. The youngest lead, dressed in jackets, shorts, and plast sandals alike. All look as alike as brothers and sisters, being cousins all. They tramp the valley from spring to fall gathering fruit and nuts. Couples await a vacant Mastership, a plot of orchard and house. There they breed or adopt the three children needed to hold it. Elders move into Town to work in factories and gossip. Henry must move his hideaway again as the group invades it.
61159-life-of-octavia-hill-as-told-in-he:
The Life of Octavia Hill tells the reformer's story in her own letters. Maurice edited the volume. Macmillan published it in London in 1913. Hill was born in 1838 at Wisbeach. A photograph of her forms the frontispiece. Portraits of her family fill the plate list.

The contents chart a life of work. Early chapters cover her childhood and first London work. Working women's classes and art training follow. A school at Nottingham Place marks the start of her housing work. Later chapters treat the open space movement. Commissioners appointed her to manage their property in 1881. The last chapter covers her final decade, to 1912. Her father opens the tale as a corn merchant at Peterborough.
6126-quotations-from-georg-ebers:
This volume gathers quotes from Georg Ebers's old tales of Egypt and the ancient world. David Widger picked them out for Project Gutenberg. Readers who know Ebers may check if their best-loved lines are here.

The editor asks for tips on lines to add, since a web book can be fixed fast. The list gives Uarda in five parts and more novels. Each is tied to a Gutenberg number, with tips for finding any quote in full by use of a word search. The book serves fans and students of Ebers, with choice lines kept in one place.
61295-little-wanderers:
Little Wanderers is a nature book for the young by Margaret Warner Morley. She was the author of Flowers and Their Friends, A Few Familiar Flowers, and Bee People. The book came out in Boston in 1899 from Ginn and Company. Its theme is the travels of seeds, as the contents set out. The first part is called Why Plants Travel.

Those That Fly with Plumes or Down stands next. Then come chapters on the dandelion, thistles, milkweeds, lettuce, and clematis in turn. Asters and golden-rod, the willow, cattails, geraniums, and cotton stand in the list as well. Other Fly-Aways and Seeds That Fly with Wings lead on to the maples, elms, ash trees, and pines. Seeds that fly with no wings or plumes close the part shown. The book tells how plants spread their seed on the wind.
61316-the-chemically-pure-warriors:
The Chemically Pure Warriors, by Allen Kim Lang, is a science fiction story. It ran in Worlds of If in July 1962, the note on it says. Conquerors own a planet outright yet dare not set foot on it. Lieutenant Lee Hartford marches his platoon back from three weeks in the woods.

Troopers in safety suits chant cadence as they march toward barracks and beer. Scarlet birds mimic their calls and garble them in comic echo at once. Camelopards chew leaves and watch the column pass on the road home. Native Kansans, called Stinkers, shun the occupying regiment dust in the fields. Shower, beer, and Service Company girls wait three miles ahead.
6148-narrative-and-miscellaneous-papers:
Thomas De Quincey gathers narrative and miscellaneous papers in two volumes, opening the first with The Household Wreck, The Spanish Nun, and Flight of a Tartar Tribe. The Household Wreck warns that to be weak is to be miserable, all weakness being suffering and humiliation.

The second volume adds the heavens by Lord Rosse's telescopes, modern superstition, Coleridge and opium-eating, temperance, war, and Kant's last days. De Quincey ranges from frail human tenure of joy to star systems and morals. This collected edition is described from its opening volume onward, without favoring either part.
6180-a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-1-being-a:
A Romany of the Snows continues the personal histories of Pierre and His People, offering the last existing records of Pretty Pierre. Its first volume holds Across the Jumping Sandhills, A Lovely Bully, The Filibuster, and The Gift of the Simple King.

Parker inscribes the tales to Sir William C. Van Horne, whose career belongs inseparably to the far north's life and development. Later volumes promise Malachi, the Lake of the Great Slave, the Red Patrol, and the Going of the White Swan. The first continuation set alone is examined in this entry, while its later continuation sets await separate entries.
6181-a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-2-being-a:
Malachi opens Parker's second Romany volume, as Freddy Tarlton gravely says he'll swing just the same tomorrow, exit Malachi. A door opens on gossips, a man takes the only vacant seat near the fire, stretches hands to heat, and looks at coals with drooping, introspective eyes.

Exit Malachi, he says presently in a soft ironical voice, without looking up, and Tarlton asks Pierre where he sprang from. Pierre answers that the wind bloweth where it listeth, and does not tell where it has been. The Lake of the Great Slave, Red Patrol, and White Swan follow.
6182-a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-3-being-a:
The Bridge House opens Parker's third Romany volume, standing on a wide wall between two small bridges, approaches to a big covered bridge over the Madawaska's main channel. When spring thaws swell the river, flanking channels divide at the house foundations and rustle toward rapids.

From any window one can watch the ugly rushing current, gorged with logs, batter the wall, jostle between piers, and race to rocks, dam, and slide. The Epaulettes, The House with the Broken Shutter, The Finding of Fingall, and Three Commandments follow. This entry takes up the third continuation set by itself, and the other continuation sets are not taken up.
6183-a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-4-being-a:
Little Babiche opens Parker's fourth Romany volume. A narrator corrects the governor: they did not tell you right, for he was with Little Babiche fifteen years, as long as he has known the governor. It was near Noel, the day of the Great Birth, with feastings, grand songs, and many candles.

The governor of the great Company settles back, powerful face seamed by years, hair grey and thick, keen eyes burning under shaggy brows. The Spoil of the Puma, The Trail of the Sun Dogs, and The Pilot of Belle Amour complete the volume.
6184-a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-5-being-a:
The Cruise of the Ninety-Nine opens Parker's fifth Romany volume, with a big gulf yawl a man and boy could manage at a pinch, old-fashioned high bulwarks, lying clean in water. She holds a tolerable record for speed and for other things sometimes considered by the government at Quebec.

The cure named her Ninety-Nine with humor, after telling owner and captain Tarboe the smuggler he came to seek one lost sheep, leaving ninety-nine in the fold at Isle of Days. A Romany of the Snows and The Plunderer complete the volume.
62-a-princess-of-mars:
A Civil War veteran wakes on a dying planet of green warriors and red cities. Edgar Rice Burroughs' A Princess of Mars sends John Carter from an Arizona cave to Barsoom. Lower gravity gives him great strength and leaps.

Captured by Tharks, Carter befriends the chieftain Tars Tarkas and rescues Dejah Thoris, princess of Helium. Arena fights, air scouts, and an atmosphere factory fill his adventures. Love and war pull him between two peoples. The book launched the Barsoom saga. Sequels followed Carter across Barsoom, and the series shaped science fiction adventure for decades.
62085-pied-piper-of-mars:
Pied Piper of Mars is a science fiction tale by Frederic Arnold Kummer. It ran in Planet Stories in the spring of the year 1942. A blurb says Elath Taen made mad music for the men of Mars. The red planet lived and would die to his fiendish piping tunes. Mercis, capital of Mars, opens the tale as a city like no other.

Solis on Venus may be more beautiful, and Earth cities more driven. Still Mercis holds a strange, inscrutable air that baffles twenty year residents. White plastoid buildings, rich gardens, and whispering canals greet tourists there. A darker side hides ever present beneath that bright tourist face. Silent little reddies follow ancient laws no Earth logic can shake.
62124-sanitation-of-mofussil-bazaars:
Sanitation of Mofussil Bazaars is a practical manual by Disney, late sanitary engineer to the government of Eastern Bengal and Assam, in its third edition of 1914. Written for municipal officers in up-country India, the manual deliberately leaves aside great waterworks and drainage schemes. It shows instead how existing arrangements in a bazaar town can be improved with the means at hand.

The introduction states the secret of sanitation plainly: the prompt removal of refuse and waste from near inhabited buildings before it decays. It adds the common fly as a carrier of disease from infected matter to the food supply. The third edition rewrites the older manual and adds chapters on road making and building construction. Disney thanks officers of the Indian Medical Service and the Bengal sanitary engineer, Silk, among his helpers: the book is a working tool of the colonial sanitary department.
62134-london-in-the-time-of-the-tudors:
London in the Time of the Tudors is a volume of a series on London in past centuries, sold at thirty shillings net. The front matter advertises its companions in the same uniform dress. London in the Time of the Stuarts carries 116 illustrations and a reproduction of Ogilby's map of London in 1677. The Times called that volume a mine for the student of topography and of manners and customs.

The Pall Mall Gazette praised the ready writer's fluent pen: the records of the city and kingdom, it said, had been ransacked for facts and documents. They are marshalled with consummate skill. The eighteenth-century companion, also advertised here, carries 104 illustrations and Rocque's map of 1741 to 1745. The Tudor volume itself belongs to that plan: the capital rebuilt in words and pictures age by age, from its streets, maps, and records.
62263-colorado-wild-flowers:
Colorado Wild Flowers is a Museum Pictorial booklet issued by Roberts with a nineteen fifty-three copyright held by the Denver Museum of Natural History. Colour plates show fifty flowering plants, each abundant somewhere in the state and most found in other areas too. The names can be learned, the book promises, without the use of any botanical key, and two plates reuse films from a nineteen forty-nine Van Nostrand book with permission.

Mary Chilton Gray of the museum staff drew the pen and ink diagrams. The entries begin in the lily family with yucca, or Spanish bayonet. Its flowers hang like drooping bells by day, spread three to four inches wide by late evening, and can be pollinated only by the deliberate work of a small pronuba moth.
62297-the-patchwork-papers:
E Temple Thurston wrote these short papers, printed by Dodd, Mead and Company of New York in 1910 and issued in February 1911. Thurston had won readers with The Apple of Eden and The City of Beautiful Nonsense. Eight of the papers appear in print for the first time. Others come from The Onlooker and The Ladies' Field, with thanks to their editors.

He gives the set to Norman Forbes Robertson in a frank letter. He dares not call the pieces essays, since a novelist should not reach for letters, nor short stories either. In serial form they ran as Beauties Which Are Inevitable. The name, he says, still holds: the papers set down things that of late have become real to him.
62321-the-flame-breathers:
The Flame Breathers is a tale of space flight by Ray Cummings. It first ran in a pulp magazine in March of nineteen forty three. Its scene is a doom world named Vulcan in the tale. One crew has gone there and vanished with no trace at all.

A second crew sails in the path of the lost men to learn their fate. The teller writes to set the true facts down past press hype. News men hail him as a new Columbus, a tag he shrugs off. He says he just did the job his backers sent him to do. Dark gorges and a hid threat stalk the crew on the small world.
62357-message-from-mars:
Message from Mars is a science fiction story by Clifford D Simak, taken from Planet Stories for Fall 1943. Fifty-five pioneers have died flying to Mars. The men at the base call the road the bridge of bones.

Scott Nixon means to be the fifty-sixth, alone. The pilot Jack Riley is sick, and the rocket blasts in fifteen minutes. Scott's brother Hugh was fifty-fourth on the roll of honour. His name stands on a bronze tablet with Harry Decker's. A radio message repeats from the red planet, over and over. No, no, no come, danger, it says. Scott stares at the crimson eye of Mars and keeps his faith anyway. The magazine's blurb carries him further than the opening does. He reaches Mars, his only ship a total wreck. Earth is doomed unless he can send a warning within hours.
62418-the-amazing-years:
The Amazing Years is a tale by Pett Ridge, out from a Hodder house in nineteen seventeen. Weston, a house maid, tells the tale in her own plain voice. Her house folk plan a cross sea trip as the tale first part opens. Miss Muriel frets at a week delay set by the house chief word. Crowd cars of trip firms are her dread for the late start date.

Mrs Hillier lays a hand on Weston arm and wishes her with them. Weston pleads sea hate, far folk hate, and one tongue lack as bars. A nephew with a fresh school prize will stay with her at home. Blue tags, wash lists, and class grumps fill the house leave fuss. Worry gnaws the wife that her man lost his old sure hand.
62421-frank-merriwell-jr-s-helping-hand-:
Frank Merriwell Junior's Helping Hand, or Fair Play and No Favors, is a boys' sporting novel by Burt Standish, from the Merriwell series. The series list in the front matter runs past a hundred titles, all by Standish. Its publishers claim a half million enthusiastic followers of the Merriwell brothers. They attest the unfailing interest and wholesomeness of the adventures. Frank and Dick Merriwell are lads of high ideals who play fair.

The stories are rich in fun and thrills in all branches of sports and athletics. They are extremely high in moral tone, the publishers promise, and cannot fail to benefit every boy who reads them. They fire a boy's ambition to become a good athlete and grow into a strong, right-thinking man. This number turns on a helping hand: fair play extended to a rival or friend in need, with no favors asked.
625-ponkapog-papers:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich gathers notes and essays from Ponkapog, Massachusetts, in this modest volume. Leaves from a notebook, asides, queer names, plot and character, the cruelty of science, and writers and talkers fill the pages. Aldrich chose the Ponkapog name for its modest air, fitting papers that claim no rivalry with great literature.

Aldrich writes with light, polished wit, turning a Kropotkin note on photography into a fantasy of a man photographed out of his good traits. The book charms as a leisurely miscellany, where a New England writer muses on books, folk, and fame without strain.
62501-great-zimbabwe-mashonaland-rhodesi:
Great Zimbabwe, Mashonaland, Rhodesia is Hall's account of two years of examination work, 1902 to 1904, carried out for the Government of Rhodesia and first published in 1905. Hall had already written on the ancient ruins of Rhodesia, and Professor Keane supplies an introduction. The volume carries two hundred illustrations, maps, and plans of the great stone ruins.

Chapters describe the author's arrival and first impressions, days at camp, the surrounding district and its people, and the relics and finds uncovered in the work. Long sections study the building itself: the walls, drains, passages, soapstone monoliths, and the great Elliptical Temple with its conical tower. Whatever later scholars made of its theories, the book remains a detailed early record of the ruins, made while digging was still fresh.
62928-child-whispers:
Enid Blyton wrote wee verse for children in a book called Child Whispers. The book came out in London in 1923. She gave it to four small brothers: David, Brian, Peter, and John. Rosamunda in the yard leads the list of small songs. She hears fairies talk ere the sun is high in the sky.

She looks on bug and bee and finds no fairies on them. By the tulips, elves pop out and wish her a good morn. One song finds a wet fairy in a cup of tea at home. Dolls on strike ask a penny for their Saturday fun. Each song is short and bright for small ears.
63032-one-against-the-stars:
Vaseleos Garson wrote One Against the Stars, a short tale first printed in Planet Stories in summer nineteen forty four. The head note says the tale came from that magazine. Earth faces a vicious radio plague, and a bright ship is its last hope. The ship must race to Venus and bring back a cure. A thirteenth man hides on board. His touch brings screaming death, for he bears the plague.

Workers who built the ship stand and watch her lift with pride. Riveters, welders, draughtsmen, and engineers all gave sweat and tears to each plate. One worker flings dust at the shining ship for luck. Pilot John Bairn sits in the glass bulge on top, with black hair and grey eyes. His stubby fingers race over the control keys. Suspense rides with the crew from the first page.
63150-the-soul-eaters:
The Soul Eaters is a science fiction tale by William Conover, printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1944. Its hero, Dennis Brooke, is a firebrand who has one last chance to redeem himself by capturing Koerber, whose ships are the scourge of the Void. The note at the head warns that his luck has run out, and that he will be marooned on a rogue planet against a menace weapons cannot kill.

The tale opens on Venus, booming on the discovery of radioactive fields, where Brooke rereads a farewell letter. Marla has bowed herself out of his life, and he is grounded from space as well as bereft. A dancer's performance in a pleasure palace cannot hold him; he craves solitude to salvage his heart and career.
63209-decatur-and-somers:
Elliot Seawell wrote Decatur and Somers, for Appleton in a third edition of 1896. Rights were held in 1894 by that New York house. Seawell had written Paul Jones and Midshipman Paulding before it. A front plate shows the meeting of the two young captains. Other plates show a privateer sinking and a pirate taken.

The expedition to destroy the Philadelphia gets a plate of its own. The exploding of the infernal at Tripoli closes the pictured list. Chapter one opens on Delaware Bay one evening in June 1798. The blue bay, bathed in a faint haze, looked its loveliest then. No moon shone, but the stars were coming out brilliantly, it says. The tale follows two young officers into the Tripolitan war. Decatur and Somers stand as friends and heroes of the young navy.
63479-the-three-lovers:
The Three Lovers is a novel by Frank Swinnerton, printed in 1922. Doran of New York held the rights and brought the book out. Swinnerton had writ Coquette, September, Shops and Houses, and Nocturne. Twenty chapters in two parts run from the studio to babies. Part one opens on a suddenly cold evening late in September.

London pavements shivered as summer vanished in a few hours' time. Street-lamps stood as sharp brightnesses in the black rainy night there. New friends, Patricia, and the reaction fill the early chapters told. Edgar moves, evenings with Harry, and a day in Patricia's life follow. Mischief closes part one of the young folk's tangled loves. Part two brings a wiseacre, change, encounter, and the sibyl onward. Playing with fire, the visitor, Blanche, and a night call follow. Babies close the tale of the three lovers of the title.
63529-mists-of-mars:
Mists of Mars, a science fiction tale by George Whittington, ran in Planet Stories in summer 1945. Special Investigator Barry Williams waits in the Martian desert at sunset. Orders in the tale call Martians savages with no rights. Williams and Princess Deisanocta hold other plans, says the head note. A white mist brings death to Earthmen who walk the night sands.

Ships have seen the pale patch once and sped past. A man on foot inside it was found dead next morning. Williams crouches with a ray gun he knows is useless. Deimos and Phobos light the red waste. The tale sets human greed against an old justice hid in the Crypts. Its close promises ruin for those who came to despoil Mars.
6354-italian-hours:
Henry James gathers his Italian notes, first collected with other impressions, now placed together for the first time in this November 1909 volume. Venice opens the contents, with the Grand Canal, an early impression, two old houses and three young women, and Casa Alvisi. From Chambery to Milan, the old Saint Gothard, Italy revisited, and a Roman holiday follow, with Roman rides, neighbourhoods, and a notebook from the after season.

A chain of cities, Siena early and late, autumn in Florence, Tuscan cities, and Ravenna close the run. James writes of porticoes at Turin, soft warm air, and the look of the written word itself, which tricks lovers of art into Italian satisfactions on easy terms. The book is travel writing as observation, where a street, a canal, and a facade carry a whole history of feeling.
63605-the-beast-jewel-of-mars:
The Beast-Jewel of Mars is a science fiction story by V E Thiessen, printed in Planet Stories for spring 1955. Its opening fixes a man face down at the edge of a Martian canal. He wears faded one-piece dungarees and an odd metallic hat, and little winds sift red dust into his collar.

Below him the fabled city spreads its spires and minarets, fantastic and beautiful, and one part of his mind insists he must go down there. A deeper part warns him off. They have a part of your mind now, the warning runs. Get away before your body becomes a soulless husk, walking the low canals with sightless eyes like those who came before. Thiessen builds the tale on that pull between the city's beauty and its hunger.
63609-beer-trust-busters:
Beer Trust Busters, a comic science fiction story by A R Stuart, ran in Planet Stories in the fall of 1945. Three asteroid miners, Doc, Listless, and Outhouse Murphy, tow in a platinum rich rock and sell it for a tidy sum. They head for a bar to start a bender.

Their round of beers costs twice the old price. The bartender shrugs: his supplier charges more, so he charges more. One man, it seems, controls the beer supply of the spaceport. The trio swears to do the trust dirty, and empty bottles mark their trail. The tale plays the fight against a monopoly for broad laughs.
6361-making-good-on-private-duty-practic:
Harriet Camp Lounsbery, president of the West Virginia State Nurses' Association, writes for graduate nurses on private duty, under the motto not to be ministered unto, but to minister. Though technique changes and teaching grows better, she says, the old problems of private work remain, and young nurses still face them. Her chapters run from nurse and patient, nurse and doctor, and nurse herself, to family, friends, and servants.

Foods and feeding, training school ties, complaints, teaching, convalescence, and waiting days follow, with hints for obstetrical nursing, washing the baby, and the valley of the shadow. Lounsbery advises patience with talkative helpers, never rebuking an amateur nurse harshly, but suggesting gently what would serve the patient more. The book is practical wisdom for a nurse alone in a home, where tact matters as much as skill.
63670-50-wonderful-ways-to-use-lucerne-s:
Recipes from the test kitchen of the American Dairy Association fill a booklet on fifty ways to use Lucerne sour cream. A letter to Mrs Homemaker opens it. The writers say the full story of sour cream's range has not been told. It does wonders, they claim, from soups to desserts.

They note that the word sour can mislead buyers. Modern sour cream is made from Grade A cream, pasteurized and homogenized, with lactic culture added. Recipes start with dips such as anchovy chip and shrimp chip. Breads, cakes, candies, and cookies follow. Pineapple coffee cake and chocolate sour cream fudge show the range claimed.
63704-some-impressions-of-my-elders:
Some Impressions of My Elders collects literary portraits by Ervine, the Irish playwright and novelist. The Macmillan Company published the book in New York in 1922. The pieces first appeared as a series of articles in the North American Review during 1920 and 1921.

Ervine dedicates the book to Elizabeth Cutting, who, he says, would give him no peace until he overcame his idle habits and wrote the impressions. His subjects are the giants of his generation. Russell, the mystic poet known as A E, opens the gallery. Then come Arnold Bennett, Chesterton, Galsworthy and George Moore. Bernard Shaw, Wells and Yeats close it. Ervine begins by mocking his younger self, whose cheery conceit held that anything he wrote ought to be published in a handsome volume. The portraits are personal estimates, not formal criticism.
63803-the-forms-of-water-in-clouds-and-r:
The Forms of Water in Clouds and Rivers, Ice and Glaciers is a work of popular science by John Tyndall. It was first copyrighted in 1872 and reprinted by Appleton of New York in 1899. Twenty-five illustrations, drawn and engraved under Tyndall's direction, support the text. The book opened the International Scientific Series.

The American preface sets out the series' plan: sound popular science by leading thinkers, against the shoddy marvel-mongering of careless book-makers. Its fields run from the physics and chemistry of common nature to the new biology and the study of mind. Tyndall's volume takes water as its thread, following it through cloud and river, ice and glacier. The aim is to give plain readers the latest reading of familiar things. Trustworthiness, the preface insists, is the first need of such a series.
63872-the-beast-jewel-of-mars:
The Beast-Jewel of Mars is a science fiction novelette by Leigh Brackett, first published in Planet Stories in the winter of 1948. Its hero, Burk Winters, is a deep-space pilot who has flown his ship, the Starflight, for years and is no longer master of himself. The story opens as the ship lands at Kahora Port on Mars and Winters stays in his seat.

Young officer Johnny Niles sees him down the ramp and urges him to enjoy his leave, hiding his pity badly. Winters looks across the tarmac toward the glassite dome of Kahora, the trade city of Mars. His hands shake, and the little sun seems to bear the port with patience. The bleak opening sets up the tale the title promises, of a proud Terran debauched into something that crawls.
63968-some-immigrant-neighbors:
Some Immigrant Neighbours is a study book on the new folk of America, for the young of the church schools. It stands in a home task course run by all the sects in joint work. A list at its front names that whole run of books.

Those books take the flag first, then the weight of the city and the red and brown folk of the land. The inrush of the new folk, the folk of the next day, and the call of the seas fill the mid run. A book on the faith of the west saints, as the Islam of America, stands in the list. A front print shows where the lads of the slums must play, from a famed photo house.
63972-the-watchers:
Roger Dee wrote this short tale of hidden aliens and a man set to kill. The tale ran in Planet Stories in September 1951. Peter Manson spent ten years to prove the watchers exist. Now he creeps round a villa at night with a blast gun.

Manson calls himself a pacifist and preacher of peace in print. He means to kidnap the alien who calls himself Leonard Havlik. He fears their meddling will spark a fourth great war soon. The tale asks what a man of peace will do at the brink.
64-the-gods-of-mars:
Edgar Rice Burroughs returns John Carter to Barsoom, the Mars of his earlier romance, twelve years after Carter's strange burial in Virginia. Plant men, a forest battle, and a chamber of mystery open the quest. Burroughs wrote The Gods of Mars as the second Barsoom book, after A Princess of Mars.

Carter seeks Dejah Thoris and Thuvia through corridors of peril, black pirates, and the prison isle of Shador, toward Issus, goddess of life eternal. The novel is fast pulp adventure, with sword fights, air battles, and escapes at every turn. Thuvia and the black pirates widen Carter's world, adding new peoples to the red planet.
64073-dateline-mars:
Dateline Mars is a science fiction story by Richard Wilson, taken from Planet Stories for May 1951. Wilson makes his hero a news man on Mars, Scott Warren of the Galactic News Service. Scott cannot yet write the big story he holds, on the fate of Rockhead Rastol.

The tale opens as Scott snaps off a vision screen and sits at his typewriter in Iopa on Mars. Through glass walls he sees the lights of the Landing Day holiday, at its mid point in a three day feast. He starts his roundup, then scores out a line with too many days in it. Mars has Earth folk and natives, searchlights, and a government house. News fans get crime and fate told from a press desk on Mars.
64174-wireless-telegraph-construction-fo:
Wireless Telegraph Construction for Amateurs is a manual by Alfred Powell Morgan. Morgan edited the mechanical and electrical department of a boys' magazine. One hundred sixty seven pictures go with the text. The third edition, revised and enlarged, was issued at New York in nineteen fourteen. A complete description of the new wireless law is included, its title page promises.

In his preface Morgan says he aimed at practical information for builders. Readers may wish to build a set for private or experimental use, he writes. Such a set should be more than a toy, he adds. Yet it should not cost as much as the commercial apparatus. Many books on wireless slight the builder's interest, he argues. The tiresome how to make style is avoided as far as possible, he says. Concise explanations of each instrument's part take its place.
64362-the-prison-of-the-stars:
Stanley Mullen wrote this short story, printed in Planet Stories in November 1953. Wilding, a trespasser, watches a supply ship's jets flame and die away, leaving him alone in a spacesuit in boundless black. Venus and Earth hide on the far side of the sun, and Mars hangs as the faintest red lantern. He takes Saturn and Jupiter on faith, not sight.

The hook names his need: to head out beyond Pluto a man needs folk as desperate and freedom-hungry as himself. He found them on Alcatraz, the rogue asteroid called the prison of the stars. Legends on Venus and Mars say the name Wilding suits him, for he was always more or less than a man. The tale opens in utter solitude.
64373-the-industrial-republic-a-study-of:
Upton Sinclair wrote The Industrial Republic, a study of the land ten years on, put out in New York in 1907. Sinclair had just won fame with The Jungle, his tale of the meat yards. He gave this book to H G Wells, whom he calls the next most full of hope. Plates show child work in glass shops and coal mines.

Sinclair first warns of a crash to come, then traces how trade grew to its vast scale. Parts on markets and want, and on rot in town life, build his case. He then sets trade next to rule by vote and finds them at odds. A part on revolt leads to his plan for a shared way of work. The book asks readers to see the clash in the terms of the Civil War.
64422-shining-hours:
Shining Hours is a book of verses and tales for young children. Its opening rhyme, Come and Play, is printed with the words split into syllables for new readers. Playful kittens spring up a favorite tree and scramble into a swinging hammock. They call down to Spot, the patient dog below, to join the party. Spot will not climb; he has his master's stick in charge.

A prose tale follows, of Edith and her dolls. Edith insists on taking the old idol to bed as of old. She loves it bushels, she tells it, though it lacks two arms, fine clothes, and a parasol. The new dolly may sit in the parlor; the old one is her everyday chum. In the Meadow, a verse of a girlie, a maiden, and a kind old dog, follows.
64485-the-origin-of-the-mound-builders:
Origin of the Mound Builders is a thesis by Alfred Coffin of Mississippi. Coffin taught at Alcorn Agricultural and Mechanical College at Rodney. An Elm Street press at Cincinnati printed the thesis in 1889. A verse from Milton fronts the first chapter on the Mississippi Valley. Coffin invites the traveler to cross that valley to the Gulf.

From Wisconsin to the Gulf, and from the Alleghenies to the plateau, mounds rise. Thousands of earth mounds with cone or pyramid tops dot that course. Inside them lie relics of human remains and of human inventions in bulk. Travelers ask the origin and reason of those strange earthworks at once. Coffin marshals the learning of his day to answer that old question.
6453-the-potiphar-papers:
George William Curtis gathers The Potiphar Papers as satire on fashionable manners. It opens with Goldsmith on parlor splendors and Burke on manners as air we breathe, vexing or soothing by constant, insensible operation. A prefatory letter to the Reverend Cream Cheese sets the tone, with Walton's angler preferring a temperate poor man to a drunken lord. Curtis writes as a watcher of New York society, amused and sharp.

A mid passage argues with Mr. P. about style of living: is his manner inferior to old Mrs. Podge or Mrs. Croesus, and will cutting back make people suspect his affairs? Do not make rash vows, the narrator advises, but go to sleep, recalling Mrs. Croesus said the same to her husband. The papers mock wealth, display, and the fear of seeming poor, in a city where manners are the real currency.
6472-on-the-pampas-or-the-young-settlers:
G. A. Henty sends young settlers to the pampas in a tale whose frontispiece shows the fight with the puma. Mrs. Hardy's resolution opens it, as her husband wonders one evening what he should make of the boys, a train of thought about their circumstances carrying him far. The start, a new life, the pampas, and the settler's home follow, with a tale of the Mexican War told by Seth and continued across two chapters.

Farm work and amusements, neighbourly visits, lost cattle, quiet times, and a steady hand fill the middle, before an Indian attack, terrible news, and the pampas on fire. A mid passage finds captives plotting escape, gnawing through each other's thongs if only their guards would leave them alone ten minutes. Henty writes settler adventure with cattle, fire, and frontier danger.
64772-the-rocketeers-have-shaggy-ears:
The Rocketeers Have Shaggy Ears, by Keith Bennett, ran in Planet Stories in spring 1950. The tale opens with a prophecy: one day, from Venus or Mars, awed words will tell of the glory of the Men of Terra. Then the scene drops to a crashed patrol rocket in Venus rainforest.

Hague, dazed since the crash, hears Commander Devlin lay out a five-hundred-mile march to the mother ship Odysseus. Hunting parties will shoot food, all water will be boiled and treated, and scientists will march and write reports as they go. No specimens can be carried, for weight is life. Five men sit cool at the chart table, ready to walk. Grit and pride carry the pulp tale.
64828-the-french-and-british-at-three-ri:
The staff of the Public Library of Fort Wayne and Allen County made this pamphlet on the old frontier post of Three Rivers in 1953. It stands in the library's historical series, under its two boards. Geyer heads the school board list; Kramer keeps its minutes.

Three Rivers, where the St Joseph and St Marys join to make the Maumee, was Fort Wayne's first ground. French traders and soldiers held it first, then the British after them. Kekionga, the Miami town on the spot, stood at the heart of the old Northwest. The pamphlet tells that first age of the place: missions, forts, and the long trade in furs. Local print for a city's own roots.
64941-supplement-to-harvesting-ants-and-:
Supplement to Harvesting Ants and Trap Door Spiders adds fresh matter to Moggridge's nature studies. Reeve published it in London in eighteen seventy four. Pickard Cambridge, a clergyman and spider man, supplies the formal descriptions of species. Three parts divide the book: ants, trap door spiders, and the descriptions.

Plates show silk tubes, nest doors of cork and wafer kinds, and whole nests. One Californian spider's nest is drawn in its bank of clayey earth entire. Doors are hinged lids of silk and earth that shut the burrow from hunters. The diagrams sort nests by single or double doors, branched or plain in plan. Eyes, claws, and body measures of each kind are figured at large size. Moggridge wrote from years of watching these builders on the Riviera shore.
65100-the-builders:
The Builders, by Fox Holden, is a science fiction story from Imagination, February 1951. Markten and a young companion fly over the dead cities of Earth, hunting old plans and diagrams. Their home, New City, holds twelve million people who live for one purpose only: to build.

The Elders, Holden says, wandered so long after the fall that they lost all memory of the past, and no one reads the old writings without diagrams. The teaser warns that what the builders finally construct gets up and runs away. The tale asks what a society loses when only making things counts.
65121-hindu-magic-an-expose-of-the-trick:
Hereward Carrington exposes the tricks of yogis and fakirs of India here. Sphinx printed the pamphlet at Kansas City in 1913 with pictures. Contents open with the mango tree trick and the basket trick. Dry sands, coloured sands, a diving duck, and jumping egg follow.

Snake charming, burial alive, and the rope trick close the contents. Carrington asks if the feats show powers beyond known science laws. He tells each feat as seen, then gives its method plainly. Handcuff Tricks and Boys Book of Magic stand among his past books. The Sphinx house at Kansas City issued the book in 1913.
65122-you-ll-like-it-on-mars:
Tom W. Harris wrote this tale of the films, first printed in a journal of such tales in August 1958. A note at its head gives the knot of the plot. No man could tell how Kettering had shot his scenes of Mars so true to life. His film was too good to be true, the note says. And it was far too grim to boot. The man who tells the tale is set a task by a chief of the films, Myron Ferdinand.

Get the facts, Myron tells him, and you can have all you want. Fail, and I wash you out of the trade for good. The chief has a plan: a tale has been spread that the man wants to leave Myron and go to work for Kettering.
65208-death-walks-on-mars:
Death Walks on Mars is a short tale of the red world and its risks. Alan Ramm wrote it for a pulp book of the year 1958. A man and his wife came to Mars as the first folk came west. They sought their luck, but hard men came to that world too.

The tale opens with death on all sides of a lone camp. A sand bird with a foul tail hangs in the thin air of Mars. A man lies shot in the red sand, his air ball holed and spent. The gun hangs loose in the tall man's glove as he stands by. The wife takes the death of her man with a frontiersman's calm. Two long years on Mars had tried the love of the pair.
65254-we-re-off-to-mars:
We're Off to Mars, a science fiction story by Carlton Furth, opens with a delivery at a shabby door. It was printed in Imagination, a magazine of science and fantasy, in September 1951. The tag line tells of a strange little robot machine that would create anything Joe Linger wanted. The catch was that he was being told what to create, and did not know it. The tale opens at the door of Joe's shabby room.

A delivery man from Time Deliveries, Incorporated, brings a large square package and asks Joe to sign. The name above Joe's on the list is Pontius Pilate, Rome, in the year twelve. He says he comes from the year 3428 by the present calendar. The firm, he chants, guarantees deliveries to anyone, anywhere, any time.
65259-early-english-water-colour-drawing:
Early English Water-Colour Drawings by the Great Masters, edited by Geoffrey Holme, was issued by The Studio in London in 1919. Its text is a set of articles by Finberg on Turner, his forerunners, and his fellow painters. Bound with the articles is a descriptive catalogue of an exhibition of chosen water-colours held at the galleries of Thomas Agnew and Sons in March and April 1919.

Plates in colour and monotone reproduce works after Turner, Cotman, Cozens, Girtin, Prout, Sandby, Varley, and others. Turner's Castle of Chillon, Saumur, Lake Nemi, and the Blue Rigi stand among the colour plates. The catalogue sorts hundreds of drawings by artist, so a reader can walk the show on paper. The volume preserves a moment when the early English school was being gathered, named, and praised as a national treasure.
65283-the-friendly-killers:
Tenneshaw wrote The Friendly Killers, a science fiction story printed in Imagination in June 1958. Its problem is stated on the cover lines: how do you fight an alien race invisible to Terran eyes, when your enemy may be masquerading as an ally? The story opens with a long extract from a galactic history.

The Kel, the history says, came from nowhere known. Their silver globeships desolated Cadar and other outlying worlds without a word. The FedGov rallied, built a defence net, and passed compulsory conditioning laws. For nearly two hundred years the war stalled, since the Kel held no fixed base. Then the Kel broke through and wiped out Bejak Two. On the bastion world of Rizal, mankind faced the worst thought of all: enemies within.
65294-legends-of-the-black-watch-or-fort:
James Grant, who wrote The Romance of War, gathered these tales of the Black Watch. Routledge brought out a new edition in London in 1860. The front plate shows the regiment in Canada, kilt and all.

Grant says in his preface that the warlike facts and many names here belong to true record. Woven in with them are tales and old beliefs gleaned among the hills the soldiers came from. He praises the kilted regiments for keeping Scotland's warlike name alive in Europe. From the wars of Marlborough to those of Wellington and since, he claims, the Highlands' fame rides on such men. Pride and legend mix in these pages.
65331-the-cosmic-looters:
