Cosmic Looters is a science fiction story by Alexander Blade. It first reached print in a magazine of science and fantasy in February nineteen fifty eight, the hosted note says. Its headnote warns that its hero Wyatt faces a hard place. He cannot stop an alien invasion, it says. Worse, if he warned Earth, nobody would believe him.

Duncan Wyatt wakes to an explosion at his lonely post in New Mexico. He grabs his gun and runs to the door of his shack. The shock wave still shakes the walls as he peers out. He thinks the third world war has started. His gear for sending tight beam signals looms over the mesa, marked with a red light for planes. His partner has flown to the coast for parts. Alone under a blazing sky of stars, he searches for where the bomb fell.
65415-the-yellow-frigate-or-the-three-si:
The Yellow Frigate, or the Three Sisters, is a Scots tale by James Grant. Grant had written The Romance of War before this sea story. Routledge of London put the book out in print. The tale opens in the broad valley by the river Allan in Scotland. Dunblane, an old cathedral city, lies among great trees in that vale.

Ruins of the vast cathedral of King David rise over the town. An old bridge there was built in the time of Robert the Third. A bishop of the see raised it over the clear Allan water. Crows flap in the deserted walls where swallows nest in carved stalls. That sad, quiet scene sets the stage for the frigate's tale. Grant then turns from the ruin to the men of his story.
65437-beware-the-usurpers:
Beware, the Usurpers is a science fiction story by Geoff St Reynard. It appeared in Imagination in November 1951. The opening warns that monsters may walk the streets. Your best friend could be one of them, it says. The narrator drives to an ancient castle in a black Jaguar. Rotted leaves choke the drive. Blank windows stare over the groves and moors.

Inside, a dead rook with pecked-out eyes greets him. He crosses the empty hall by torchlight. Moonlight patterns the floor of the great room. Guests of strange kinds gather as the tale proceeds. A tanned old officer and a one-armed man are among them. The usurpers of the title wear human shapes. Reynard builds dread from a country-house frame. The tale is a fair sample of fifties magazine horror.
65512-lasers:
Hal Hellman wrote Lasers, a booklet in the Understanding the Atom series of the Atomic Energy Commission. The Commission's Division of Technical Information made the book for lay citizens. Its card number dates it to 1968, revised in 1969. The series holds that nuclear energy touches each man, woman, and child in the land. All Americans, it says, should grasp this vital force to act wisely as citizens.

Contents move from the spectrum of waves to radio waves and light and the atom. A part asks what is special about coherent light, the heart of the laser. Controlled emission, the birth of a laser, and the new word lasing follow. Uses, a multitude of lasers, and communications fill the late pages. The book gives a new marvel in plain, pictured terms.
65548-how-to-have-bird-neighbors:
How to Have Bird Neighbors, by Louise Patteson, author of Pussy Meow, the autobiography of a cat, was copyrighted in 1917 and published in Boston by Heath. Photographs by the author fill the book, and the dedication is simply to boys and girls. A front plate shows strings, cotton, and chicken feathers set out for the birds' nestings.

Twelve chapters run from My First Bird Neighbors through bluebirds, wrens, chimney swifts, and martins, to the cardinals and My Bird Family. Directions for making bird houses and a glossary close the book. The picture list tells the method in miniature: suet and doughnuts for the downy woodpecker, corn for the cardinal, cereal for the song sparrow. Patteson teaches children to feed, house, and watch the birds at their own doors.
65563-nuts-in-family-meals-a-guide-for-c:
Nuts in Family Meals, a Guide for Consumers is Home and Garden Bulletin Number One Hundred Seventy Six of the United States Department of Agriculture. The Consumer and Food Economics Institute prepared the guide. It was issued in May nineteen seventy, slightly revised in nineteen seventy one, and approved for reprinting in nineteen seventy eight. Buying, storing, preparing, and recipes structure the booklet.

Nuts contribute rich flavor and crunchy texture to many foods, the guide says. They are tasty and nutritious as well, and familiar dishes take new interest when nuts are added. Nuts are filling from their fat content, it notes. Sections treat kinds available, how nuts are marketed, cost, form to buy, and signs of quality. Shelling, skinning, roasting, and cutting lead into recipes that fill most pages. Home cooks get a plain federal guide to a rich food.
65589-journal-history-of-the-twenty-nint:
Journal History of the Twenty-Ninth Ohio Veteran Volunteers is a regimental history by Secheverell, late of Company B, printed at Cleveland in 1883. A committee of comrades supervised the work for the regiment's twentieth anniversary. A portrait of Lewis Buckley, late colonel of the regiment, fronts the book. Its title runs from 1861 to 1865.

The title page lists the campaigns in which the Twenty-Ninth bore an honorable part. Winchester, Port Republic, and Cedar Mountain stand in the Valley. Chancellorsville and Gettysburg follow, then Lookout Mountain and Atlanta. The March to the Sea and the campaign of the Carolinas close the roll. Secheverell gives the regiment's victories and its reverses in a journal's day-by-day spirit. It is a veteran's memorial, written while the survivors still marched together.
65812-survivors:
Arthur Savage wrote a short tale of life after a last great war. The tale ran in a science tale monthly in May 1952. Two men, Oluf and Bowron, meet by a hid lake in wild land. Each had thought the other lost in the wreck of the world.

Oluf is a hunter, young, strong, and used to the wilds. Bowron is a teacher from New York who heads south for warmth. Food from old ruins grows scarce, and wolves roam the north ridge. Their talk asks who can live, and how, when towns are gone.
65923-little-rifle-or-the-young-fur-hunt:
Little Rifle, or The Young Fur Hunters, is a pocket novel of the backwoods by Captain Bruin Adams. Beadle and Adams published it in New York, entering it for copyright in 1873.

The boy trapper of the title is fifteen or sixteen, handsome, swift, and sure of his body. The first chapter finds him creeping along a branch of the Upper Columbia, alert for danger in any form. His dress is pure backwoods: fringed buckskin leggings, beaded moccasins, a broad belt with a knife, and a small revolver hidden in his breast for need only. A powder flask and bullet pouch hang from his shoulders. There is no game bag, since the game of that country is too big for a boy to carry. Adams had written other pocket novels of trappers and scouts.
66085-old-ruff-the-trapper-or-the-young-:
Old Ruff, the Trapper, or The Young Fur-Hunters was issued at New York in 1873. Beadle and Adams printed the pocket novel. Its author signs as Captain Bruin Adams. The tale follows his earlier Little Rifle. Twenty chapters carry the story. Young Harry Northend waits by a lonely camp-fire at dawn. Little Rifle, his promised bride of the wilderness, has vanished. Snow has stopped falling, and no moccasin print marks the ground. She must have gone before the snow came, he reasons.

Blackfeet raiders may strike at any time beyond gunshot of the fort. Harry guesses she went back to old Ruff Robsart, her guardian. Contents promise the Cascade Range, the Columbia River, and a leap for life. The dime novel moves fast, in the Beadle house style.
66086-chester-water-colours:
Harrison Compton made a plate book of Chester in water colors. The book came out in London in May 1916. It sits in a line of such books for shire after shire. The great church from the north-east fronts the book. A list names each plate in the set in order.

Watergate Street and its old row come near the start. Stanley House, the Cross, and the Falcon Inn show old town life. The Abbey gate, Pepper Gate, and the castle bridge fill the mid set. A canal view and the Phoenix Tower close the walk. Town fans get Chester's old stones in soft hues. Each plate is a calm, true view.
66093-cotswolds-water-colours:
Cotswolds is a book of water-colours by G F Nicholls, printed at London in the spring of 1920. It belongs to Black's Water-Colour series, which also held volumes on Cambridge, Cornwall, the English Lakes, and Oxford. The frontispiece shows a Cotswold village store. Twenty water-colours are listed in all.

They take in old houses at Broadway, the north Cotswolds from Willersey, and a Cotswold sheep pasture. Market Hall at Chipping Campden, Ebrington, and Saintbury Cross follow. The village green at Broadway, Winchcombe, and Painswick Church are pictured, as are Fairford and the church porch at Northleach. Lower Slaughter and Burford come later in the list. Cirencester, on the cover, closes the set. Nicholls painted the stone villages and churches of the Cotswold hills for the armchair traveller. The book is mostly pictures, with the plates doing the work of the text.
66194-the-wright-brothers:
The Wright Brothers tells how Wilbur and Orville Wright first flew a powered plane. On December seventeenth, nineteen hundred three, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, their craft flew. It rose from its track and held the air for twelve seconds. The flight ran one hundred twenty feet in that short span.

Orville held the controls while Wilbur steadied the wing at launch. Seven men in all saw the first flight that day. The work began in a small Dayton bicycle shop, the tale notes. Tires, wheels, and pumps framed their long dream of flight. Set plane lore proved wrong when they put it to test. A crude wind tunnel and balances of saw blades gave true data. Their wire to their father and sister told of four flights in one morning. Twenty one mile winds blew against each launch that day.
66245-ticket-to-the-stars:
Ticket to the Stars is a science fiction story by Raymond E Banks, printed in Imagination in February 1954. Its narrator sits in the dining bar of the Thousand Lights in New York. He watches Kelly at the bar as a woman walks in and stirs the room. The stir is not for her looks or her dress. She is an Ideal.

People hate Ideals, the narrator explains, and the better looking they are, the more they are hated. This one stands right on top of the scale. Kelly's face in the mirror scowls with hate. He crushes his empty cigarette pack in his fist and cannot look away. The story's premise, set by its headnote, joins deep space to these manufactured perfect people. Earth stops being good enough for a man who has tasted space and met his Ideal.
6625-the-coming-of-the-friars:
Augustus Jessopp, a canon of Norwich, gathers historic essays first printed in The Nineteenth Century, now revised with additions. The title essay on the friars' coming leads to village life in Norfolk six hundred years ago, daily life in a medieval monastery, and the Black Death in East Anglia. A university's building and a prophet of Walnut-Tree Yard close the set.

Jessopp writes as a scholar who loves a good story, with vivid detail on monks, peasants, and plague. His essays make medieval England feel close and human, not distant and dry. The Coming of the Friars is a lively, learned book for readers who like history told with warmth and wit.
66287-the-frogs-of-mars:
The Frogs of Mars is a science fiction story by Roger Dee, taken from Imagination magazine for April 1954. It opens in a bar after closing time. A little man comes in just as the first Marscast is about to start. He scoffs at scientific facts and keeps mumbling about something else. Six newsmen are already at the bar, and none of them knows him.

Larry the bartender is trying to bring in the first broadcast from Mars on the television set bracketed above his whiskey stock. He is not pleased at his after-hours party being crashed, and tells the stranger the bar is closed by city ordinance. The little man looks at the clock, which says a quarter past three, and at the shuttered windows. A passage preserved in the copy shows him ordering at last: water on the side, and do not mix it.
66387-pink-ears:
Pink Ears is a story by Murray Leinster. It opens at the Stratford, a hotel for men only with the quiet air of a conservative club. Its lobby is small, its smoking-room large and comfortable, and its kitchen worth a special trip. James Craig has enjoyed it to the full.

An hour before the story starts, Craig rose from a well-cooked meal in deep content. He chose a cigar with care and spent twenty minutes over his newspaper. Then, methodical in all things, he wrote a note and took a stamp from a small notebook. Leinster sets this scene of perfect routine before the twist his tales are known for.
66407-the-scarlet-shoulders-or-the-miner:
Harry Hazard wrote The Scarlet Shoulders, or the Miner Rangers, a Beadle and Adams pocket novel issued in New York. Frank Starr and Company entered it for copyright in eighteen seventy. Hazard had earlier written The Heart Eater, The White Outlaw, and Arkansas Jack. Chapter one is The Tragedy. Indios, Indios bravos, Manuel Navaja yelled to open it.

He discharged his escopette full at the glowing disk of old Sol, the tale says. Then he rushed through the outer gates, sounding the terrible words at every step. All the peons who heard him swarmed to the main building, it adds. There is a spell, a fascination like that of a rattlesnake, in the land of the sun, it notes. But a clear, stern voice soared above the din, it says. Dime novel readers get a Mexican mine adventure.
66435-eight-million-dollars-from-mars:
Eight Million Dollars From Mars, a science fiction tale by Winston Marks, ran in Imagination in November 1954. Pauker has killed ten men to get eight million dollars, and a flight to Mars should put him beyond justice. The blurb asks: or will it? The tale opens in a spaceport with a high, vaulted roof.

Pauker crosses the concourse in perfect poise, his robot luggage carrier trotting at his heels, steered by a bone he holds. The clerk whistles at the excess baggage charge of $4,175.00 for four heavy leather bags. Pauker pays and watches the man's bland face for doubt, well aware that most space travelers pack light. Marks builds a tight crime tale in a future port.
6672-the-caesars:
Thomas De Quincey opens on the Roman emperors, whose condition, he says, has never been fully grasped in its unique grandeur. There was but one Rome, he argues, no other city of ancient or modern times matching it in size, and few in display. London, he jokes, should be called a nation, not a city, yet even London cannot match Rome at her height.

A million and a half souls lived in Rome at her peak, a scale that shaped the emperors' lonely power. De Quincey writes with learned fire, mixing history, logic, and high rhetoric. The Caesars is a bold, brilliant essay on empire, power, and the strange fate of men who ruled the world.
66743-the-sacred-beetle-and-others:
Henri Fabre wrote The Sacred Beetle and Others, in Teixeira de Mattos's translation. Hodder and Stoughton put it out at London, New York, and Toronto. Fabre's own preface opens the book on the building of the nest. Nest building shows instinct at its highest, he holds. The clever bird teaches that lesson, he says.

The insect, with its still more diverse talents, repeats the lesson. Maternity is the supreme inspirer of instinct, Fabre declares. Care for the species outweighs care for the single life, he adds. The wasp kind bear the cares of maternity in their fullness. They prepare board and lodging for offspring they will never see. One turns cotton-spinner and makes cotton-wool bottles for her young. Another sets up as a basket-maker and weaves her cradle. Fabre gives insects as master craftsmen of the cradle.
66843-battle-for-the-stars:
Battle for the Stars, by Alexander Blade, ran in Imagination in June 1956. Kirk commands a squadron he has thrown into a deadly passage. The Dragon's Throat, he thinks, is well named: a throat of fire, a cosmic blind alley. A blurb at the head says Kirk had never seen Earth. Yet his squadron is ordered there now, to stem a galactic war. Joe Garstang watches the radar beside him. Nothing has been monitored yet, he reports, with stress on the yet.

The cluster crowds the scanners with a thousand suns, green, violet, white, and smoky red. Radar fails in such fields of force. Rumours told of Orion cruisers gone in before them, and of a secret base on a hidden world. Only a fool, or a cruiser, would enter. Kirk commits his hundred men to the gamble.
66996-cactus-and-rattlers:
Cactus and Rattlers is a western novelette by H Bedford Jones. A puff at its head calls it a double action, big caliber tale of adventure. Jones is billed as author of Sixteen Miles and other noted stories. The hero of the piece answers most days to the name Sagebrush. Twice a year, coming into Stovepipe Springs for mail and flour, he answers to George Beam.

Sagebrush boasts he is the only man between Death Valley and the Colorado who keeps abreast of the times, the tale says. He subscribes to several weekly magazines. Twice a year he collects the pile and answers advertisements for circulars. Then he reads magazines for six months and circulars for the next. A strange female at the hotel and a pilgrim due by stage crowd his quiet town, to his disgust.
67093-sidelights-on-negro-soldiers:
Sidelights on Negro Soldiers, by Charles H Williams, was published at Boston in nineteen twenty-three by the B J Brimmer Company. Benjamin Brawley supplied the introduction. Williams had served as a special investigator of conditions among Negro soldiers in the World War. A War Department letter of February nineteen nineteen opens his credentials.

The chapters move from the call to the colors into camp life. The Negro officer gets a long chapter of his own. Hopes and fears, the lure of the uniform, and the welfare organizations follow. The stevedore, the Ninety-second Division, and the Ninety-third Division take three chapters. Home-fires closes the account. Williams interviewed officers and men fresh from overseas service. His book is a first survey of Black America's war, written while memories were raw.
67190-the-asbestos-society-of-sinners:
The Asbestos Society of Sinners, a comic fantasy by Lawrence Daniel Fogg, was published at Boston in 1906. Its full title promises the diversions of Dives and others on the playground of Pluto. A newspaper man picks up broken threads of history in Hades and weaves them into a Stygian nights' entertainment. The book is dedicated to John Kendrick Bangs, who first made Hades a pleasant place in fiction.

Chapters begin with a summons from Satan and move among the shady sinners of the Styx. John Brown's body and the bones of John Paul Jones get a chapter. So do Henry the Eighth and his harem in Hades. Methuselah gives his thoughts on a modern doctor, and Boss Tweed discourses on tainted money. Fogg plays the afterlife for laughs, seating famous sinners and heroes side by side for talk and mischief below.
6727-england-under-the-tudors:
Arthur Innes writes England under the Tudors in a fourth edition, with a general editor's note on the flood of new historical material. Standard histories, the note says, need revision or even replacement, as monographs, letters, and records pile up faster than scholars can absorb them. Yet few have tried to rewrite history on a large scale.

Innes takes up that task for the Tudor age, from Henry the Seventh to Elizabeth, with a clear, scholarly narrative. His book suits students who want a full, orderly survey. England Under the Tudors is a solid, early twentieth-century history of a dynasty that remade England.
67412-the-corsican-lovers:
The Corsican Lovers is a novel by Charles Felton Pidgin, subtitled a story of the vendetta, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap in 1906. Pidgin had earlier written Quincy Adams Sawyer and Blennerhassett. Thirty-two chapters carry the tale between Corsica and England.

Brotherly love opens the contents, and a duel in the dark, an avenger of blood, and a double vendetta follow. The first chapter starts with defiance. A girl of eighteen tells her brother Pascal that he has no right to command her to marry a man she does not love. A dying wish and a stabbing lie behind the command. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
67550-troubled-waters:
Bertrand W. Sinclair wrote this tale of the north woods. The man who tells it opens with a hard word on life. Life is a grim jest at times, he says: it lifts a man to the peak of his dreams, and then blows up the peak. His case in point is a town man turned to the felling of trees, Joe Galloway. The first time the teller met Joe past his wed day, he felt envy of him.

It was a kind envy, he is quick to say. Joe had won what looked like true gain in life, in goods and in soul alike. He had a post that gave him funds in full for his needs, and a fat stake in the trade that grew year by year.
67577-we-women-and-our-authors:
We Women and Our Authors is a book of essays by Laura Marholm Hansson, in Hermione Ramsden's English rendering from the second German edition. John Lane published it in London and New York in 1899. Hansson had earlier written Modern Women, with studies of Sonia Kovalevsky, George Egerton, and Eleonora Duse.

The opening essay argues that German women once took pride in being an appendage of man and now ask who they are, not whose they are. Their first fight, she says, is for the right to support themselves, though it can cost them their womanliness. Essays then read famous male authors through their women: Gottfried Keller, Paul Heyse, and Ibsen, whom she calls the author in a cul-de-sac. Björnson is the high priest of purity. Tolstoy and Strindberg are paired as the women-haters, and Maupassant and Barbey d'Aurevilly follow.
67606-the-slaves-of-society-a-comedy-in-:
Slaves of Society is a comedy in covers by an unnamed author. Harper and Brothers published it in New York and London in 1900. The author signs himself only as The Man Who Heard Something. Fifteen scenes run from A Mother's Cares to A Misfortune for Society. The Course of True Love and the slave of Alderman Dobbin follow.

The notorious Belle Yorke, a person of importance, and what people said ensue. A question of chemistry, Cinderella, and the prince vary the middle scenes. A marriage has been arranged, and will shortly take place, heads two more. Scene one opens with a marchioness nibbling muffin from a silver dish. After all, she sighs, what are we but slaves of society.
67672-the-wright-brothers:
The Wright Brothers is a life of the two first men of the fly craft, by Fred Kelly. Orville Wright gave his leave for the book, as its title leaf says. It was put out at New York with rights held in nineteen forty three. The book is sworn to the brave fly men of the lands in the great war of that day. They fought past the whole world for man kind and for grace past the hosts of brute rule.

The first words of the hand set out his aim. That aim was to meet the ask of the plain, non craft reader on the work of the two men. He would do so in the most plain way he could. No try is made to go to the fine points of the craft.
67674-the-druidess-a-story-for-boys-and-:
The Druidess is a historical story for boys by Florence Gay. Ouseley published it in London. The tale is set in sixth-century Britain and Ireland. Ethne, a druidess, leads the action. Ethelbert of Kent and Saint Columba both appear.

A preface confesses the liberties taken with history. Ethelbert walks farther west than records allow. A league of Britons and Saxons in the Severn valley suggested the plot. The first chapter opens with the Britons' old appeal for Roman help. A battle closes on the western shore in 577. Saxons hold the winning side. The losing Britons face the sea behind them. Chapters then follow Ethne's hatred of the Christians and her errors.
67681-arthur-blane-or-the-hundred-cuiras:
James Grant wrote Arthur Blane, or The Hundred Cuirassiers, published by J and C Brown at London in 1858. Grant was the author of The Romance of War. An old proverb heads the title. The Pretty Mask opens it, and a case of rapiers follows. The Chateau and the Bond of Makrent come next.

Madame opens the trenches, and the Scots in France march in. War, the campaign in Alsace, and a charge of the Scottish Guard raise the middle. The Bastille and a haunted forest follow. Taken prisoner and defiance lead on. Husband and wife and a catastrophe close toward the end. Grant writes the Scots guards of old France, in the reign of the cardinals, as high romance.
67809-the-climbers:
The Climbers is a tract tale on boys who aim to rise in the world. A tract house in New York put the small book out for home use. Rights date the work to the year eighteen sixty six. Its first voice is that of a small inn keeper with a grudge.

He holds that tales of rise spoil boys for plain work at hand. His own stable boy hides with a book at each spare breath he gets. The man calls that book bent the ruin of the fine young lad. Talk at the inn then tests that claim gainst faith and thrift. The tract pleads that grit and study are a boys true due path.
67829-a-floating-city-and-the-blockade-r:
A Floating City and The Blockade Runners are two tales by Jules Verne, bound in one volume. The text is part of a uniform edition of his works, with pictures. It came out in New York in 1904 from Charles Scribner's Sons. A picture shows a ship of which one would have taken her for a small island, as its caption runs.

A note by the transcriber states the shape of the text. Italics are marked by the underscore sign, and captioned pictures stand in brackets. The few small slips of the printer have been set right. The table of contents was added by the transcriber for this form of the book. The first part of the volume is A Floating City, as the contents begin. The volume pairs a tale of a great ocean liner with a tale of blockade running.
68-the-warlord-of-mars:
John Carter has haunted the Temple of the Sun for six Martian months. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Warlord of Mars, third in the Barsoom series, opens with Carter trailing a shadow toward his entombed princess. Dejah Thoris may live or lie dead below.

Carter crosses the river Iss, the Kaolian road, and carrion caves toward war. New allies join him against yellow men and old foes. Battles, a magnet switch, and a tide of fighting lead to rewards. The novel crowns Carter's long quest on the dying planet. Burroughs's Mars books continued to shape planetary adventure for later writers and filmmakers.
68037-with-the-movie-makers:
John Amid wrote With the Movie Makers in nineteen twenty-three, a tour of film work with fifty-one pictures. The pictures come from famed studios and from Amid's own productions. Early pages show a crew on location, with two cameras raised for a long shot.

Chapters cover trick shots, how a set is built, and work inside the studios. Amid walks through the full making of a film, step by step. He recalls the early days of the movies and asks what makes a good picture good. Later chapters look at American films abroad and at the films of the near future.
68038-with-our-army-in-flanders:
With Our Army in Flanders, by Valentine Williams, was published in London in 1915. Edward Arnold issued the book that year. Williams gives it to the British soldier. Seventeen chapters make the volume. The war of positions and the fight for the Salient come early. Silent Ypres takes chapter four, with a drawing of the ruined town as frontispiece. Billets, Flanders castles, and headquarters follow. The Chief gets a chapter of his own; troops march past Sir John French in one plate.

Into the firing-line and the comradeship of the trenches mark the middle. The Prince of Wales and the Guards in Flanders follow. Children of the Raj treats the Indian troops, cavalry and infantry both. The eyes of the army and the new army close the book.
68051-mr-carteret-and-others:
David Gray wrote Mr. Carteret and Others, a book of stories published by the Century Company in New York in 1910. Gray was known for Gallops, his earlier sporting tales. The title character is an American gentleman moving in English country house society. A frontispiece shows a hunting field, with a guest calling it one of the smartest packs in England.

Six stories make up the book. Carteret appears among his fellow Americans abroad and proposes marriage in the second tale. A locket brings him an adventure, and a golf club figures in the matter of a mashie. Other stories treat the Evanstons and retell a tale of the Medal of Honor. The opening scene puts Carteret at a house party where a Wild West show is under debate. Gray writes light, well-bred comedy about rich Americans at play in England, their manners, courtships, and sport.
68290-the-berkeleys-and-their-neighbors:
The Berkeleys and Their Neighbors is a novel by Molly Elliot Seawell. Appleton published this revised edition in New York in 1892. Seawell had written Throckmorton, Maid Marian, and Midshipman Paulding. The front pages carry press praise for those earlier books. The New York Sun praised Throckmorton's charm of expression. The Critic called it a novel to linger over.

Reviewers marked Seawell as a past master of plantation tales. Her brisk fancy and turn for the odd drew notice too. Negro dialect in her stories won special mention from the Tribune. The novel itself belongs to her Virginia plantation world. Neighbours, manners, and local colour supply its matter. The revised edition shows the book still found readers four years on. Appleton kept it in cloth and in cheap paper alike.
68319-out-of-the-briars:
Out of the Briars is the autobiography of A H Newton, published in nineteen ten. The A M E Book Concern of Philadelphia issued it at one dollar and twenty-five cents. Newton was a minister of the African Methodist Episcopal Church. He joins his life story to a sketch of the Twenty-ninth Regiment, Connecticut Volunteers.

The contents move from his life before the war into his war record and the regiment's history. His ministerial labors follow, then essays on the church and the Negro problem. Sermons, articles, and resolutions close the volume. The Twenty-ninth Connecticut was a Black regiment in the Civil War. Newton's double record preserves both a soldier's war and a pastor's peace. An introduction by J P Sampson places him among the antislavery advocates of the older generation.
68389-in-the-grip-of-the-hawk-a-story-of:
In the Grip of the Hawk, a story of the Maori wars, was written by Reginald Horsley and published in London by T C and E C Jack. Horsley also wrote Stonewall's Scout and Hunted Through Fiji. His prefatory note lays out the historical ground with unusual candor.

The note explains the Pai Marire religion, called good and peaceful by its founders. In practice it preached deadly hostility to the Pakeha, the white man. Its votaries, the Hau-haus, followed prophets such as the rebel chief Te Kooti. Horsley recounts Te Kooti's imprisonment on Chatham Island, his escape by brig, and the Poverty Bay massacre. He warns that the tale is built on history but is not itself history.
68439-neva-s-choice-a-sequel-to-neva-s-t:
Neva Choice is a sequel novel by Mrs Harriet Lewis of the Select Library. Street and Smith of New York issued it as Select Library number two thirty two. Copyright dates run eighteen seventy one and eighteen ninety two on the tale. A synopsis of Neva Three Lovers opens this sequel for new readers.

A fair young widow, Octavia Hathaway, wed the rich widower Sir Harold Wynde. Her admirer Craven Black shared her plots against the baronet and his heirs. His son George was reported killed by a tiger in India, but lived captive. After false mourning, Lady Wynde married Black and eyed Neva fortune next. Neva must wed Black son to secure that fortune, the pair schemed.
68497-the-boy-scout-pathfinders:
The Boy Scout Pathfinders is a boys' novel by George Durston, published in 1921. Saalfield of Chicago and Akron issued it as one of twelve volumes in the series. The first chapter is called The Iron Box. Two boy staff members, Beany and Porky Potter, have vanished. The office fears foul play, since no sentry saw them leave the building. General Pershing himself orders couriers and scouts to search.

Every cranny that could hold a boy, alive or dead, is combed. The tired staff wait through the night in silence. Then a faint tapping sound catches one man's ear. The message comes quickly and accurately by signal. The boys are alive, trapped in a closed chamber below. They report spies and dynamite and ask for help at once. The rescue plot drives the rest of the tale.
6852-venus-in-furs:
Leopold von Sacher-Masoch's Venus in Furs, in Fernanda Savage's translation from German, was printed in only 1225 copies for private circulation, with type then distributed. An introduction traces Sacher-Masoch from Lemberg in 1836, through law at Prague and Graz, to teaching, then to a full literary life. He edited a Leipzig review, lived in Paris as a Francophile, and died at Lindheim in 1895.

His marriage in 1873 to Aurora von Rumelin, who wrote as Wanda von Dunajew, mirrors the novel's own tangle of love, power, and surrender. The tale that follows is frank, strange, and famous. Venus in Furs is a landmark erotic novel, best read with its history in mind.
68599-the-unseen-blushers:
A science fiction story by Alfred Bester. Astonishing Stories printed it in June 1942. The narrator is a pulp writer among pulp writers. Plots twist in his head after a late night's work. Wind has blown his story's pages out the window. Only part of the carbon survives, and he is not sorry.

A special luncheon anchors his week. Every Tuesday the writers meet in a second-rate restaurant. They gossip about stories, editors, and slow-paying magazines. A cent a word is their common wage. A few have graduated to movies or the slicks. Belcher, a science-fiction specialist, hosts and talks too much. Bester, then near the start of his career, writes the hacks with affectionate bite.
68626-untimely-papers:
Untimely Papers is a posthumous collection of essays by Randolph Bourne, published by Huebsch in New York in 1919 with a foreword by the editor James Oppenheim. Bourne, the most brilliant critic of the younger American generation, had died in December 1918 at thirty-two. The volume gathers his war-time essays from The Seven Arts.

Oppenheim's foreword is a memoir of the circle. The Seven Arts spoke for a young world, until its subsidy was withdrawn in 1917 and it died. Bourne, silenced and unwanted, began his unfinished book on the State. Its surviving essay, Oppenheim says, is the most terrible indictment of that institution the war produced, and it closes this volume as climax. The book is the record of America's suppressed anti-war minority, written by its sharpest voice.
6865-four-years:
William Butler Yeats looks back on 1887 to 1891, when his family had lately come from Dublin to settle at Bedford Park in London. The red brick house, its garden under a great horse chestnut, and streets shaped by Pre-Raphaelite taste set the scene for a young writer finding his place. He recalls the gap between the suburb's high ideals and its plain daily life, from shops that looked common to a church he never liked.

Friends, talk, and art fill these years, as Yeats measures the hopes of his circle against small letdowns close at hand. The memoir moves through rooms, streets, and gatherings rather than through great public events. It keeps returning to how a place can stir the mind even while it fails its promise.
68669-proxy-planeteers:
Proxy Planeteers, a science fiction tale by Edmond Hamilton, ran in Startling Stories in July 1947. Doug Norris guides a Proxy robot deep inside Mercury. The fissure rocks run to hundreds of degrees in heat. Shifting rock rumbles close by. Six small clouds of glowing gas drift toward the Proxy. A flash of light ends the link at once. Norris tears off his television helmet back at the control station near New York.

Seven Proxies have been wrecked in two weeks. Each blacked out with no sign of falling rock. Signals take eight minutes each way between Earth and Mercury. That lag can strand a Proxy in trouble, Norris knows. The tale sets remote control, time delay, and an unseen foe in the hot depths.
68683-american-literary-masters:
American Literary Masters, by Leon Vincent, is a set of studies of the classic authors of America, issued in 1906. Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York published the book. Vincent dedicates it to George Edward Woodberry, a critic of the age. Washington Irving heads the contents in four short parts.

Irving’s life, his character, and the writer himself are taken in turn. His early work, from Knickerbocker’s History to the Sketch Book, closes that study. Other masters follow in the same pattern through the volume. Vincent writes for readers who want the lives behind the school classics. His tone is warm, plain, and full of anecdote. The book is a parlour guide to the first age of American letters.
6876-the-british-association-s-visit-to-:
Lady Rayleigh gathers letters on the British Association's 1884 visit to Montreal, a meeting planned long in advance for a far city. The introduction, drawn from the Times, notes that the Dominion government and Canadian men of science had chosen presidents and fixed steamship and rail deals. Excursions were planned, and full guidance was drawn up for members before the ships sailed.

Much of that readiness is credited to the High Commissioner, Sir Charles Tupper, and his zeal for the visit. The letters that follow record the crossing, the welcome, and the work of the sections. They give a private view of how a great body of British science carried its yearly meeting across the Atlantic to Canada.
68908-mother-bunny-and-her-flowers:
Mother Bunny and Her Flowers, by Laura Rountree Smith with pictures by Penny Ross, was published at Chicago in 1922. Verse opens the tale and invites young readers to stay till the story is done. Happy hours with Mother Bunny and her flowers are the promise of that rhyme. Chapter one is called Planting the Garden in the contents.

One bright spring morning Old Mother Bun talks to herself about the garden. It is time the garden was begun, she says in rhyme. Old Father Bun calls for the rake and the hoe at once. Healthy Bunny and Pretty Bunny ask if they may help the seeds to grow. A garden tale in verse and prose for small children fills the book.
68994-lightning-thunder-and-lightning-co:
Gerald Molloy, a Dublin professor of science, wrote these illustrated lectures on lightning, thunder, and lightning conductors. The Humboldt Publishing Company published them at New York, with an appendix on the recent controversy over conductors. Plates show the electric spark, the brush discharge, and a Leyden jar battery at work.

Lecture one argues the identity of lightning and electricity through Franklin's experiment and Richman's fatal one. It asks what a flash is and how long it lasts, and sorts forked, sheet, and globe lightning from Saint Elmo's fire, before explaining the rolling of thunder. Lecture two turns practical: the destruction lightning works on buildings, ships, and powder magazines, Franklin's rods, the battle of balls and points, and rules for personal safety in a storm. The appendix reports Professor Lodge's challenge to the received theory, debated at the British Association in September 1888.
6901-the-happy-adventurers:
Lydia Miller Middleton tells a tale she calls strictly true, of children who find adventure in building, digging, and play. The chapters name their games one by one: a little house built by small hands, a cherry garden, a duke's nose hunt, a miracle, grape gathering, and a fateful stone. A Kipling verse at the head claims little has changed in the building trade since things were made.

Grannie opens the story with the old saying that woes cluster, and the children answer trouble with pluck and humor. Illustrations catch moments like a wish for a bridge to a brother and a watch kept on a kangaroo. The book keeps a warm, homely tone, and it ends as it began, with the joy of making.
6914-the-last-of-the-huggermuggers:
Christopher Pearse Cranch tells a giant story of Little Jacket, a boy who longs to go to sea. Luck at sea, good and bad, brings him to shore and then to the giant Huggermugger, whose boot becomes his strange shelter. He escapes from the shop of Kobboltozo, learns to use the giant in travel, and at last leaves the giant's island with friends.

Later chapters bring Mister Nabbum, Zebedee and Jacky plotting together, and a return voyage to the island. The Huggermuggers appear in a new light at Huggermugger Hall, while Missus Huggermugger grows thin and fades and the giant's sorrows deepen. Cranch mixes fairy tale wonder with jokes about size, pride, and home.
69175-the-seven-stairs:
The Seven Stairs, by Stuart Brent, is a memoir of life in the book trade. Houghton Mifflin issued it at Boston in 1962, first printing that year. Brent tells how a young man set out to be a book dealer. A torn up first draft and Will Cuppy joke open his tale of himself.

Chapters trace getting started, building the Seven Stairs shop, and hard years. The day his accountant cried and the man with the golden couch stand out. Farewell to the shop, a move to the Avenue, and Bark Point follow. Theatre life, writing, and publishing fill the later chapters in turn. Books and Brent closes this warm trade memoir.
69342-troubled-waters:
William MacLeod Raine wrote a western printed at New York, with rights of 1918 and 1925. Raine had written Bucky O'Connor, Man Size, The Big Town Round Up, and Gunsight Pass. Among the apple blossoms opens the tale, then Tim Flanders offers information and opinions. A challenge and the bringing of Rowan McCoy to Ruth Trovillion follow.

A ride, champion of the world, and fate flinging open a closed door fill the early chapters. A cold trail, a rift in the lute that widens, Larry going calling, and across the dead line lead to a night raid. The young man drew up his horse by a dusty road and looked across the barbed wire into an orchard, the tale begins. Blue mountains rim the far view. Love and feud ride the range here.
69365-zephyrs:
Kate R Stiles gathered a small volume of poems called Zephyrs. A B Adams printed the book at Worcester in the year 1879, from Congress entry. The poems are given to her angel Effie, whose life inspires the work. Friends pressed her to print the verses, her front note states.

Stiles offers the book with low hopes, not expecting it to bear a stern test. The title speaks of soft west winds, light and passing. Small, earnest verses on faith, loss, and love fill the slim pages. Readers gain a tender keepsake of private grief and hope from its time.
69627-thoughts-selected-from-the-writing:
An anthology of uplifting quotations compiled in Oakland, California. Jessie K Freeman and Sarah S B Yule hold the 1901 copyright. Ladies of the Fabiola Hospital Association made the selections. Dodge Publishing Company issued the book at New York. A portrait of Edwin Markham fronts the volume. Come, let us live the poetry we sing, his caption runs.

Bovee supplies the first maxim. The pleasantest things in the world are pleasant thoughts, he writes. Ruskin follows with his nests of pleasant thoughts. Gladstone praises the thrift of time with interest. Edward Everett Hale advises bearing one trouble at a time. Age is opportunity no less than youth, another verse adds. Hospital ladies compiled the book as a gift of cheer. Such thought books furnished parlours and sickrooms alike.
69703-the-master-mind-of-mars:
Master Mind of Mars is the sixth Mars novel by Edgar Rice Burroughs. A cover scene shows battle damage aboard a Toonolian flyer in flight. Dar Tarus cries that the ship is useless and cannot turn course. The narrator shoots out the enemy searchlight as they rush to collide. He vows they shall take the enemy craft for their own escape.

A list of Mars novels fronts the book from A Princess of Mars on. Gods, warlords, Thuvia, and chessmen fill the sequence before this sixth tale. The Master Mind was first published in Amazing Stories magazine. John Carter's world of Barsoom frames the new hero's adventures in red deserts. Science, swords, and strange minds mix in Burroughs' swift pulp manner.
6984-the-pothunters:
Wodehouse's Pothunters opens with Tony Graham looking up from his bag as a voice asks where it has seen a face before. Allen's arrival sets the school tale moving, and the contents promise patient perseverance producing pugilistic prodigies, thieves breaking in to steal, and certain revelations. A mutual friend, a literary banquet, and Barrett's exploring lead to a sleuth hound and Mister Thompson's inquiries.

The sports, an interesting interview, and Sir Alfred's scoring give way to a long run, explanations, and the disappearance of J Thomson. A search follows, whether he be above the ground, and the affairs of various persons are wound up at the close. Wodehouse mixes school sport, theft, and detection with light humor.
6991-across-the-years:
Eleanor Porter gathers stories across the years, reprinted by leave from the Ladies Home Journal, Ainslee's, the Century, Harper's Bazaar, and other magazines. The contents list When Father and Mother Rebelled, Jupiter Ann, the Axminster path, Phineas and the motor car, and the most wonderful woman. The price of a pair of shoes, the long road, a couple of capitalists, and the bridge across the years follow.

Later tales give a summons home, black silk gowns, a belated honeymoon, and the giving thanks of Cyrus and Huldah. When Father and Mother Rebelled opens a month before Christmas, with Lyddy Ann hearing the news. Porter writes New England life with warmth, humor, and a keen eye for small revolts of the heart.
6995-ghosts-i-have-met-and-some-others:
John Kendrick Bangs meets ghosts with humor in this collection, dedicated to choice spirits everywhere. The contents list ghosts that haunted him, the mystery of his grandmother's hair sofa, the mystery of Barney O'Rourke, and an exorcism that failed. Thurlow's Christmas story, the Dampmere mystery, and Carleton Barker first and second follow, with illustrations by Newell, Frost, and Richards.

Captions catch the tone: grotesque attitudes no one ever saw, a thing grinning in a chair, a friendly spectre standing by, and a flight madly through wainscoting. Bangs tells of gold and silver ware in the Elysian fields, empty chairs, and cooking sherry drained to the dregs. The book is a comic ghost book, where dread gives way to laughter.
70019-the-female-impersonators:
The Female-Impersonators, by Ralph Werther under the name Jennie June, is a sequel to the Autobiography of an Androgyne. The Medico-Legal Journal published it in New York in 1922, in a first edition of one thousand copies. Alfred Herzog, the journal's editor, supplied an introduction.

Werther recounts six years spent as an instinctive female-impersonator in New York's underworld. The book adds the life stories of androgyne associates and an outline of the author's knowledge of kindred questions of character and psychology. Sale was restricted: copies went only to physicians, lawyers, clergymen, teachers, writers, psychologists, sociologists and legislators, and each copy was numbered. Werther inscribed the book to nature's step-children, in the hope that their lives might be made more tolerable. It remains a rare firsthand document of a hidden world.
70328-bobby-and-betty-with-the-workers:
Bobby and Betty with the Workers is a school reader by Katharine Elizabeth Dopp, a former University of Chicago Extension instructor. Rand McNally published it in Chicago and New York, with copyright from 1923 and an edition of 1928. Mary Spoor Brand illustrated the lessons.

Two children visit the workers of their town, trade by trade, and learn where things come from. The milkman and his horse come first, then the iceman. Mother wants a cherry pie, so apple pies are made and the baker's shop is visited. A penny poses the question of what to buy. The grocery store, the banana man and the fruit and vegetable man follow, then the meat market. Shoes take the children to the shoemaker's shop and the shoe store. The dressmaker and the tailor fit them with new clothes. Scissors-grinders, broom men, newsboys and policemen complete the civic round.
70438-women-compositors:
The Victoria Press of Praed Street, London, issued this guide to the composing room for women in 1880. It came from the Office for the Employment of Women, under the patronage of Her Majesty. The writer hides behind the initials of the title page alone.

Outlines of compositors' work open the teaching. Frames, cases, type, the composing stick, rule, galley, chase, and galley-press are named and shown. Corrections and imposing close the round. Three appendices hold the craft's sums: sizes of type, leads to equal a line, ems to a page, and the laying out of sheets, from folio to sixteens. The Victoria Press was Emily Faithfull's famous house, run to give women a trade; this is its own textbook.
7044-in-the-courts-of-memory-1858-1875-f:
L de Hegermann Lindencrone draws In the Courts of Memory, 1858 to 1875, from contemporary letters of court life. Illustrations name Madame Charles Moulton, the Fay house at Cambridge, Emperor Napoleon the Third, Empress Eugenie, and composer Auber. Facsimiles show letters from the Duke de Morny, Jenny Lind, and Liszt, with signatures and answers from Merimee, Metternich, Napoleon, and Eugenie to Madame Moulton's questions.

Views of Compiegne and Pierrefonds, their music hall and hall of fetes, and the hall of heroes set the stage. Elihu Washburn and Raoul Rigault appear among the figures of the age. The letters carry readers into Second Empire salons, concerts, and courts, through the eyes of a woman who lived among princes and artists.
7053-pages-from-a-journal-with-other-pap:
Mark Rutherford gathers pages from a journal with other papers in this 1901 Unwin volume, second impression. The contents open with a visit to Carlyle in 1868, then early morning in January, March, June, August, and the end of October. November, the break up of a great drought, and Spinoza follow, with a supplementary note on the devil, injustice, and time settling controversies.

Later papers treat talking about troubles, faith, patience, an apology, and belief, unbelief, and superstition. Judas Iscariot, Scott's use of the supernatural, September 1798, and notes on Milton lead to the morality of Byron's poetry and Byron, Goethe, and Matthew Arnold. Rutherford writes a quiet, reflective journal of reading and conscience.
70540-skulls-in-the-stars:
Skulls in the Stars is a tale by Robert E. Howard. It was put out in Weird Tales in January 1929. A verse from Hood stands at its head, on how murderers walk the earth beneath the curse of Cain. Crimson clouds stand before their eyes and flames about their brain, the verse runs, for blood has left its lasting stain upon their souls.

A picture shows a fen from which a single shriek of dire laughter sounded. The tale then opens with a road. There are two roads to Torkertown, it says. One, the shorter and more direct, leads across a bare upland moor. The other winds its long way in and out among the mounds and bogs of the swamps, by the low hills to the east. Solomon Kane, the tale's figure, halts on that road as the account begins.
70600-wanted-leaders:
Theodore DuBose Bratton, an Episcopal bishop of Mississippi, wrote Wanted Leaders, a study of Black growth issued in New York in 1922. The book came from the church's board for missions and church work. Bratton starts with Africa five hundred years back, when sea powers first cut into its tribal life.

Eight parts move from Africa to Liberia and Haiti, then to the slave and the freedman in America. War and the rebuilding years get a part of their own. Later parts treat school training and church growth, and ask what the years ahead may hold. A large book list and an added set of notes close the study. Its call is for trained Black leads in church and school.
70623-the-deadly-thinkers:
William Beyer wrote this feature novel of machine and man, Urei. The tale ran in Science Fiction Quarterly in May 1951. Urei is a huge unified reflexive electronic integrator machine. Men suspect the vast machine has gained a mind of its own.

Benton tells Doctor Albie he felt a compulsion turning a page. Albie calls it fantasy, born of too much science fiction reading. Urei cells and circuits fill near a square mile of ground. Five hundred feet tall with its depths, it need not move. Science fiction was Urei father, Benton contends, or at least a distant ancestor of it.
7082-lives-of-the-necromancers:
William Godwin writes Lives of the Necromancers as an account of the most eminent persons in successive ages who claimed magical power or had it imputed to them. Published in London in 1834, the book aims to exhibit a fair picture of human credulity, which Godwin holds cannot fail to teach salutary lessons. One view of the subject, he argues, teaches a useful pride in the abundance of our faculties.

Without pride, he insists, man is of little value, since pride stirs great undertakings and the secret persuasion of extraordinary talents. Footnotes, numbered in sequence and moved to the end, support the narrative. Godwin's lives run through magicians, prophets, and pretenders, showing how wonder and fraud shaped ages before science.
70962-the-sentinel-stars:
The Sentinel Stars is a science fiction novel by Louis Charbonneau, published by Bantam Books in 1963. Its hero is TRH-247, the two hundred and forty-seventh citizen to bear the name Thomas Robert Hendley, in a future where the Organization uses numbers instead of names. Hendley rebels: he quits work, samples a Freeman Camp, uses a false number, and is punished with banishment, taking a girl whose crime equals his.

The opening shows the morning after the Merger that united the world. In underground streets, automatic cleaners snuffle at the cups and bottles outside the vending bars while marquees still blink last night's slogans: One for all, all for one. The Organization is one, and its slogans declare freedom for all. Against that polished unity stands one man lying motionless in bed, refusing to rise.
70972-the-man-killers:
The Man-Killers is a western novel by Dane Coolidge, author of The Fighting Fool and Wunpost, printed at New York in 1921. The first chapter, The Trap, opens in Deadman Canyon. A hush of boding silence lies there, and hawks settle on the cliffs to watch. A man rides up the Maverick Basin trail.

Ahead of him, like hunting animals, two men skulk to cut him off at the creek. Above them the white houses of cliff-dwellers, now desolate, gaze down on the age-old tragedy. The captive is tall and slim, as befits a Texan, with a red freckled face and a huge black hat. The chapters run through the sheep war, the man-killing Bassetts, and a man back from the dead. The Eagles' nest and the honour of the McIvors follow. Coolidge writes of feuds and ambushes in cattle country.
71080-the-rag-pickers:
The Rag Pickers and Other Stories, by Mrs Madeline Leslie, is a book of moral tales for children, published in Boston. The text was entered for copyright in 1863. Leslie had written Tim the Scissors Grinder and other stories of poor children.

The first tale follows little Dilly Hogan, aged six, who picks rags and coal with her father, mother, and brothers after a breakfast of porridge or dry bread. Tired and homesick, she begs her hard-faced father to go home. Other stories in the book tell of Eddy and his fishes, Willie's grave, a substitute soldier, a hospital child, and Johnny's fretting. Each short tale turns on a lesson of patience, kindness, or repentance for young readers. The pictures and plain talk suit the Sunday school trade of the day.
71170-modern-daughters:
Modern Daughters, by Alexander Black, holds conversations with various American girls and one man. Scribner of New York issued the book in 1899 at two dollars and a half. Photographs taken by the author illustrate the conversations throughout. Miss America, his earlier book of pen and camera sketches, stands in his list.

A Capital Courtship and Miss Jerry complete that list of his works. Black toured with a camera and a notebook among the new women of his age. College girls, workers, and society daughters speak in these pages. The one man of the subtitle answers for his sex at the end. The book is a snapshot album of the American girl of 1899. Her talk, dress, and ambitions are caught as she wished to be seen.
71174-the-nugget-finders:
Alger's The Nugget Finders, a tale of the gold fields of Australia from the London house of Shaw, follows two boys of sixteen, Harry Vane and Jack Pendleton. Harry, an orphan, had crossed the sea as assistant to a stage magician who billed himself as the Magician of Madagascar.

The boys meet on a ship that is wrecked, and they spend some weeks on an uninhabited island before rescue. In Melbourne the magician sails home, but Harry stays with Jack to try the mines. Chapters carry them to Bendigo, where a struck nugget brings luck, danger, a trial, and captivity before the claim is sold. Alger shapes the gold rush into a brisk boys' adventure of friendship and fortune.
71219-the-manufacture-of-earth-colours:
Josef Bersch wrote this trade manual on making earth colours, turned into English by Charles Salter from the third German edition, as revised by Wilhelm Bersch. Scott, Greenwood and Son of London issued it in 1921 with thirty-one illustrations. Chapters open with the raw materials: limestone, chalk, gypsum, barytes, talc, and clay among the whites.

Yellow earths follow: brown ironstone, ochre, yellow earth, and terra di Siena. Red earths bring red ironstone, bole, alum sludge, and mine sludge. Blue and green earths, azurite, vivianite, and malachite round out the raw stock. Later chapters treat the finished colours, from native ferric oxide and hematite to caput mortuum and burnt ochres. The book serves paint makers with recipes and tests.
71285-dead-letters:
Maurice Baring wrote Dead Letters, issued in Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin Company in nineteen ten. The letters first ran in the Morning Post. Baring dedicated the book to Lord Lucas. These letters are in no wise meant to be either historical documents or historical studies, he warns his friend. They are the fruits of imagination rather than of research, he says.

The word research is not even remotely applicable here, he admits. His sources are the hazy memories of a distant education, a few hurried references to Smith Classical Dictionary, and a map of Rome. If you tell me my account of the Carthaginian fleet is full of inaccuracies, I shall answer that I do not care, he declares. Yet a few grains of historical truth remain, he claims. Readers get invented letters from the dead.
71324-a-dictionary-of-american-authors:
Oscar Fay Adams compiled A Dictionary of American Authors, here in its fifth edition, revised and enlarged, published by Houghton Mifflin at Boston and New York in 1904. Adams wrote a life of Jane Austen and edited Through the Year with the Poets. Here he arranges American writers alphabetically, with birthplace, dates, a line or two of career, and their chief books. The opening pages run from Cleveland Abbe, the Weather Bureau meteorologist, through a cluster of Abbeys, Abbots, and Adamses, clergymen, verse writers, and scholars.

Entries stay compact: Ezra Abbot gets his Harvard divinity professorship and Bible dictionary work; Francis Ellingwood Abbot gets his advanced religious thought and editorship of The Index. Cross-references point to memorial volumes where a fuller life exists. The dictionary served as a quick who's-who of American letters at the turn of the century. A Gale Research reprint followed in 1969.
71407-nature-s-carol-singers:
Richard Kearton wrote this book of England song birds, Nature Carol Singers. Cassell printed it in London in 1906 with photographs from nature. Cherry and Richard Kearton took the pictures direct from life. A nightingale and its mate front the small volume here.

The preface quotes Cook verse praising nightingale, robin, and thrush song. England stands rich in song birds despite thick crowds, he writes. Furze clad commons and game preserves shelter the feathered singers there. Rich and poor alike hold kind feeling toward the wee birds. British birds nests and Cock Robin adventures stand in the Kearton works list in front.
71462-nature-readers:
Julia Wright wrote this first Nature Reader for children just learning to read. The book, Sea-Side and Way-Side, came out in Boston in 1896. A Longfellow verse to Agassiz stands as its motto at the front. Wright says nature is a story book God wrote for children.

Her preface argues first lessons should hold real facts, not trivia. She picks strong short Saxon words to teach reading and nature at once. Lessons come from the shore and field, where life lives free. Habits, homes, and forms of small animals fill the simple pages.
71696-recollections-of-full-years:
Helen Herron Taft, wife of William Howard Taft, wrote Recollections of Full Years, a memoir put out in New York in 1914. Her tale starts in Cincinnati, the town of her birth. She tells of a large home on a plain wage, and of song and study in her youth. She met her mate there amid the stir of votes and rule.

A first trip to Washington brought a call on President Hayes and his wife. The pair wed, went abroad, and set up a first home with a loan on it. Later parts trace court work, a move to Washington, and the birth of their young. The tale then sails to the Philippines on a troop ship. A stay in Japan, with inns, shops, and a bout of ill health, fills a long part.
71707-the-africanders:
Le Roy Hooker wrote this history of a century of Dutch English feud. Rand, McNally printed the book in Chicago and New York in 1900. Contents open with the Dutch at the Cape from 1652 to 1795. First contact in diplomacy and war in 1795 follows at once.

The first trek north, Natal contact, and Orange River contact come next. Slavery, the Free State, and the Transvaal fill the middle chapters. A first war of independence and its causes get long treatment. Plates show Kruger, Steyn, Rhodes, Cronje, and Majuba Hill views. Le Roy Hooker wrote the century long feud account.
71779-the-language-of-flowers:
The Language of Flowers, also called The Floral Offering, explains what bouquets say. Henrietta Dumont compiled the token book. Peck and Bliss published it at Philadelphia in 1851. Coloured illustrations come from original drawings. A motto picture opens it. Roses and violets confess love in its caption.

A preface asks why flowers cover the earth so richly. They enter every scene from cradle to grave, it answers. Flowers bear a real and natural significance. They correspond to actual human emotions. The East has understood their language from remote ages. Europe knew it long among the common people. Shakespeare shows it in Ophelia's madness, the preface notes. The little volume makes the code complete for its readers.
71909-west-o-mars:
Charles Fontenay wrote West o' Mars, a science fiction story printed in Infinity in April 1958, illustrated by John Schoenherr. Its hero, Peache, is a salesman whose territory is the inhabited planets and moons. Of all the planets, he likes Mars best, for its gentle gravity, which makes walking feel like flying without frightening him.

In 2081 Peache sups with Samlaan Britt in the tower of West o' Mars, an experience he ranks with taking tea with Shah Jehan in the Taj Mahal. They smoke foot-long cigars from the Hadriacum Lowlands as the sun sets over the Aeolia Desert. Peache has heard many tales of the founding: wealth won on one throw of dice, a woman's hatred, a wife's memorial. The blurb hints that behind every man lies the influence of a woman, in odd forms.
72-thuvia-maid-of-mars:
Carthoris, son of John Carter, loves Thuvia of Ptarth, but custom and war stand between them. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Thuvia, Maid of Mars, fourth in the Barsoom series, opens in the royal gardens where a suitor presses his case. Thuvia is soon swept into slavery, treachery, and a war between cities.

Chapters carry her through phantom bowmen, the Jeddak of Lothar, and the hall of doom. Carthoris fights green men and white apes to reach her, aided by the bowman Kar Komak. A glossary of Martian names and terms closes the volume. The romance keeps Burroughs's Mars vivid with duels, escapes, and strange cities.
72022-the-unpretenders:
The Unpretenders, a novel by Anne Warwick, was published by John Lane Company of New York in 1916. Warwick also wrote The Chalk Line, Victory Law, and Compensation. The contents name each chapter for a person with a deflating label: Anne, just a plain woman; Timothy, only a writer; Gladys Marie, merely a maid. Sheila is simply a society person, and Warner what else but a wag. The joke of the title is that nobody pretends to be more.

The first chapter opens on a book being written. Michael and his sister Doromea have one chapter left and need Anne's help. Anne is trimming a hat on the west porch, though she never wears one herself. Michael calls the manuscript the best she has ever helped to write. The talk runs quick and bright, and the hat, meant for a sunbonnet, comes out an incoherent cloche.
72056-how-to-know-the-wild-flowers:
How to Know the Wild Flowers, by the wife of William Starr Dana, came out in eighteen ninety-three as a guide for walkers. Marion Satterlee drew the pictures. The author quotes Richard Jefferies on the joy of learning a flower's name for the first time.

John Burroughs had wished for a handbook that sorts flowers by colour, not by hard study. Dana answers that wish, grouping white, yellow, pink, red, and blue blooms in turn. Each entry gives the name, the haunts, and the habits of a common wild flower. A short opening chapter explains terms and the chief plant families.
72356-the-caravaners:
The Caravaners is a comic novel by the author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden, printed at New York in 1910. The same writer's other books listed here are The Solitary Summer, Princess Priscilla's Fortnight, and Fraulein Schmidt and Mr Anstruther. The tale is told by a husband who finds his flat dull once a few fine days come in June.

The flat, a nice well-planned one on the second floor, looks over a cemetery, yet the fine weather makes it feel a dull place. The couple long for the country, and a caravan trip follows. The picture list shows the party at their troubles: rapidly cooling eggs by lantern light, forgotten paper, and a debate over how best to treat a sausage. Edelgard, the wife, leaves her husband to bear the whole burden of opening and shutting their things.
72390-i-bring-fresh-flowers:
I Bring Fresh Flowers is a science fiction story by Robert F Young, taken from Amazing Stories for February 1964. A house note calls it a touching tale of an astronette, and links it to the line on the gentle rain from heaven and the quality of mercy.

Young opens by telling the reader that they know Rosemary Brooks, and have known her for years. As a small girl her favorite poem was Barbara Frietchie. She would poke her head from her bedroom window and cry the famous line about sparing the flag. Rosemary grew into a lovely young lady, yet the young men rarely asked her to dance. Her short, dedicated life took her through many windows, from Girl Scouts onward. Readers get a tender tale of a space age saint in a suburb key.
72473-spellbinders:
Margaret Culkin Banning wrote this novel of politics and marriage for Doran of New York in 1922. She gives Spellbinders to her father, William Culkin, who taught her of politics and philosophy. At the Brownleys' opens the tale in a drawing room.

Gage Flandon puts his wife's fur cloak round her and stands back to watch. Freda, on the stump, and City Mice follow. A husband, an ugly glimpse, and work for Freda build the middle. The convention, Gregory lectures, and Mr Sable starts something fill the climb. Gage finishes it. Barbara breaks loose and Walter's solution close the list. Banning knew the speech-making world from inside, and her spellbinders work crowds with words as their trade.
72496-the-small-bears:
The Small Bears is a science fiction story by Gene Henderson, from Fantastic Universe of nineteen fifty three. Its aliens look cute as koalas, the headnote warns, but a graveyard waits. Dead spaceships of earth litter the mystery planet that no ship returned from. The cruiser Assault dives through a gap in the planet's cloud blanket.

Below lie woods and green meadows under thin, sunlit cloud two miles high. The planet blocks earth's road to the next star system and must be cleared. The lookout cries that a plateau ahead is covered with ships at rest. They are earth ships, and one is the Conquest, first sent to scout the world. Her crew were friends of men aboard the Assault now watching in silence. A small lake of boiling lava smokes at the plateau's centre.
72504-finders-keepers:
Finders Keepers is a science fiction story by Milton Lesser. The tale appeared in Fantastic Universe in the summer of 1953. Its hero, Eddie Amhurst, wants to get married. An unseen girl moves in on his wedding day, the blurb promises.

Eddie sits on his bed in his underwear, watching a pair of scissors. The scissors rise from the dresser and march across the air of the room. They snip his new black silk socks in half, then march back. His roommate George comes in with shaving soap on his face. George lays out the plain reading: Eddie cut the socks himself. Eddie tells how the shears walked on their own legs. Wedding nerves, says George, and tells him to calm down. Lesser plays the marvel for laughs.
72508-nature-readers: Nature Readers is a school reader on the natural world, and the hosted pages open with a chart of the earth's crust. The chart lines up eras, ages, periods, and strata in columns. Beside them it sets the great groups of life, from early invertebrates to birds, mammals, and man. Such charts taught children the deep order of earth history at a glance.
72826-the-foster-sisters:
The Foster Sisters, a story of the days of Wesley and Whitefield, is a novel by Lucy Ellen Guernsey. It belongs to her Stanton Corbet Chronicles and opens in the year 1728. A Highland proverb stands on the title page: kindred to six degrees, fostership to a hundred. Early chapters recall a childhood at an old convent and move through troubles and a bishop's visit.

A midnight raid, a summons, and a flight from the nest follow in quick order. The sisters reach Lady Throckmorton and the world of Highbeck Hall, where much of the tale unfolds. Winters, surprises, and visitors fill the hall's life, with news from the north stirring the plot. Guernsey sets her story in the years when Wesley and Whitefield were remaking English religion. Her tale mixes family loyalty with the stirrings of the great revival, in a warm historical style.
72913-beyond-the-stars:
Beyond the Stars is a science fiction novel by Ray Cummings, shown here in the Ace Books edition of 1963 at New York. The tale first ran as a serial in Argosy All-Story Magazine, and Cummings gives the book to Donald Wollheim with affectionate regard. A note at the front, drawn from the tale, pictures stars as mere electrons streaming through a vehicle larger than the universe itself.

The story opens in May 1998, with the narrator as third commander of Liner 40 N, running twenty-eight minutes late at the Azores. A saying in the Service holds that when Liner 40 N runs late, the whole world waits. The first chapter is a call for help, and the voyage turns toward a cosmos beyond the stars.
72919-the-gold-hunters:
The Gold Hunters is a first-hand picture of California mining camps by Borthwick, printed at New York in 1917. Horace Kephart edited the account for the Outing Adventure Library. Its scenes belong to the early fifties, when the gold rush stood at full height. Twenty-seven chapters run from the isthmus crossing to the resourceful Americans.

The opening chapter dates the fever to the start of 1851. Men of all ages left their work to chase sudden wealth in the land of gold. The Panama steamship office in New York was mobbed for tickets. Later chapters treat miners' law, lynch law, and a bull and bear fight. Borthwick writes as one who was there.
73001-rube-burrow-king-of-outlaws-and-hi:
G W Agee wrote Rube Burrow, King of Outlaws, and His Band of Train Robbers as a true record. The Henneberry Company issued the book in Chicago. Agee ran the western arm of the Southern Express Company. He wrote at Memphis in December eighteen hundred ninety.

Agee says wild press tales had warped the facts for years. He built his account from reports by the men who hunted the gang. Full statements by men who rode with Burrow fill key parts. Eight train raids span close to four years. Lamar County in Alabama was the home ground of the Burrow kin. Texas raids at Bellevue and Gordon open the chase. Pinkerton men join the hunt soon after.
7304-the-life-of-captain-matthew-flinder:
Ernest Scott, professor of history at the University of Melbourne, tells the life of Captain Matthew Flinders, who died one hundred years before this book's 1914 publication. Within forty years Flinders discovered a very large area of what is now an important region of the earth. He took part in stirring events memorable in modern history, and applied a vigorous, original mind to knowledge with useful results.

Scott adds that Flinders was the victim of circumstances peculiarly unfortunate, whatever way they are stated, and bound to win sympathy from any reader who takes the trouble to understand them. Portraits, maps, and facsimiles support the text. The biography honours an explorer whose charts outlived his troubles.
73139-books-and-authors:
Books and Authors is a set of notes on books by Robert Lynd, out in nineteen twenty-three. The book is given to a friend by his marks. Two quotes at the front praise the joy of high views of great work. A note to the readers of the United States opens the text with a jest at books on books.

Lynd grants that such books are past the least needful of all. No man would pick a book of notes for a lone isle shelf, he says. Yet no shelf of one thousand best books would lack one, he holds. As town life grows, men write on books as they write on birds or flies, since books are part of the world men live in. His notes live by that rule.
73145-the-thought-feeders:
R R Winterbotham wrote The Thought-Feeders, printed in Future combined with Science Fiction for October 1941. Dr Kempster Duerkes has built the stratosphere scout, and Captain Lewis Hawes flies it. The ship stands eight miles up when the tale opens. Duerkes beams that the job is perfection itself. Hawes grants it is a neat job, no more. The two men hold each other in cheerful contempt.

Inventors think pilots over-rated, and pilots think inventors crackpots, yet the stratosphere binds them. The head note promises the living clouds they meet on high. Up there the pair find what it means to eat your words, literally. Winterbotham wrote for the pulps under several forms of his name. His stratosphere tale turns a squabble about credit into a meeting with thought-eating life above the weather.
73288-the-survivors:
Hamm wrote The Survivors, a science fiction story printed in Amazing Stories in August 1961. The tale opens after a crash on Mars. A spaceship came down on the thin roof of a cave sector in a plateau, and the ground gave way beneath it.

Soames and Rutherford went down with the ship when the fuel tanks blew. Four men remain: Bradford, Canham, Palmer, and Rodriguez. They pull themselves up, stunned and deafened, under a tower of dust. Bradford stops Palmer from rushing to the chasm, since nothing can be left of their shipmates. The four must now cross hard country toward a safety that may not save them. The magazine's blurb asks the sharp question of the piece: whose survival will it be?
73434-prof-e-h-crane-s-manual-of-instruc:
A trade manual of embalming by Professor E H Crane. Crane and Allen held the 1888 copyright at Kalamazoo, Michigan. The firm sold embalming fluid under the Excelsior name. Only its customers received this book. It was never offered for open sale. Crane promises a complete course between its covers. Lectures alone add just one thing, a live demonstration. The plates and chapters replace even that.

The contents march through the whole craft. Ancient embalming comes first. Ordinary cases and cavity injection follow. Chapters treat failed results, disinfection, and operator safety. Separate plates locate the carotid, brachial, and femoral arteries. The manual marks a turning point. Undertaking was becoming a chemical, professional trade.
73504-the-abysmal-invaders:
The Abysmal Invaders, by Edmond Hamilton, is a tale from Weird Tales, June 1929. Its record opens with the vanishing of Doctor Walter Morton in May. Morton led the world in fossil study, based at Chicago Northcote Museum. He found a rare Mesozoic bird in a Kentucky cavern in his rise.

Alone by habit, he sought old life traces in Sutter Swamp in Illinois. That swamp lay a few miles from Brinton, a tangle of pools and streams. The narrator warns that much of the invasion tale stays unknown forever. Only known facts will be told, with no theories to fill gaps. Huge shapes in the art promise death riding across a town.
73506-empty-chairs:
A memoir by Squire Bancroft, published at London in 1925. John Murray issued the first edition in March of that year. A reprint followed within a month. Bancroft was a famous actor-manager of the Victorian stage. His wife Marie appears in the frontispiece portrait. The title mourns friends now gone from their chairs.

The first chapter honours King Edward the Seventh. Bancroft was born in 1841, the king's own year. He recalls the prince's 1868 visit to his theatre. The prince came behind the scenes for the first time. A costume detail caught his exact eye. Later chapters range over church, law, painting, and literature. Two chapters return to the stage itself. One other empty chair closes the book.
73511-the-hartley-brothers:
The writer known as ALOE wrote The Hartley Brothers, or The Knights of Saint John. Gall and Inglis put it out at London and Edinburgh. The book is a sequel to two earlier volumes. Pictures of Paul and of Peter in an English Home came before it. Readers of those books know the Hartley brothers, the preface says.

Contents open with starting for India, then contrasts and balking the bear. A battle and its result, a rescue, and an attempt to serve follow. Malta and its knights give the book its second title. A desert ride, a night attack, a dark deed, and slavery fill the middle. Only one lamb, a bitter cup, and a promise stand in the later chapters. A plate shows a captain silent while a lady trembles. The tale mixes travel and faith for young readers.
73606-the-art-of-decorating-dry-goods-wi:
The Art of Decorating Dry Goods Windows and Interiors is a trade manual by Frank Baum, printed at Chicago in 1900. Baum calls it a manual of window trimming, designed as an educator in all the details of the art. The Show Window Publishing Company issued it, fully illustrated.
