Baum is better known now for Oz, but this was his bread and butter.

His introduction goes back to the packmen of ancient days, the first recognized merchants. A packman who won entry to a castle spread his goods on the floor to best advantage. If he could not open his pack, his visit bore no fruit. In old Bagdad arose the custom of open booths before the houses, with merchandise attractively displayed. From those booths Baum derives the modern shop window, without which no store, village or city, is.
73611-the-life-masters:
The Life Masters is a horror tale by Hamilton, first set in a famed pulp sheet for weird tales in the first years of the age of sound film. A note tells that no proof was found its rights were made new in law. Its doom comes first as news print.

The first word the world had of the life masters, it says, came in a wire from the great press guilds of New York. That brief note told just this. In the past day or so, the beaches round the great city had been shut to bathers. A thick scum of clear grey jelly stuff, left by the ebb tides, was the cause. The slime showed a few signs of rude life and stir. It lay too on sea walls and dock piles, and word of it came from far towns.
73703-the-devil-downstairs:
Devil Downstairs is a fantasy story by Costello, from Fantastic magazine of January 1958. A blurb gives the Devil boast as the theme of the tale in its head. Without me, you mortals would be in trouble, the Devil says in that boast. Your whole world would go to hell, he warns the reader in the blurb.

And he proved his point, the blurb goes on to say of the story. Before long the world was crying: come back, Lucifer, all is forgiven, it promises. The tale opens in a bedroom at night, where a wife shakes her husband awake in alarm. Joe, there is a burglar in the house, she cries in the first lines of the text. Costello plays the old bargain for laughs and shivers: a world that dismisses its devil, and finds the vacancy worse than the tenant.
73731-tar-and-feathers:
Victor Rubin wrote Tar and Feathers, a novel dated nineteen twenty-three and here in a third edition of nineteen twenty-four. The title page calls it a fact-based post-war romance in which the Ku Klux Klan figures largely. Reviews quoted in front praise its attack on prejudice.

The tale opens in a packed ward of an American hospital in Paris as the armistice bells ring. Robert Hamilton of Georgia lies there with McCall, a Catholic reporter from Chicago. Doctor Levin and Williams, a Harvard graduate, join the cast. Dorothy Meadows is the nurse. The Boston Transcript called the book a protest against prejudice of every kind. The New York Evening Post praised its force.
73940-life-histories-of-north-american-w:
Arthur Cleveland Bent wrote Life Histories of North American Woodpeckers, first issued in nineteen thirty-nine as a museum bulletin. The Dover edition of nineteen sixty-four reprints the work whole and unchanged. Bent wrote a long shelf of such bird life histories.

His series covers birds of prey, marsh birds, jays and crows, and wood warblers, among many others. Each volume gathers what was known of a group's haunts, nests, eggs, and habits. The woodpecker volume stands with its mates as a storehouse for bird watchers. Prices and codes on the back pages list the set. Bent's patient gathering made the series a standard work.
74022-little-sally-waters:
Ethel Calvert Phillips wrote a story book for young children, printed in Boston and New York in 1926. Edith Butler drew the pictures. Sally Waters is a merry girl with bright blue eyes, red cheeks, and a quick laugh. The first tale finds her lonely after her father and mother leave for a day in the city.

Twelve short tales follow Sally and her friends through small daily joys. A garden party, a doll named Tilly Maud, a sailor called Jolly Jack Tar, and a trip to the shore fill the pages. Mud pies, brown mice, a mermaid, and a present for Aunt Bee give each tale a fresh turn. The tales stay close to home, play, and kindness.
74104-literary-values-and-other-papers:
Literary Values and Other Papers is a book of literary essays by John Burroughs, the nature writer. The front pages list his many books, from Wake Robin and Winter Sunshine to Whitman, a study. Burroughs turns here from birds and fields to the worth and fate of books themselves. One essay opens with the writer's end.

The day inevitably comes to every writer, he writes, when he must take his place amid the silent throngs of the past. No new work from his pen can then call attention to him afresh. The partiality of his friends no longer counts, for they too are gathered to the same throng. Even the spirit of the day in which he wrote has given place to another. His essays weigh fame, style, and the use of reading, with the plain wisdom of a man who lived close to nature.
74184-the-negro-workers:
The Negro Workers is an address by Eugene Victor Debs, the American socialist leader, delivered on October 30, 1923. He spoke at Commonwealth Casino, at 135th Street and Madison Avenue in New York, under the auspices of a Socialist Party branch. The Emancipation Publishing Company issued the speech at ten cents. Randolph, editor of The Messenger, stood among the speakers who presented him.

The chairman calls it an enviable honour to present this great character and modern crusader to the audience. He notes the segregated section of the city in which they meet, and speaks with bold pride of his socialism. Debs then addresses Black workers directly, as the title promises. The pamphlet preserves a moment when the ageing Debs, freed from prison not long before, carried his message to Harlem. It is a primary record of socialist outreach to Black labour in the nineteen twenties.
742-editorials-from-the-hearst-newspaper:
Arthur Brisbane, the leading editorial voice of the Hearst newspapers, gathers his daily pieces on politics, business, and American life at the turn of the century. Brisbane wrote for millions, in short, punchy paragraphs. Brisbane edited Hearst papers in New York, where his column reached millions daily.

The editorials show Hearst journalism at its most confident, urging reform, praising progress, and scolding power. Historians of the press value the volume as a record of what ordinary readers were told, day after day. His plain style, short sentences and bold claims, set the tone for popular journalism.
7422-roman-holidays-and-others:
W. D. Howells published these travel sketches in 1908, after a lifetime of writing about Europe and America. The journey begins up and down Madeira, passes through Spain, and comes ashore at Genoa. Naples and her joyful noise, Pompeii revisited, and a week at Leghorn follow, with Pisa and Genoa again before the close.

The title piece, Roman Holidays, sits at the center: Rome seen not as a museum but as a living city on holiday. Howells writes as a familiar visitor, amused by crowds, ruins, and modern streets in the same paragraph. The book ends with Eden After the Fall, a wry coda. It is travel writing for readers who like their ruins mixed with people.
74302-the-universe-wreckers:
The Universe Wreckers, subtitled A Tale of Neptune, is a science fiction story by Edmond Hamilton. An editor's introduction frames the tale for magazine readers. It asks why so much of Neptune stays a mystery, and whether distance alone explains it. Life two thousand million miles from Earth, the editor says, opens a rich field for writers of scientific fiction.

The introduction poses a second puzzle: what if the sun, for some reason, began to spin faster and faster? Hamilton, readers are told, needs no introduction to fans of Amazing Stories. His story turns chiefly on the trip to Neptune and on the life found upon that planet. The wreckers of the title and the fate of worlds hang on what the travellers meet at the far edge of the solar system.
74496-dave-porter-s-war-honors:
Dave Porter's War Honors is a boys' novel by Edward Stratemeyer, published at Boston in 1919. Its sub-title puts Dave at the front with the fighting engineers. The frontispiece shows him bringing a gun butt down on a German's head. A foreword walks old readers through the whole series. Dave began at Oak Hall school, went west to the gold fields, and took a camp holiday in the Adirondacks. Then he gave up school for civil engineering, on the Mexican border and in Montana.

The great war in Europe then drew him in. America joined the fight, and Dave became an army engineer. A past volume told his adventures under fire in France. In this book he is still at the front with his unit. The tale is one of the long Dave Porter run, made for boys who liked war work told plain and fast.
74528-an-essay-on-the-preservation-of-sh:
An Essay on the Preservation of Shipwrecked Mariners is a prize essay by Fothergill, a physician and fellow of the Royal Society. It was printed in London in 1799 for the Royal Humane Society, at two shillings and sixpence. The society had offered prizes for answers to three questions.

The questions stand on the title page. What are the best means of preserving mariners from shipwreck? How can the vessel be kept afloat? And how can help reach the crew when boats dare not venture out to their aid? Fothergill dedicates the essay, under the king as patron, to the society's president and officers. The book belongs to the first age of organized lifesaving, when doctors and seamen joined to make the sea less deadly by method rather than by luck.
74529-thirty-one-brothers-and-sisters:
Reba Paeff Mirsky wrote Thirty-One Brothers and Sisters, for Wilcox and Follett in 1952. Mars drew the pictures for the Chicago book. The tale is set on the South African veld, the cover copy says. Gentle rolling hills and green meadows, watered by streams, form its ground. Nomusa, daughter of a Zulu chief, stands at its heart.

Nomusa is warmhearted, generous, and fond of her many little brothers and sisters. She loves helping to care for them, the copy adds. But she is strong, brave, and daring too, and finds girls' work dull. Boys' work seems far more exciting and fun to her. More than all else, she yearns to join the men on the elephant hunt. Girls never go on elephant hunts, her mother tells her. A fierce wild boar gives her the chance to prove her courage.
74652-the-world-s-leading-conquerors:
The World's Leading Conquerors, by Bevan, professor of history at the University of the South, was published at New York in 1913 by Henry Holt and Company. The book belongs to the World's Leaders set of biographies, edited by Trent, with companion volumes on the leading poets and painters. Portraits illustrate the lives.

Six subjects make the volume: Alexander the Great, Caesar, Charles the Great, the Ottoman sultans, the Spanish conquistadors, and Napoleon. The Alexander chapters run from the conquest of Greece through Persia to the invasion of India and the shape of his empire. The Caesar chapters open with his beginnings and his alliance with Pompeius and Crassus, then take up the conquest of Gaul and the break with Pompeius and the senate.
74809-stokers-and-pokers:
An anonymous author, signing as the writer of Bubbles from the Brunnen of Nassau, published rough sketches of railway life at London in 1849. The sketches cover the London and North Western Railway. They also treat the electric telegraph and the railway clearing house. John Murray issued the book at Albemarle Street. The dedication addresses railway travellers. It also addresses the proprietors of a dozen British railways, from the Great Western to the Caledonian.

The sketches delineate the difficulties of building, maintaining, and working a railway. Stokers and pokers were the men who fired engines and tended signals. The book explains the new railway system to its users. The clearing house divided receipts among companies. Murray sold many such railway guides.
74925-the-greek-orators:
Dobson, a professor of Greek at the University of Bristol, wrote The Greek Orators. Methuen of London first published the book in 1919. Twelve chapters trace public speech in ancient Greece. The story runs from the beginnings of oratory to its decline.

The first chapter roots oratory in early society. Where no king's word settles a question, the side that argues best prevails. Dobson then treats the great speakers one by one. Antiphon and Lysias stand early in the line. Isaeus and Isocrates follow, with lesser rhetoricians between. Aeschines gets a chapter before the giant of the field. Demosthenes fills the longest study in the book. Phocion, Lycurgus, Hyperides, and Dinarchus share the closing lives.
75015-flood-waters:
Flood Waters, a tale by Leland S Jamieson with drawings by Paul Lehman, tells of flight and flood in hard rain. Jamieson was a Kelly Field pilot. He had earlier written The Affair of the Juxacanna and other tales. The head note calls the piece a stirring tale of adventure. Rain is the first foe in the tale.

For a week rain falls with scarce a break from low grey skies. Roads turn to mire and cars sink deep and stick fast. Horse teams drag wagons piled high with the goods of folk who flee their homes. Gaunt men with blackened faces trudge through the wet. A plate shows a plane tipping as its right wing tip strikes a bank. Air skill and flood peril drive the action.
7504-tom-of-the-raiders:
Austin Bishop's Civil War story follows Tom with the Second Ohio into one of the war's boldest strokes. The chapters map the adventure: the raiders start, Tom is arrested, Tom goes alone, Tom arrives at the Beeghams', and on to Chattanooga and Marietta. Then the train is captured, and the race begins.

Pursuit, speeding northward, fighting with fire, and fighting the river follow, as Tom and his companions run for the Tennessee line with the enemy after them. Morgan Dennis's illustrations picture Tom feeding logs into the flames. The book is a boys' tale of the great train raid, told at full gallop, ending with Tom reporting at headquarters.
7509-the-logbooks-of-the-lady-nelson-wit:
Ida Lee, author of The Coming of the British to Australia, gathered the logbooks of the Lady Nelson in one volume. The little Australian discovery ship's story comes with the journal of her first commander, Lieutenant James Grant of the Royal Navy. Sixteen charts and illustrations from the originals in the Admiralty Library accompany the text. Lee dedicated the book to her grandfather, William Lee, one of Australia's pioneers.

Grant's story is paraphrased in places, since he sometimes writes in diary form under date headings and sometimes inserts the date into his narrative. The Lady Nelson's voyages, undertaken for discovery, make her logbooks of more than ordinary interest. The volume preserves the working record of early Australian coastal exploration, in the words of the men who sailed it.
75191-opposite-neighbours:
Opposite Neighbours, or The Two Lives and their End, was written by Lucy Ellen Guernsey. The American Sunday-School Union issued it at Philadelphia in 1867. A frontispiece shows a question: Letty, are you really going to be married? Chapter one opens on that point. Mrs Trescott, paring quinces in an old wrapper, talks with her chambermaid. Letty Bright has served her long and won her high regard. John Caswell has courted Letty for six months and more.

Mrs Trescott calls him a good, steady young man, worthy of her maid. Eighteen chapters follow the two households of the title. A will, losses, a baby, and restitution mark the turns. Mischief-making and a removal darken the middle. Peace at last and a last glimpse close the tale of neighbours set side by side.
7542-quotes-and-images-from-the-novels-o:
Georg Ebers, the German Egyptologist turned novelist, wrote historical romances once read across Europe, and this volume collects short passages and pictures from them. Portraits and illustrations introduce the novels: Uarda, Cleopatra, Margery, Homo Sum, the Recluse, and In the Fire of the Forge. Any passage can be searched to find its full context in the eBook below.

Read together, the passages sketch Ebers's moral world: Egypt and Germany, ancient and modern, seen through private choices. First impressions, small joys, timely words, and the claims of honor recur across them. The pictures help a new reader tell the novels apart. It is a pleasant way into Ebers: short, vivid samples before choosing a romance to read whole.
75488-the-purple-sickle-murders:
The Purple Sickle Murders is a detective novel by Freeman Wills Crofts, copyrighted in 1929. It features Inspector Joseph French of Scotland Yard. The first chapter opens with French writing steadily in his room on Victoria Embankment. His desk is covered with sheets of memorandum paper in his small, neat hand.

The contents promise an inquest, a trip to Lee-on-the-Solent, and a grey car's round. French makes assignations, plays the cracksman, and studies the car's freight. Crofts built his tales on timetables, routes, and patient checks of fact. French, his quiet inspector, solves by method what others miss by brilliance. This case turns on transport and supplies, in the author's best manner.
75499-the-star-jewels-and-other-wonders:
The Star Jewels and Other Wonders is a book of tales for the young by Abbie Farwell Brown. Pictures by Ethel C. Brown go with the tales. The front pages list the other works of the author, with their prices. Among them are The Flower Princess, The Curious Book of Birds, and A Pocketful of Posies. In the Days of Giants and The Book of Saints and Friendly Beasts stand in the list as well.

The title tale is called The Star Jewels, and the rest of the book holds more wonders, as its name states. A picture of Wavilocks and the Crab, from a page of the book, is named in the front matter. The volume is a set of fancy tales for children, from a writer known for her books of myth, saints, and beasts for the young.
75729-the-river-of-stars:
The River of Stars is a novel by Edgar Wallace, printed at London and Melbourne. Ward, Lock issued it among his popular novels, after Sanders of the River and Bones. Wallace dedicates the book to his sister Gladys Gane. Nineteen chapters and a prologue carry the tale, from Amber to the chapter the last.

The prologue opens on a bush road from Alebi, a track scarcely marked. Sutton is warned that the affair has already cost a lot of money. If he locates the mine, he must bring back samples and exact bearings. Above all he must fix where the River lies. Wallace builds his tale of diamonds, maps, and double dealing in the African bush.
75908-music-and-bad-manners:
Carl Van Vechten wrote a set of bright essays on music, issued by Alfred Knopf in New York in 1916. The lead essay gives the book its name and rounds up tales of rude acts by famed singers and players. Beethoven's storms, Wagner's spite, and Chopin's sulks all get a place in the tale.

Van Vechten is fair and blames crowds too, for fans sit mute through weak shows far too often. Other essays treat music for the movies, Spain and its music, and the aims of Wagner. One long piece weighs a new rule in music, and one treats the bold young player Leo Ornstein. The tone is witty and well read.
75913-no-stop-overs:
John Thompson wrote No Stop-Overs, a tale of railroading in Alaska in the days of the gold camps. The lure of the diggings on the Kougarok pulls every able man from his job, and the railroad from Nome faces a spring rush short-handed. Firemen are given regular runs, and call boys stout enough to lift a slice bar are set to firing. Still the new drivers keep quitting at the far end to dig for gold.

Sam Tebbetts and Plapp stand out as men who stay. One runaway brakeman even staked his claim with signal flags stolen from the road. The worn superintendent at Nome, bent over his morning reports, gets a strange visitor: a pint-size man in overalls cut for a giant, with cuffs rolled near knee-high. The tale mixes the hard facts of rail work with frontier humor.
76085-rival-ocean-divers:
Rival Ocean Divers, or The Search for a Sunken Treasure, by Roy Rockwood, was copyrighted as a serial in 1900 and published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Thirty-one chapters promise an ocean monster, a prisoner underground, a jaguar, a gorilla fight, a diving bell, and the treasure at last. Dave Fearless, a lad of seventeen, leads the hunt.

Chapter one has Dave pressing his father, Amos Fearless, once a sea captain and marine architect. A million dollars, the captain says, lies at the bottom of the sea, and more may be there. The money would belong to the finders. But the Hanker family claims the Washington fortune too, through the same kinship. Rockwood launches a boys' sea adventure of rival divers and deep-water perils.
76211-mamba-s-daughters:
Du Bose Heyward wrote a novel of Charleston printed at New York in 1929 by the Literary Guild. Heyward had written Angel, Skylines and Horizons, and Porgy, both as novel and as a play with Dorothy Heyward. Because regional writing, even avowed fiction, should be plain in its tie to its place, he has used the correct names of the city, streets, and districts, he says.

Lest this lead the reader to confuse the tale with history or biography, he stresses that the work is purely imagined. It treats certain social and spiritual values in Charleston and its environs. The phosphate mining camp stands for more than one industry in his synthesis. It was no mere chance that brought Mamba out of the darkness of the underworld into the light of the Wentworths' kitchen, the tale begins. Race and caste turn on that door.
76284-paul-and-his-interpreters:
It was translated by Montgomery. Schweitzer was a lecturer in New Testament studies at the University of Strassburg. He had already written The Quest of the Historical Jesus. The German title of that earlier book, From Reimarus to Wrede, is named at the head of this one.

In his preface Schweitzer lays out the great task of his field. Strauss and Renan, he says, saw this duty and tried to trace the path. Since their time, no writer on the life of Jesus has followed it. The history of dogma, for its part, starts with the Greek period and leaves the steps from Jesus to Paul unexplained. So the whole building lacks a firm base. This book takes up Paul and the men who have read him, to lay that base.
76653-the-patriarch-of-one-hundred-years:
Patriarch of One Hundred Years gives the reminiscences of Henry Boehm. Wakeley wrote the life, with chapters added on the hundredth birthday. Nelson and Phillips published it in New York in the year 1875. Boehm was born on June 8, 1775, and died in 1875 at one hundred. An engraving by Ritchie shows his signed portrait at the front.

Extra chapters print his centennial sermons at Jersey City and New York. Addresses then delivered stand phonographically reported for the reader verbatim. His sermon before the Newark Conference joins that record of honour. Wakeley inscribes the volume to the bishops of the Methodist Episcopal Church. They are hailed as worthy successors of the apostolic Asbury in faith.
76857-i-mars:
I, Mars is a short tale by Ray Bradbury of a man lost in time. Old Emil Barton sits alone on Mars in the year 2097. No rocket has come from Earth to save him in sixty years. On his eightieth birthday his dead phone rings at last in the dark. The voice on the line claims to be Barton himself at twenty.

His younger selves live on in that strange link of years. They hate the old man for what his long life proves true. Their hopes are dead, and his lone age is the proof of it. He begs to warn the boy of the lone years ahead of him. Kill yourself, he cries, rather than turn into what I am. The tale turns on time, age, and a self that can warn itself.
76965-the-counterfeiters:
The Counterfeiters is a novel by André Gide, translated from the French by Dorothy Bussy and published by Knopf in New York in 1927. The French original, Les Faux-Monnayeurs, appeared in Paris in 1925, and seven printings followed within months of this edition. Gide dedicates it to Roger Martin du Gard in token of profound friendship, calling it, remarkably, his first novel.

The first part is set in Paris. Its chapters move from the Luxembourg Gardens to the Profitendieu family, then Bernard and Olivier, Vincent and the Comte de Passavant, and Edouard and Laura. Edouard's journal interrupts the narrative, recording visits and a wedding. A passage preserved in the copy catches Bernard alone at home. The time has now come, he says to himself, for me to hear a step in the passage.
77004-the-story-of-the-sun-moon-and-star:
The Story of the Sun, Moon, and Stars is an astronomy book for general readers by Agnes Giberne, issued in an edition of 1898 with additions. Giberne had written other sky books, named on the title page. A front picture shows an ancient astronomer in his observatory at Alexandria. An Oxford professor of astronomy supplies the introduction.

In that introduction the professor tells how the pages came to him while passing through the press. A friend asked him to mark any points that might improve the work. At first he took up the task with hesitation, he admits. But a rapid reading of the first sheet woke his interest, and then held it fast. The book, he judged, had features of no ordinary kind and promised to supply a clear want.
77320-fatal-fingers:
Fatal Fingers, A Mystery, by William Le Queux, was published by Cassell in 1914. The first chapter mainly concerns Richard Goodrick, a thin, white bearded old man in a stuffy little room where he has hidden for eighteen years, believed dead. A stout visitor offers him fifty thousand pounds.

Goodrick calls the offer bribery and throws it back, though the money touches his son Gordon, a girl named Maidee, and a secret carried to the supposed grave. Thirty chapters of confessions, treachery, and faded ink follow. Le Queux, the tireless thriller writer of his day, opens at full pressure and never lets the parlour cool.
77346-strange-waters:
Strange Waters is a sea story by Kingsbury Scott, opening with a threat in a ship’s fire hole. A voice vows to brain the first man who tries to get out of that place. Old Tim Donahue is the hero of the piece. The blurb says he shows that not all sea fighters are in the navy.

Captain Daniel Sullivan and little Tim Donahue had little in common. Their lives had never touched in fifty years on earth. Then came a day on board the Aurora, and a brief flash of contact. That short meeting had no direct bearing on the career of the captain. For Tim it swept him out of the ranks of everyday men. It set him in the pages of history itself, the tale promises.
77379-the-twin-seven-shooters:
The Twin Seven-Shooters is a Civil War memoir by Charles Manderson. Manderson had been colonel of an Ohio volunteer regiment and a brevet general. Neely published the book at New York and London in 1902. A portrait of the author in uniform faces the title page.

The book tells the true story of a pair of revolvers, the author writes. The two guns were presented, captured, and at last brought together again. They had spent a quarter century apart, carried under two flags. Comrades who knew the tale urged him to print it. Manderson praises both sides for fighting without personal hatred. The story frames accounts of two great battles. Murfreesboro, one of the hardest fought fields, and Chattanooga supply the scenes.
77415-american-lace-lace-makers:
American Lace and Lace-Makers, by Emily Noyes Vanderpoel, was published at New Haven in 1924. Yale University Press issued it on a memorial fund. Elizabeth Buel edited the work. Vanderpoel had written Color Problems and Chronicles of a Pioneer School. A front plate shows black net stitched with coloured carnations. Caroline Canfield made that piece, held at Litchfield in Connecticut. Contents promise an introduction, then plates and descriptions.

A list names each plate, its maker, and the owner of the original. Museums in New York, Boston, and Salem hold many pieces. The memorial fund recalls Amasa Stone Mather, of the Yale class of 1907. The book honours hand work by American women and keeps their names with their lace.
77464-a-fishing-trip-on-the-planet-mars:
A Fishing Trip on the Planet Mars is a short tale by Sidney, framed as a true trip told by the man who made it. An editors note at the head asks how a trip to Mars feels. It points to the tale as the reply. The teller sets out on a fine day in his summer rest, rod and lunch in hand.

He fishes a stream till noon with no bite at all. Then he sits to eat in the shade of a tree. A strange flower near his seat draws his eye. As he steps to it, the flower is gone. He feels himself drawn up into space. With no soul in sight to aid him, he yells in vain as he shoots up through the clouds.
77500-the-talkers:
Talkers is a novel by Robert Chambers, published by Doran at New York, copyrighted in 1923. Chambers is named as author of The Flaming Jewel, The Slayer of Souls, and The Common Law. The book is dedicated to his friend Robert Davis, the editor, in its front pages. Chapter one introduces a man called Sadoul to the reader at once.

Sadoul only experiences in love had been gross, the first line says of the hero. The cynic in him admitted nothing better, the narrator adds of his temper. Saturnine, without delusions, he went about his business in life in the account.  Chambers, famous first for tales of the unseen, fills this late novel with the talk of studios and salons, and with a cynic who talks better than he lives.
776-hermione-and-her-little-group-of-ser:
Don Marquis creates Hermione, a fashionable young woman who takes up every serious thought of the day and talks it to death. Her little group of thinkers meets to discuss art, souls, and the new psychology, with great earnestness. Marquis created Hermione for the New York Sun, where her chatter delighted readers.

Marquis writes the sketches as Hermione's own chatter, and the comedy lies in her confident misuse of big ideas. The book satirises a whole generation of drawing-room intellectuals, and its heroine remains delightfully unaware. Her group, earnest and vague, mirrors real drawing-room fashions for Bergson, Freud, and souls.
7762-wanderers:
Knut Hamsun's Wanderers, translated by W. W. Worster, joins two volumes, Under the Autumn Star and A Wanderer Plays on Muted Strings, under one title. Its center is Knut Pedersen from the Northlands, through whose eyes the fates of Captain Falkenberg and his wife slowly unfold.

Worster's introduction calls the books close to diaries, mirroring Hamsun's moods and known life events with unusual candor. Read with the sequel The Last Joy, they form a psychological record as much as a story, tracing a wanderer's mind through autumn roads and muted music.
77644-the-troubadours:
The Troubadours is a history of Provençal life and literature in the middle ages. Francis Hueffer wrote it, and Chatto and Windus published it in London in 1878. A verse from Keats serves as its motto. Hueffer's preface claims a first for the book. He calls it the first continuous and adequate English account of the subject. Magazine pieces of his own fed into it, but the book is no reprint.

English neglect of the langue d'oc struck Hueffer as glaring. English critics had honoured old French literature for generations. Yet the troubadours flourished in lands then tied to the English crown. Only a poor version of Millot's work stood on English shelves. Hueffer sets out to give the poet singers of Provence their due. Their loves and lyrics form the heart of the survey.
7766-a-dog-of-flanders:
Louisa de la Ramee, writing as Ouida, tells of Nello and Patrasche in A Dog of Flanders, with color pictures by Maria L. Kirk. A Flemish boy and a big Flemish dog, both orphaned and poor, share a hut a league from Antwerp, among pastures, cornlands, and poplar lines.

Their bond, closer than brotherhood, grows from a shared rescue and daily toil pulling a cart. Nello draws with charcoal and dreams of art, while Patrasche pulls beside him. The tale is a tender classic of loyalty, poverty, and a child's hope, known to readers far beyond Flanders.
77665-the-man-who-had-spiders:
Roger Dee's story The Man Who Had Spiders opens with an editor's note comparing him to Saki, the master of whimsical fantasy. Its hero is Adrian, a new boarder whose way with spiders is the centre of the tale.

Marcus, a travelling salesman who has sold novelties to novelty shops for forty years, comes back to Maysville on the 8:04 train for his regular April week of selling. At the Ponder boarding house he finds blind Kitty at the piano, playing Delibes, her face lighting up at the hope that the step she hears is Adrian's. The editor's note promises that Adrian's cure for a tragic addiction to alcohol is as shuddery as a smiling Medusa. Dee lets a quiet boarding house hold the strangeness.
77842-microbe-hunters:
Microbe Hunters is a popular history of the men who first tracked germs, by Paul de Kruif. It was published in New York by Harcourt, Brace in 1926. Plates show the hunters at their work, from Leeuwenhoek's lenses to the last portrait of Ehrlich.

The chapters march in time. Leeuwenhoek comes first, the obscure Dutchman who saw a new world of tiny beings two hundred and fifty years ago. Spallanzani proves that microbes must have parents. Pasteur shows them as a menace, and then masters the mad dog. Koch fights death in his laboratory. Roux and Behring, Metchnikoff, and Theobald Smith follow. Bruce trails the tsetse fly, Ross fights Grassi over malaria, and Walter Reed works in Cuba. Ehrlich and his magic bullet close the tale.
78051-borrowed-feathers:
Borrowed Feathers, by Ruth Lamb, appeared in London in 1886 as an extra summer number of The Girl's Own Annual, volume 7. Only three chapters make up the short tale. The heroine, Annette Clifford, opens the story alone in a large house, talking to herself at the sound of the doorbell.

Annette calls herself Cinderella and plans to pull the front blinds so callers will think no one is home. She is bright, lively, and full of spirits, with no one to talk to but a deaf, makeshift servant. A humble cab, not a grand carriage, waits at the door. Lamb sets up a tale of pride, show, and a girl who must face callers and herself.
781-sinking-of-the-titanic-and-great-sea:
Logan Marshall edited this account of the Titanic's loss and of other great sea disasters, written soon after the event. The Titanic, the largest and finest steamship of her day, struck an iceberg on her maiden voyage, 600 miles southeast of Halifax, with more than 2,300 souls aboard. The book tells of the collision, the boats, and the rescue.

Other chapters gather wrecks and heroics from the age of steam, with portraits of captains, crews, and passengers. Marshall writes for a popular audience, with a moral eye on pride, speed, and the lack of boats. The book is a vivid, if partisan, record of how the world first learned of the disaster, and why it shocked the age.
78112-astronomy-for-beginners:
Astronomy for Beginners is a primer by Hereward Carrington, issued in 1925. Haldeman-Julius published it as Little Blue Book number 895. Carrington had written other beginner books in the same series. His contents run from astrology to curved space in some fifty pages. The solar system is taken planet by planet. Sun, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars come in order.

Jupiter through Neptune follow, then the minor planets and the moon. The origin of the solar system gets its own short chapter. Constellations, meteors, comets, and nebulae fill the middle. Star distances, temperatures, and double and variable stars come next. Eclipses, telescopes, and the spectroscope close the survey of tools. Tides, gravitation, calendars, and the aurora end the book. Egyptians and Babylonians open it as the first astronomers.
78235-sea-whispers:
Sea Whispers, a book of tales by Jacobs, was published at New York in 1927. Scribner issued it with copyright taken in 1926 and pictures by Bert Thomas. Twelve tales make up the contents of the volume for his readers. The Bravo opens the set, and Taking Pains follows as the second story.

His Brother Keeper, Trust Money, and Kitchen Company fill the middle of the list. The Model, Artful Cards, and Handsome Harry carry the Wapping world of the tales. The Blindness of Captain Ferguson and Wapping on Thames close the named heads. A dedication keeps the memory of his friend James Pinker at the front. Jacobs sailors, night watchmen, and riverside rogues fill these comic sea tales.
78356-the-andaman-islanders:
Brown wrote The Andaman Islanders, a study in social anthropology, for Cambridge in 1922. The work grew from the Anthony Wilkin Studentship research of 1906. Brown had been a fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge. He gives the book to Haddon and Rivers, whose teaching and kind encouragement made it. Whatever value it holds, he says, is due to them, as a work of apprenticeship. A front plate shows an islander shooting fish with bow and arrow at Port Blair.

Parts treat social order, ceremonial customs, and beliefs in religion and magic. Myths and legends get a full part, and two more parts interpret all the rest. Appendices treat the tools and craft of the islanders and the spelling of their words. Plates show dress, clay paint, villages, and bows. Brown gives a deep, careful record of a small island people.
78481-miss-bracegirdle-and-others:
Stacy Aumonier published a volume of short stories at Garden City in 1923, with copyrights running back to 1916. Miss Bracegirdle Does Her Duty heads the contents. Where Was Wych Street follows, then The Octave of Jealousy. The Funny Man's Day and The Beautiful, Merciless Lady come next. The Accident of Crime closes the visible list.

Aumonier's other books are listed at the front: Olga Bardel, Querrils, and The Golden Windmill among them. Doubleday issued the collection in a first edition. Aumonier wrote polished short fiction of English middle class life. His stories turn on small incidents and quiet ironies rather than large events.
78529-a-little-girl-in-tears:
A Little Girl in Tears is a comic story by Ellis Parker Butler. The hosted text opens in a rich man's club in New York. Morley Smith, a clubman close to fifty, has caught a taste for adventure from a chance book.

One night he let the check-boy help him into his costly fur-lined coat and took a cab to a house picked at random. The small thrill fed his hunger for a week. Then the urge came back. After a good dinner and his favourite wine, he sits in the smoking room in drowsy ease. Restlessness stirs under his waistcoat. The opera bores him, and the musical comedy leaves him cold. He rings the bell to go out and hunt a fresh adventure, by the rules of his private game.
7856-the-cheerful-cricket-and-others:
Jeannette Marks's The Cheerful Cricket and Others, pictured by Edith Brown and dedicated to her nephew Henry Douglas Bacon, tells insect tales for children good and bad, big or little. The cheerful cricket runs anxiously through grass, while Mrs. Cricky hunts food for Chee, Chirk, and Chirp.

Other stories bring a slothful toad, sullen caterpillar, green inch worm, mean spider, noisy fly, dizzy moth, honest ant, walking stick, ladybug, and tuneful hummingbird. A marsh grass vesper quartette sings late at night. Through small creatures, Marks teaches cheer, work, and kindness.
78722-the-toll-keepers:
Toll-Keepers and Other Stories for the Young is a tale set by Benjamin Clarke. Nimmo, Hay, and Mitchell published it at Edinburgh for young readers. Clarke also wrote My First and Last Voyage for that market. Sixteen tales fill the contents, led by The Toll-Keepers at page five. Chips from a Naval Officer's Log follows as the second piece.

A note swears those naval chips are all strictly true as told. Officers who bore witness related them to the writer himself, it says. A short account of Gibraltar, a generous enemy, and Thirsty Jack ensue. Visits to Malta, a fat captain, a convict story, and pups vary it. Bushgrove farm house, snug and rich, opens the title tale in warmth.
79007-founding-fathers:
Founding Fathers is a humorous science fantasy tale by Robert Bloch. The Founding Fathers appear in gangster roles in the opening scene. An editor's note calls it an outrageous distortion of history at first sight. Yet a turnabout climax sets history by the ears, the note promises. Dissolving that distortion into dazzling humor is Bloch's trick here.

Early on July 4, 1776, Thomas Jefferson pokes his head into Independence Hall. Come on, you guys, the coast is clear, he yells inside. John Hancock follows, puffing nervously on a cigarette in that chamber. Ditch the butt, Jefferson warns, or you will louse us up. Charles Thomson scowls at being called Nunzio by his fellow conspirator. Straighten that wig, he growls, digging Hancock in the ribs hard. Sign and keep your yap shut, Jefferson orders the signer.
79124-the-best-jokes-about-preachers:
George Milburn edited a small joke book on preachers for the Little Blue Book series, number 879 in that run. Haldeman-Julius printed it at Girard, Kansas, in 1927. Each page holds short jokes, most of them built on a brief scene and a punch line. Clergy, sermons, and church life supply the whole stock of fun.

One joke turns on a long winded preacher whose sermon, a judge says, passed all understanding and seemed to last forever. Others play on church notices gone wrong, on converts with limits to their zeal, and on frank words from the pews. The humor is broad and quick. It shows what a cheap paper book of that era thought the general reader would laugh at.
79178-monkeying-with-ancestors:
Monkeying with Ancestors is a west jest tale by Tuttle. It is told in the broad tongue of the range, in the voice of a cow hand. He and his mate Chuck sit on a truck at the stage of a town they are sick of. No coin is left for a pass on the train that rolls in, and no fair card game can be found in town, they moan.

As the goods car halts, a man is hurled out and skids past his hands and knees. A great ape comes past him, and the two roll in a clinch. The man flees past the brush with threats of a law suit in a thick tongue. The bag man grins, kicks at the ape, and boards as the train pulls out. Two broke hands and one loose ape are left on the stage.
79243-death-between-the-stars:
Death Between the Stars is a science fiction story by Marion Zimmer Bradley. The editor's note recalls her earlier story, Jackie Sees a Star, and readers' pleas for a sequel. This new tale, the note promises, charms in a somewhat different vein. Its motto says that sympathy, in the gulfs between the stars, may work a miracle.

The story opens with Miss Vargas boarding the starship Vesta. Its captain explains, again and again, that his ship is no passenger liner but a cargo carrier. Strict rules divide human from nonhuman across the western sector of the galaxy. Bradley builds the tale on that rule and on the sympathy that breaks it.
79294-clay-shuttered-doors:
Helen R Hull wrote a story of a marriage watched by a close friend. Clay-Shuttered Doors ran in Harper's Magazine, Volume 152, in May 1926. The narrator has tried for months not to think of Thalia Corson. Thalia's thin wrists, long eyelids, and blue, intense eyes haunt her still.

A glimpse of Winchester Corson's grand car showroom starts the tale churning. Summers on the Cape root the friendship, when Winchester was a rising young man. Fletcher, born too soon at seven months, marks the family's hard start. Readers gain a fine, sad study of love, pride, and distance.
7932-brook-farm-historic-and-personal-me:
John Thomas Codman wrote these memoirs of Brook Farm, the famous community founded near Boston in the 1840s. His chapters trace the movement from its Transcendentalist beginnings under George Ripley, through its reorganisation on Fourierist lines, to its industrial period. Along the way he describes Ripley, Charles Dana, Margaret Fuller-era friends, and Nathaniel Hawthorne, who lived at the farm.

Codman writes as a participant, mixing the community's constitution and daily rules with personal memories of work, walks, and wild flowers. The book is therefore both a history and a first-hand account of an American experiment in shared living. It remains a key source for anyone studying Transcendentalism, utopian communities, or Hawthorne's early circle.
79336-twisted-bars:
Twisted Bars, a western tale by Erle Stanley Gardner, opens on the Circle C outfit. Pug Parry is such a gorilla of a man that he can twist iron bars into loops. Phil Dunton is such a little fellow that the hands call him Big Hat. With the other men Phil acts respectful before the strength of Pug.

That respect lasts only until Pug trespasses on private range, the head note warns. Bill Carson, called Old Walrus for his grey drooping moustache, opens the tale in town. He casts mild blue eyes over the sun swept street and spits as he thinks. Something is going on, he says, as sure as shooting in his view. The Bar Y boys have devilment up their sleeves, he holds.
79345-stories-of-adventure-as-told-by-ad:
Stories of Adventure, as told by adventurers, is a collection made by Edward Hale for young readers, first copyrighted in 1881. A new edition, revised and illustrated, was issued at Boston in 1905. A front picture shows a great khan of Cathay at table. In his preface Hale explains the aim of this volume and its four companions in the series.

The set was proposed at a congress of librarians in Boston, he says. It was made to teach boys and girls how to use the treasures now at their hands in public libraries. The public spirit that built those libraries should be matched, he argues, by care in guiding young readers. Librarians cannot do all the work of introduction. Friends of education must show the young how to choose and enjoy good books.
7941-mrs-day-s-daughters:
Mary E. Mann set this English provincial novel in the household of Mrs William Day, opening at a New Year's party that dances into the small hours. The chapters that follow trace the Day daughters, Bessie and Deleah among them, through an office disaster, family misfortune, and the suitors, neighbours, and callers who crowd a market-town social world. Names like the Manchester man and the importunate Mr Gibbon hint at the comedy and worry mixed into the plot.

Mann writes with a keen eye for class, money, and reputation in a small community, where one setback can unsettle a whole family. The novel moves between drawing room, tea-party, and office, and its interest lies in how ordinary people recover their footing. It is a warm, observant example of the late Victorian domestic novel at its most readable.
79489-the-grandmothers:
Grandmothers, by Glenway Wescott, is a family portrait in narrative form. Harper and Brothers issued the book in New York and London in nineteen twenty seven. A grandmother line fronts it, urging children to get out the photographs. Fifteen chapters trace Alwyn Tower knowledge of his kin and his land.

Contents move from Alwyn as a small boy and his grandmother keepsakes. Grandfather Tower character, a soldier sweetheart tale, and great aunts follow in turn. A deserter uncle, a minister uncle, and his mother girlhood fill later parts. Maternal grandparents Ira and Ursula Duff earn their own late chapter. A memorandum on the Tower family tree guides the reader through.
79490-on-the-theory-of-light-and-colours:
On the Theory of Light and Colours is a lecture by Thomas Young, read to the Royal Society on November 12, 1801. It was printed in the Philosophical Transactions in 1802 as the Bakerian Lecture. Young was then professor of natural philosophy at the Royal Institution.

Young argues that light moves in waves, as sound does, rather than as a stream of particles. He draws older writers, above all Hooke, into his case, and sets the wave view against the system of Newton. The lecture is one of the founding papers of the wave theory of light. Later work on interference grew from the path it opened.
79497-the-radio-gun-runners:
Ralph Milne Farley spun a tale of crime on the sea that ran in Argosy from February 22 to March 29, 1930. Tom Jones had just taken his degree at Harvard with high honors. He was sailing his seventy five foot yacht Miami toward Labrador to visit friends in Grenfell's colony. Then fate, in the shape of a gangster called Scarface Boston Jimmy, changed his plans.

The yacht lay at anchor off Belle Isle on the Newfoundland coast. Jones fished in the shade of the pilot house with a crewman, Mike Murphy, a Cambridge policeman asked along for fun. A strange boat bumped the Miami, and Mike went to look. He did not come back. Jones found him bound and gagged, with gangsters at work on deck. Boxes marked canned goods were coming aboard from the raiders' craft. The tale is a brisk pulp yarn of hijack, radio, and nerve.
79566-seven-brothers:
Seven Brothers, the Finnish novel by Alexis Kivi, opens on Jukola farm. Alex Matson turned the tale into English from the Finnish tongue. Faber and Faber of London first put this version out in 1929. Jukola stands on a hill slope north in the province of Häme. Fields, a clover meadow, and vast wild woods ring the old farm.

Seven sons of that farm are the heroes of the long tale. Juhani is the eldest at twenty-five, and Eero the youngest of all. Tuomas and Aapo are twins, and so are Timo and Lauri. Broad Tuomas is famed for the great width of his shoulders. Brown skin and stiff, hemp-like hair mark all seven alike in looks. The farm's founder won its wide woods by a shrewd land deal.
79737-myself-and-others:
Jessie Millward, a famed stage actress, tells the story of her life with help from Booth, in a book printed in London in 1923. Eighteen pictures fill the book. Her father Charles Millward opens the tale, and her early days follow. The stage world of London and America in her time stands behind every chapter.

Millward writes of Henry Irving, the Lyceum, the Adelphi, and Drury Lane. She tells of her first trip to America, of William Terriss, and of Charles Frohman. A list at the end names the parts she played. Readers who love the old stage will find names, houses, and plays recalled by one who lived among them at the top.
7994-the-crayon-papers:
Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. , the pen name of Washington Irving, gathered these miscellaneous papers under his familiar byline. They range widely: Mountjoy, or passages from the life of a castle-builder; the Great Mississippi Bubble, a time of unexampled prosperity; Don Juan as a spectral research; Broek, or the Dutch paradise. Sketches in Paris in 1825, including the Tuileries, Windsor Castle, and the field of Waterloo; American researches in Italy; and early experiences of Ralph Ringwood, plus Seminole traditions.

The collection shows Irving in his most roaming mood, mixing travel, history, legend, and humour. Each paper stands alone, so the book can be dipped into anywhere. For readers who know The Sketch Book, it offers more of the same urbane pleasure, and a reminder of how widely Irving travelled in search of stories.
8004-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Numbers, the fourth book of the Bible, takes its name from the censuses that open and close it, counting Israel's tribes in the wilderness. Between the counts lies forty years of wandering: complaints about food, rebellion against Moses, the report of spies who feared Canaan, and the death of the generation that left Egypt. Only Caleb and Joshua, of that generation, will enter the land, and the book ends with Israel camped across the Jordan.

The book is frank about a people's failures, showing how fear and grumbling delay promise. Its laws about priests, vows, and inheritance sit inside a travel story that never quite arrives. In the King James Version, Numbers reads as a long, honest middle chapter: between deliverance and home, with a whole generation lost on the way.
8110-lincoln-letters:
Abraham Lincoln's letters, published by the Bibliophile Society, are presented as so characteristic of the man and so self-explanatory that they need no comment. The editor notes philosophical admonitions to Lincoln's brother Johnston written on the same sheet as a letter to his father, and an unequivocal order to the Attorney-General. Endorsed on a pardon request, showing how promptly Lincoln despatched affairs during the most turbulent scenes of the Civil War.

The letters range from family counsel to presidential orders, and their plain, direct style is Lincoln's own. Readers meet the president without a biographer's filter: patient, humorous, and decisive. For students of Lincoln, the volume is a compact source, and for general readers, a moving introduction to his character in his own words.
8140-lectures-of-col-r-g-ingersoll-volum:
Robert G. Ingersoll's first volume of lectures gathers his famous freethought orations, including Gods, Ghosts, Hell, Individuality, Humboldt, Which Way, The Great Infidels. Talmagian Theology, and The Mistakes of Moses, with his answers to the clergy and his oration at his brother's grave. The lecture on Gods opens with his claim that an honest god is the noblest work of man, and that each nation creates a god resembling its creators.

Ingersoll, the Great Agnostic, drew huge crowds with eloquence, humour, and moral argument against orthodoxy. His lectures made freethought respectable in Gilded Age America, and his defence of reason still reads with force. For readers interested in American religious debate, this volume is the essential Ingersoll, in his own rousing voice.
8154-revolutionary-heroes-and-other-hist:
James Parton, author of lives of Horace Greeley, Andrew Jackson, and Benjamin Franklin, wrote these historical papers for the Historical Classic Readings series, number ten. His subjects include General Joseph Warren, Captain Nathan Hale, Washington's spies, Robert Morris, Valley Forge, John Jay, John Adams, Fisher Ames, and the Pinckneys. Parton himself was born in Canterbury, England, in 1822, brought to America at five, and educated in New York.

The papers are short, vivid lives and episodes from the Revolution, written for schools and general readers. Parton was a popular biographer, and his sketches favour anecdote and character over theory. For students of the Revolution, the volume offers an old-fashioned but engaging gallery of its heroes, in the style that once taught American history.
8157-esther-waters:
George Moore published Esther Waters in 1899, opening with a young woman of twenty on a railway platform, watching a receding train. She wears a faded yellow dress and a black jacket too warm for the day. And beside her lies an oblong box tied with rope, while the bundle she carries bulges with dead weight. From that arrival, the novel follows Esther, a servant girl, through work, seduction, single motherhood, and the struggle to keep herself and her child respectable.

Moore wrote with the frankness of French naturalism, refusing to soften Esther's hardships or to condemn her. The novel's power lies in its heroine's endurance and in its picture of domestic service and horse-racing society. It remains one of the great English novels of working-class life, and Moore's most humane book.
8231-the-world-english-bible-web-numbers:
Numbers, in the World English Bible, opens with Yahweh speaking to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the Tent of Meeting, in the second year after the Exodus. Commanding a census of Israel by families and fathers' houses, every male from twenty years old and upward able to go to war, numbered by divisions with a head of each tribe. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book follows the wilderness wanderings that give it its name.

The modern version keeps the counts, camps, and complaints in order, so the forty years of delay read as a coherent journey. Numbers here shows a people learning, through failure, toward the promised land. For readers working through the Pentateuch, this rendering makes a long book easier to follow.
8377-the-water-ghost-and-others:
John Kendrick Bangs, the American humorist, gathers ghost stories with a comic twist in this volume. Contents include The Water Ghost of Harrowby Hall, The Spectre Cook of Bangletop, and A Speck on the Lens. A Midnight Visitor and The Ghost Club follow, along with the literary remains of Thomas Bragdon. Bangs treats the supernatural as a chance for jokes rather than terror.

His ghosts complain, cook, and join clubs, and the humor lies in treating them as ordinary, tiresome company. Readers who like ghost stories without dread, in the vein of Bangs's popular humorous fiction, will find the book light and clever. It is a good introduction to a writer who made the afterlife funny.
8424-mohun-or-the-last-days-of-lee-and-h:
John Esten Cooke presents this novel as the final memoirs of Colonel Surry of Eagle's Nest, a staff officer serving in Virginia, and it tells the last days of Robert E. Lee and his paladins. Two crossed swords hang over the mantel in Surry's quiet study, and the prologue turns from that peace to the closing campaigns of the Civil War.

Cooke, a Confederate veteran and prolific novelist, wrote the Surry books as romantic history, loyal to Lee and his circle. Readers meet the Army of Northern Virginia in its final months, through a staff officer's eyes. The novel is a Southern romance of the war's end, best read with its sympathies understood as those of its time and author.
8485-books-fatal-to-their-authors:
P. H. Ditchfield gathers stories of books fatal to their authors, dedicating the volume to John Walter of Bearwood. His preface, addressed to the book lover, admits a risk. To record the woes of authors and discourse on fatal books seems to court the displeasure of the fickle mistress who presides over authorship. The chapters that follow tell of writers ruined, imprisoned, or killed for their books.

Ditchfield, an antiquary and clergyman, writes literary history as cautionary tale, with anecdotes of censorship, libel, and martyrdom. Readers who love books about books will find a morbid, fascinating collection. It reminds writers that words once had sharper consequences, and that fame could be fatal.
8495-the-life-of-st-frances-of-rome-and-:
Lady Georgiana Fullerton wrote The Life of St. Frances of Rome, with lives of Blessed Lucy of Narni, Dominica of Paradiso, and Anne de Montmorency, and an introductory essay on the miraculous life of the saints by J. M. Capes. The authorities for the histories are set out at the start, grounding the lives in sources.

Fullerton, a Catholic convert and novelist, writes saints' lives for Victorian readers, with devotion and narrative skill. Frances, a Roman wife and mystic, anchors the volume, and the other lives show women of faith in different centuries. Readers get hagiography in the nineteenth-century manner, earnest and edifying, and a window onto Catholic devotion.
8546-two-summers-in-guyenne-a-chronicle-:
Edward Harrison Barker, author of Wayfaring in France and Wanderings by Southern Waters, wrote Two Summers in Guyenne as a chronicle of the wayside and waterside, with maps and illustrations. Contents follow the upper Dordogne, across the moors of the Corrèze, in the viscounty of Turenne, and on through the villages and rivers of southwestern France.

Barker writes travel as slow walking and boating, with attention to churches, doorways, and local life, like the abbey church at Beaulieu pictured at the head. Readers get Edwardian travel writing at its most leisurely, for a region less visited than Provence. The book suits armchair travelers and walkers planning a Dordogne tour.
8547-pirke-avot-the-sayings-of-the-jewis:
Pirke Avot, the Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, gathers the ethical teachings of the rabbis in the Mishnah, and this edition transliterates Hebrew letters in brackets, spelling them out where needed. A transcriber's note explains the method, so readers without Hebrew can follow the text, with rare additional notes also in brackets.

The sayings themselves are short and practical: on study, character, community, and the world to come, passed from master to disciple. Jews read Pirke Avot on Sabbath afternoons between Passover and the New Year. Readers new to rabbinic literature get a welcoming doorway, with the Hebrew kept visible beside the English.
8604-the-house-of-atreus-being-the-agame:
Aeschylus wrote the three tragedies gathered here about the cursed house of Atreus, in E. D. A. Morshead's English version. Agamemnon returns from Troy to be murdered by his wife; his son Orestes avenges him in The Libation-Bearers. And in The Furies, the avenging spirits pursue Orestes until Athens itself must judge him. An introductory note sketches Aeschylus, born at Eleusis in 525 BC, soldier and playwright, dead in Sicily in 456 BC.

Together the plays trace blood guilt from one generation to the next, asking whether revenge can ever end without law. Gods, ghosts, choruses, and courts all take part in the argument. The trilogy remains the foundation of Western tragedy. This plain translation lets a new reader follow its stark plot and fierce poetry without a scholar's apparatus getting in the way.
8697-guns-and-snowshoes-or-the-winter-ou:
Captain Ralph Bonehill sends four boy hunters into winter camp in this Boy Hunters series volume, also billed as the outing of the gun club. The contents promise a quarrel in the snow, snowballing with results, an explosion, chickens and mince pie, a dismaying discovery, and a first night in camp. Bonehill, author of Four Boy Hunters and the Flag of Freedom series, knew his young audience well.

Snowshoes, guns, tracking, and camp craft fill the chapters, with mishaps and rivalries keeping the fun moving. The boys learn to work together, handle firearms with care, and endure cold nights outdoors. It is straightforward Edwardian boys' adventure, wholesome and brisk, and a good window onto the outdoor books that taught a generation of American boys to romanticize winter camping.
8934-the-forest-lovers:
Maurice Hewlett wrote this romance of the Middle Ages, set in a green, half-magical England of knights, hermits, and outlaws. Its hero, Prosper le Gai, rides out into the forest and falls in love with a lady tied to a holy thorn and a strange vow. Around them move a dark knight, a charcoal-burner, and folk of wood and road.

Hewlett writes in a rich, old-style voice, full of chases, sanctuaries, and sudden turns, yet the heart of the book is love tested by vows and peril. It was a popular success in its day and still pleases readers who like their romance steeped in forest shade and medieval color.
8992-the-blockade-runners:
Jules Verne wrote this short novel in French in 1871 as Les forceurs de blocus, and N. d'Anvers turned it into English. It tells of the Dolphin, one of the fastest ships of its day. The Dolphin dares to run the Union blockade of the American South during the Civil War. Speed and nerve are its whole game.

First paired with A Floating City, the tale mixes sea detail with wartime risk, as captain and crew dodge guns and weather to reach port. Verne keeps the action tight and the stakes clear. The novella still reads as a brisk sea yarn from the age of steam and blockade.
9177-the-royal-game-of-the-ombre-written:
Printed in London in 1665 for Thomas Palmer, this manual teaches Ombre, a Spanish card game whose name means The Man. The player who takes the game cries, I am the Man, and Spaniards boast their Ombre beats the French game Beste as a man beats a beast. The form taught here is called Renegado.

Three players use a pack stripped for the game, and the manual sets out its rules in order. The British Library copy, Jessel 1249, preserves its old spelling. The book is a treasure for card players and historians of games, a glimpse of Restoration play.
9188-aboriginal-american-authors:
Daniel Brinton, anthropologist and member of learned societies in Philadelphia and abroad, wrote this chapter in the history of literature in 1883. Its subject is aboriginal American authors and their works, especially those in native languages. A new introduction notes its fitness for an age seeking history from the Indian point of view.

Brinton, known for The Myths of the New World and American Hero Myths, treats native writers as authors, not curiosities. He lists their books and languages with scholarly care. The book remains a pioneering survey, dated in language yet valuable for recovering Native voices in print.
9372-songs-out-of-doors:
Henry van Dyke published these outdoor songs in 1923, in four parts. Of Birds and Flowers gives the veery, the song-sparrow, and the Maryland yellow-throat, with sea-gulls of Manhattan and an angler's reveille. Of Skies and Seasons adds spring in north and south, Indian summer, and a snow-song. The Grand Canyon and God of the Open Air follow.

Wayfaring psalms in Palestine close the set, with the heavenly hills of Holland recalled. Van Dyke sings nature as a spiritual home. The book remains a pleasant volume of verse for walkers, birders, and lovers of open air.
9406-government-by-the-brewers:
Adolph Keitel, who spent thirty years inside the brewing trade, wrote Government by the Brewers as a fierce attack on that trade. He argues that brewers bought votes, bent laws, and fed crime through the saloon, all to guard their profits. The book belongs to the Prohibition fight, when reformers sought to ban drink by law. Keitel writes as an insider turned foe, naming firms and tricks.

Chapters claim beer is a habit-forming drug, not a mild temperance drink, and that saloons bred vice, broke homes, and staged crime. He tells how brewers backed cabarets, fought distillers, and spent millions to sway elections. A reader gets a raw, one-sided brief for Prohibition, useful for grasping how bitter and personal the drink war had grown.
9461-the-foolish-lovers:
St. John Ervine wrote this Irish novel in 1920, dedicated to his mother, who asked for a story without bad words, and to Mrs. Hannay, who asked for one without sex. Its epigraphs praise love as discovery. The tale opens with Ulster pride: ask an Ulster man who are Ireland's proudest people, and he answers, the Ulster people, of course.

Ask a Ballyards man who are Ulster's proudest, and a child would know: the Ballyards folk. Ervine builds a comedy of pride, love, and village honor from that boast. The novel remains a witty, warm Irish tale, clean in language and rich in character.
9501-concerning-cats-my-own-and-some-oth:
Helen M. Winslow wrote Concerning Cats in the early 1900s, a fond book about cats she knew and cats of fame. Winslow, editor of The Club Woman, opens with her own Pretty Lady, a quiet, lordly cat of fine manners. Later chapters take up other people's cats, historic cats, cat clubs, cat shows, and cats in verse and art. The book speaks to cat lovers in a chatty, warm voice.

Chapters range from high-bred cats in America to cats in England, cat hospitals, and the speech cats use with us. Winslow mixes true tales with lore on breeds, care, and shows. A reader gets a gentle, old-style celebration of feline grace, and a glimpse of how cats first won clubs, prizes, and a place in print.
9613-the-young-buglers:
G. A. Henty wrote The Young Buglers, a boys' adventure of the Peninsular War. Tom and Peter Scudamore, the most popular boys of their age at Eton in 1808, enlist as buglers and sail for Portugal. Chapters follow a coaching adventure, a tough customer, and a fall overboard, then the passage of the Douro and Talavera. Madrid, Busaco, and Albuera mark the campaign's course.

Later chapters bring Ciudad Rodrigo, Badajos, Salamanca, Vittoria, and Toulouse, with traps, rescues, and just-in-time escapes. Henty writes with brisk, factual verve for boys. A reader gets a rousing war tale for the young, rich in marches, battles, and schoolboy pluck.
9853-the-mystery-of-the-four-fingers:
Fred M. White wrote The Mystery of the Four Fingers in 1908, a detective tale of a lost mine and phantom gold. Chapters open with a black patch at the Great Empire Hotel in high London season, then a first finger, a lift, and a puzzle for Venner. A white lady, a missing person, and a house next door deepen the case. Felix Zary and Fenwick move the plot.

Later fingers, a prodigal's return, and a mouth of the net lead to nemesis and explanations, closing in a peaceful sunset. White writes with brisk Edwardian suspense. A reader gets a lively mystery of fingers, gold, and ghosts, from the author of The Crimson Blind.
9993-captivating-mary-carstairs:
Henry Sydnor Harrison's novel, first published under another name in February 1911, opens with a chief conspirator securing a pal. The pair embark upon a crime, arrive in Hunston, fall in with a stranger, and tangle themselves in local politics and other matters.

Mary Carstairs herself, captivating as the title promises, sits at the center of the plotting, while Varney meets a galling rebuff and Peter marches on. Harrison writes a light, comic romance of schemes gone sideways. Readers get a cheerful tale of rogues, small towns, and love arriving where it is least expected.
a-book-of-fruits-and-flowers: This anonymous collection teaches how to preserve fruits and flowers for the table and the stillroom. Its recipes cover sugar work, pickling, pies, cakes, broths, puddings, tarts, syrups, and salads. A further section gives ointments, waters, salves, and poultices for wounds, burns, aches, and bleeding. The book is a practical household manual from an age when kitchen and medicine chest stood close together.
a-bundle-of-letters:
Henry James builds his tale entirely from letters, in the 1887 Macmillan edition used here. The first comes from Miss Miranda Mope of Bangor, Maine, writing home to her mother from Paris on September 5th, 1879. She is boarding in a French pension with a lively set of fellow lodgers, and she reports on all of them.

Other pens join in: a young Englishman, a German musician, a French poet, and the sharp Miss Vanderbank, whose letters judge the rest. Each writer sees the same small society differently, and the comedy comes from the gaps between accounts. James, still young, practices here the art of character shown through voice that fills his later novels.
a-dog-of-flanders:
A Dog of Flanders, first published in 1872, is a short novel by Ouida, the pen name of Marie Louise de la Ramée. Ouida wrote many popular novels of adventure and romance, and also stories for young readers. This tale, set in Flanders in Belgium, became the best loved of them.

The story follows Nello, a poor and gentle boy who dreams of becoming a painter, and Patrasche, the great dog who shares his life and work. Their bond carries the book through hardship and rejection toward its famous sad ending. It is a story about loyalty, poverty, and unrecognized talent, and it has moved readers for more than a century.
a-gentleman-vagabond-and-some-others: Francis Hopkinson Smith gathers stories of gentleman vagabonds and vagabond gentlemen. Its pieces include a knight of the Legion of Honor, John Sanders laborer, the lady of Lucerne, and Jonathan. Smith says he selected these types without premeditated intent, letting readers group them as they wish. The stories mix travel, character, and gentle humor.
a-history-of-the-mcguffey-readers: Henry Hobart Vail writes a history of the McGuffey readers. Before him lie four small books, roughly bound, that taught generations of American children. Vail traces the readers' origin, authors, and place in school life. The history, with three portraits, preserves the story of America's most famous schoolbooks. The tale of these small books still charms all who love old schools.
a-little-mother-to-the-others: L. T. Meade tells of a little mother to the others in this girls story. Chapters introduce the poor innocent, the arrival of an aunt, and a punishment chamber. Bow and arrow, a baby's honor, a birch rod, and Diana's revenge follow. Meade writes of children caring for children with courage and feeling.
a-napa-christchild-and-benicia-s-letters: Charles Gunnison offers two old-fashioned Christmas tales in this small book, pairing a Napa Christchild story with letters from Benicia. Written to be read before an open fire, the tales trade modern realism for sentiment and seasonal cheer, with the author cheerfully admitting that every word is invented for entertainment. The book is offered in memory of sunny winter days spent in Germany, and dedicated to Stolterfoht's mother and sisters.
a-pair-of-patient-lovers: William Dean Howells gathers five stories in this collection, beginning with the title tale of a young clergyman met on a Canadian boat. Glendenning is first seen on the St Lawrence run from Kingston toward Montreal, handsome and alone with his guidebook, willing to know his fellow passengers. The other stories follow a piano pursuit, a difficult case, a voice with strange power, and a circle widening in water.
a-prince-of-sinners: Edward Phillips Oppenheim tells a political and social story in three parts, opening with Kingston Brooks, a political agent, and the Bullsom family at home. The contents promise a question for the country, a tempting offer, a marquis on matrimony, charity treated as crime, and a man who went to hell for fifteen years. Through Mary Scott, Lord Arranmore, and Brooks's missions and recruits, the novel weighs power, philanthropy, and ambition.
a-prince-of-swindlers:
A Prince of Swindlers, first published in 1900 by Guy Boothby, presents the adventures of Simon Carne, one of literature's first and greatest gentleman rogues. Carne predates both Hornung's Raffles and Leblanc's Arsène Lupin, the two famous gentleman thieves who followed him. The British Viceroy first meets Carne while traveling in India and, charmed, invites the reclusive hunchbacked scholar to London.

Little does society guess what the invitation brings among them. Carne's London career of elegant swindling forms the heart of the book, as the supposed scholar turns his charm and learning to crime. Boothby builds the rogue's double life into a portrait of a prince among swindlers, admired and dastardly at once.
a-princess-of-mars:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote this adventure novel as the supposed manuscript of Captain John Carter, a Virginia soldier who is mysteriously carried to Mars. The foreword, written in a family voice, presents Carter as a strange, ageless uncle. On Mars, called Barsoom by its people, Carter's Earth muscles give him great strength and leaping power. Captured by green Martian warriors, he wins standing by combat.

The contents list twenty-eight chapters of escapes, duels, and air battles. Carter meets Dejah Thoris, a red Martian princess held captive, and her cause pulls him through the wars of rival cities. Sola, his guard, tells her own sad history along the way. The book launched the Barsoom series and helped define planetary romance.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-1-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 1, by Gilbert Parker, continues the personal histories of Pierre and His People and calls itself the last existing records of Pretty Pierre. Parker's Pierre is a French Canadian half breed wanderer of the North West, gambler, philosopher, and witness to other men's tragedies. This first volume prints four of his tales, and its contents page maps the whole five volume gathering ahead.

Across the Jumping Sandhills opens the set, followed by A Lovely Bully, The Filibuster, and The Gift of the Simple King. The stories move between Hudson's Bay country, mining camps, and the borderlands where Canadian and American law both run thin. Parker was a Canadian who made his career in London. He writes the North as a moral climate. Cold, distance, and hunger strip men to what they are. Pierre, who has seen everything twice, narrates without surprise.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-2-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 2, by Gilbert Parker, gives Pretty Pierre five more northern tales. Parker opens with Malachi, in a room of gossips calmly predicting that a man will swing tomorrow. The door opens, the condemned man's friend Pierre steps to the fire, stretches his hands to the heat, and repeats the sentence himself in a soft ironical voice: Exit Malachi. The wind, Pierre says, does not tell where it has been.

The Lake of the Great Slave and The Red Patrol take the tales onto the water and the mounted police trails of the far North. The Going of the White Swan and At Bamber's Boom close the volume among river drivers and their booms of trapped logs. Parker's North West gives a hanging, a drowning, and a log jam the same weight of fate. Pierre's shrug there is a philosophy earned at forty below.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-3-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 3, by Gilbert Parker, places Pretty Pierre among the river drivers of the Madawaska. Parker opens The Bridge House with a building set on a wall between two small bridges, above channels that divide at its foundations. Spring floods batter the wall with logs, and a man can step from the back door into the river itself. The house was once a tavern, and the drivers who loved it were its true parish.

The Epaulettes, The House with the Broken Shutter, and The Finding of Fingall follow, with Three Commandments in the Vulgar Tongue to close. Soldiers, deserters, and river men pass through Parker's Ottawa valley, where French and English Canada meet on the drives. The Bridge House itself, rock like among the currents, stands for the book's method: fix one spot where wild lives converge, and let the river bring the stories past.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-4-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 4, by Gilbert Parker, opens with a Christmas tale told to power. In Little Babiche, Pretty Pierre faces the governor of the great Company, the Hudson's Bay chief, whose grey head and seamed face carry long solitary years in the northern fastnesses. Pierre corrects the record about a man he has known fifteen years, and promises the strange truth of a thing that happened at Noel, the day of the Great Birth.

At Point o' Bugles, The Spoil of the Puma, The Trail of the Sun Dogs, and The Pilot of Belle Amour complete the volume. Parker's tales keep returning to witnesses: men who were present, who knew, and who set a governor or a reader straight years later. The North of these stories is governed from fur trade posts and remembered in firelight, and its justice arrives, when it arrives, as testimony.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-5-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 5, by Gilbert Parker, closes the Pretty Pierre records with the longest tale in the set. The Cruise of the Ninety-Nine follows a big gulf yawl, handy enough for a man and a boy, with high old fashioned bulwarks and a tolerable record for speed. Her captain was Tarboe the smuggler. He named her after a parable. The parish priest came seeking the one lost sheep. Tarboe replied that he was the ninety nine, needing no repentance. He offered the cure his excellent smuggled brandy.

A Romany of the Snows and The Plunderer fill out the volume. Parker ends his northern cycle on salt water. Customs officers wink there, and priests drink with their parishioners.
a-woman-s-love-letters: Sophia Margaretta Hensley writes a woman's love letters in verse in this volume of the Fleur de Lis Poets, published at New York in 1895. The contents run from A Dream and Dream-Song through Doubt, Anticipation, Misunderstanding, Shadow-Song, and Revulsion to a Song of Dawn, Weariness, a Song of Rest, Death, and Battle-Song. Content, Sea-Song, Gratitude, Prayer, Loneliness, and To-morrow close a sequence of feeling in short lyrics.
