catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gregory-of:
Gregory of Tours, bishop and historian, wrote the Franks' story while governing a city through civil war. Born in 538 or 539 at Arverni, modern Clermont-Ferrand, to a distinguished Gallo-Roman house, he was first called Georgius Florentius. He later took Gregory for his maternal great-grandfather, bishop of Langres. Losing his father young, he was raised by his uncle Gallus of Clermont, then by the priest Avitus. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Tours to 17 November 593 or 594.

An illness turned him toward church service. His History of the Franks preserves his age's voice. As bishop he faced kings who increased power by violence, until endless civil war made might seem right itself. During Sigebert and Chilperic's war he cried that the woes of his people hurt the Church more than Diocletian's persecution. The entry joins pastor and chronicler in one troubled reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hilary-of-:
Hilary of Poitiers, bishop and doctor, turned a noble pagan's learning into the West's great defence against Arianism. Born at Poitiers early in the fourth century, he came of a noble, very probably pagan family. He mastered profane learning, then studied Scripture. There he found the truth he ardently sought, renounced idolatry, and was baptized. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Poitiers to 1 November, or 13 January 368 by the Breviary.

About 350 his learning and zeal won him governance of Poitiers' faithful, a body existing since the third century. Hilary is the first of its bishops about whom true information survives, thanks to his part against heresy. Arianism had ravaged regions and threatened invasion, while papal power in practice could neither prevent nor stop internal discord. The entry follows a convert bishop into theological war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-martin-of-:
Born at Sabaria in Pannonia around 316, Martin of Tours first served as a Roman soldier before he became one of Gaul's most beloved bishops. At Amiens he famously shared his cloak with a shivering beggar, then sought baptism and freedom from the army. He joined St Hilary at Poitiers, lived as a hermit at Ligugé, and drew so many followers that a monastic community grew around him.

Dragged almost against his will to the see of Tours in 371 or 372, he kept his plain hermit habits while ruling the diocese, founding the monastery of Marmoutier across the Loire. He preached through central and western Gaul, pleaded at Trier for condemned men, and resisted handing the heretic Priscillian to secular courts. He died at Candes, most probably in 397.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-statute-of-pr:
The Statute of Provisors, the English act 25 Edward III, statute 4, of 1350 to 1351, curbed papal appointments to English benefices. It arose from the long and angry controversy, in Lingard's phrase, between English kings and Rome. The quarrel concerned filling church livings by papal provision, whereby the pope suspended a patron's right and nominated his own candidate, called a provisor.

Possession of English livings by Italians provoked at one thirteenth-century period acts of lawless violence. Gregory IX had pronounced against provisions infringing lay patrons' rights, and Innocent IV expressed general disapprobation in 1253. From the statute's recitals it appears that papal bestowal of English benefices and their revenues had grown intolerable. The entry sets a famous act within a century of crown and papacy contention.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stedingers:
The Stedingers, Frisian peasants along the shore of northern Germany, revolted against their lord, the archbishop of Bremen, and were crushed by crusade. Their name means those living along a shore. They refused tithes and forced labour as serfs, duties demanded with considerable severity, and Archbishop Gerhard II sent troops against them.

His troops lost in 1229. The Stedingers then wrecked churches and monasteries, and abused and slew priests. A Bremen synod on 17 March 1230 accused them of contempt for church authority and sacraments and of superstitious practices, and excommunicated them. Refusing submission, they faced a crusade preached by Gregory IX's bull of 9 October 1232, after Frederick II had banned them. An army advanced and subdued them in battle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-surnames-of-f:
Medieval custom gave celebrated doctors surnames that summed up their excellence, and this entry lists the principal examples with death dates. Theology supplies Angelicus for Thomas Aquinas, dead in 1274. It also gives Arca testamenti for Anthony of Padua, dead in 1231, Eximius for Suárez, dead in 1617, and Dulcifluus for Antonius Andreas, dead in 1320.

Law supplies its own roll. It includes Speculator for William Durandus, dead in 1296, Speculum Juris for Bartolus of Sassoferrato, dead in 1359, and Pater Juris for Innocent III, dead in 1216. Dozens more names fill both lists, from Acutissimus for Sixtus IV to Subtilis for two later writers, making the entry a handy key to medieval nicknames.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synodal-exami:
Synodal examiners are chosen in a diocesan synod, and this entry sets out Trent's rules for them. Trent requires at least six, while the Congregation of the Council fixed twenty as ample. Their chief task is running competitive examinations, called concursus, though they may be assigned other examinations as well. Candidates are proposed singly each year by the bishop or his vicar-general.

Each nominee needs the synod's approval by majority vote, secret or public as the bishop decides, and should hold at least a licentiate in theology or canon law. Once appointed, examiners serve until the next synod, swear to act without prejudice or favour, and must refuse presents on pain of simony. If their number falls below six within a year, the bishop with his chapter may fill it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-apostolic:
Christian writers of the first and second centuries who knew the Apostles, or were shaped directly by their teaching, are gathered under this name. Though some use the term only for actual disciples, it stretches in practice to cover nearly all surviving primitive Christian writing before the great apologies of the second century. These works form the bridge between the New Testament and later tradition.

Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Polycarp, the Didache, the Shepherd of Hermas, and the Epistle of Barnabas all appear, with accounts of each text, its date, and its witness. Jean-Baptiste Cotelier's 1672 edition gave the group its modern label. For students of early faith, the entry maps a small but vital body of writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-crosiers:
Canons Regular of the Holy Cross, called Crosiers, are the order traced here from a Liège canonry to wide lands. Théodore de Celles, after following Frederick Barbarossa on crusade, won a canonry at Saint Lambert's, Liège. On Holy Cross Exaltation, 14 September 1211, he and four fellow canons vowed before Liège's bishop, who gave them Saint Theobald's church at Claire-Lieu near Huy for their first house.

Innocent III approved the order by word in 1215, Honorius III in writing, confirmed by Innocent IV on 3 May 1248. France, Netherlands, Germany, and England soon held Crosier houses. Preaching to Albigenses with Dominic, martyrdom in Livonia under Prague's Bishop Albert in 1246, and service with Saint Louis on crusade mark their early zeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-military-:
Brotherhoods of knights, sacred and secular, crowd this survey, numbering near a hundred once sham and stillborn orders are struck out. War and religion, the twin trades of the Middle Ages, explain their appeal. Kings later turned the idea to their own ends, founding royal orders to reward loyal nobles until no country lacked its princely order.

Private adventurers joined the trade, decking dupes with sham insignia sold at a price. Marino Caraccioli, a Neapolitan noble, passed himself off as grand master of an order in 1624, a cautionary tale among many. Genuine orders, their rules, crusading service, and decline receive the main attention, mapping chivalry's sacred and courtly faces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-ten-thous:
Two groups of ten thousand martyrs, entered in the Roman Martyrology on different days, are sifted here. March 18 reads: at Nicomedia ten thousand holy martyrs put to the sword for confessing Christ. June 22 reads: on Mount Ararat ten thousand holy martyrs crucified. The first likely honours victims at Diocletian's persecution opening in 303, as Eusebius and Lactantius confirm.

Numbers need not exaggerate, the entry argues, given the scale of that persecution. June's entry rests on a legend translated from a lost Greek original by Anastasius Bibliothecarius, who died in 886, and dedicated to Peter, Bishop of Sabina. Emperors Adrian and Antoninus marching against Gadarenes opens a tale the entry treats as pious fiction, not history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-third-orders:
Third Orders are lay men and women joined to a religious order while still living ordinary lives outside a monastery or convent. They may wear the order's habit, share in its prayers and good works, and follow a rule fitted to life in the world. The Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces this pattern from early lay associates of monks through its full growth in the thirteenth century.

Franciscans, Dominicans, Carmelites, Servites and others each get their own section, with separate treatment of secular tertiaries and regular communities. Readers also find rules for members, lists of privileges, and reports on the orders in Canada, Britain, Ireland and the United States. It suits anyone tracing how laypeople took part in monastic life without leaving home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-three-chapter:
The Three Chapters were three sets of writings condemned in the sixth century. They were the person and works of Theodore of Mopsuestia, certain works of Theodoret of Cyrus, and the letter of Ibas to Maris. Emperor Justinian's edict of late 543 or early 544 anathematized them, hoping to win back the Monophysites, who charged the Church with Nestorianism. Those who refused the condemnation were said to defend the Chapters.

The quarrel runs in three stages. They stretch from the edict through Pope Vigilius's time at Constantinople and his ratification of the Second Council of Constantinople, to the healing of the Western schisms that followed. Greek bishops mostly yielded under pressure, while Latin bishops, including Dacius of Milan and Facundus of Hermiane, stood firm. Facundus's Defence of the Three Chapters remains the classic plea for their side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tours:
Tours is an archdiocese covering Indre-et-Loire in France, re-established by the Concordat of 1801 with Angers, Nantes, Le Mans, Rennes, Vannes, Saint-Brieuc and Quimper as suffragans. Rennes became a metropolitan see in 1859, taking the last three, while Laval, created in 1855, stayed subject to Tours. Its early history rests on Gregory of Tours's chapter on the bishops of Tours.

Gregory names Gatianus, one of seven apostles sent from Rome to Gaul in the mid-third century, as founder, though Duchesne doubts the date 250 and admits only a Constantinian founding. After Gatianus came Litorius, then the great Martin, bishop from 372 to 397, then Brice. The city later opened its gates to Clovis in 507, faced Saracens in 732 and Northmen from 853 to 903, and passed to English rule until 1214.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tunkers:
A Protestant sect named from the German tunken, to dip, also called Dunkards, Dunkers, Brethren and German Baptists. Besides Baptist teaching they hold distinctive practices: the candidate kneels in the water and is dipped forward three times, honouring the three Persons of the Trinity.

Communion follows the primitive pattern, held in the evening, preceded by the love-feast or agape and followed by the kiss of charity, with foot-washing on certain occasions. Founded by Alexander Mack at Schwarzenau in 1708 with seven companions, the body emigrated to America between 1719 and 1729 and organized its first church at Germantown in 1723.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
The University of Angers probably grew from the cathedral school of that city. Early in the eleventh century the school became famous under Marbodus, later Bishop of Rennes, and Ulger, later Bishop of Angers. Both men had studied under the famed canonist Fulbert de Chartres. In 1229 the school was enlarged by students, many of them Englishmen, who fled Paris to escape the direct control of the French king. Angers then became a centre for civil law.

It counted as a studium generale, though it was officially recognized as such only in 1337 by an episcopal ordinance. In 1364 King Charles V granted it a charter with the same privileges as the University of Orléans. Only in 1432 did it gain a faculty of theology, the entry notes, with medicine and arts following. The result is a compact history of a provincial university shaped by exile, law, and royal favour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-use-of-beads-:
Beads strung in set kinds, orders, and numbers help Catholics keep count in prayers that repeat their parts, a common expedient in forms of devotion. Made from plain wood or natural berries up to costly metals and precious stones, beads may be blessed with prayer and holy water, becoming sacramentals. In that character most religious orders, of men and women alike, prescribe them for personal use or as part of the religious habit.

Today beads appear mostly as the Dominican Rosary, or Marian Psalter, but Catholics also know Brigittine beads, Dolour beads, Immaculate Conception beads, and the Crown of Our Saviour. The entry traces the counting device from early knotted cords to the modern rosary, explaining each form's prayers and indulgences. It offers a practical guide to a humble tool of prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-mathew-fl:
Mathew Flathers, alias Major, was an English priest and martyr born probably about 1580 at Weston in Yorkshire, who died at York on 21 March 1607. Schooled at Douai and ordained at Arras on 25 March 1606, he was sent to the English mission three months later. Government agents, redoubling their hunt for priests after the Gunpowder Plot, discovered him almost at once.

Tried under the statute of 27 Elizabeth on the charge of receiving orders abroad, he was condemned to death. By an unusual act of clemency the sentence was commuted to lifelong banishment, but after a brief exile the undaunted priest returned to England to fulfil his mission. After ministering a short time to his oppressed fellow Catholics in Yorkshire, he was seized again, tried, and executed at York.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vespers:
Vespers is the evening office of the Church, treated here under six headings: its sixth-century form, its origin, its medieval variations, its latest changes, its symbolism and hymns, and its importance. In the sixth century, as described in St Benedict's Rule, the evening gathering comprised four psalms. A short reading, a response, a hymn, a versicle, the Gospel canticle Magnificat, litany, Lord's Prayer, prayer, and dismissal.

Pliny's early second-century letter already mentions Christian gatherings morning and evening, making Vespers, with Vigils, among the most ancient offices known. Later sections trace how Compline reshaped the old lucernarium, the lamp-lighting service, how psalm choices varied between the Benedictine arrangement and the Roman order's five psalms. How hymns entered the Roman evening office only in more recent times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vivarini-fami:
The Vivarini were a family of Venetian painters, and the entry's centre is Alvise Vivarini, born in 1446 or 1447 and dying in 1502. Son of Antonio and pupil of his uncle Bartolomeo, little is known of his youth. In 1488 he begged the Signoria to let him prove his skill beside the two Bellini in decorating the Grand Council's hall.

Granted, his pictures there have vanished, but in 1492 he received the honorary title Painter in the Great Council and five ducats a month. Long dismissed by critics as Bellini's pupil, foreman, or unimportant Murano imitator, Alvise was restored by Bernhard Berenson's work on Lotto to his rightful place. He stands as an eminent, original Venetian master of the fifteenth century, no follower of Bellini but great in his own right. He was master of Cima, Lotto, Mantegna, and Bonsignori, exercising a great and lasting influence on his successors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-viviers:
Viviers is a French diocese covering the Ardèche, suppressed by the Concordat of 1802 and joined to Mende. Then restored in 1822 from most of old Viviers plus parts of Valence, Vienne, Le Puy, and Uzès, as suffragan to Avignon. St Andéol, disciple of Polycarp, evangelized the Vivarais under Septimius Severus and was martyred in 208, his body buried by Blessed Tullie.

The Old Charter of 950, drawn up by Bishop Thomas, is the fullest document on Viviers' primitive Church, naming five bishops at Alba Augusta, Januarius, Septimus, Maspicianus, Melanius. Avolus, the last a victim of the barbarian Chrocus's invasion. After Alba's ravages, St Auxonius moved the see to Viviers about 430. Later canonized bishops include Lucian, Valerius, Venantius, present at councils in 517 and 535, Melanius II, Eucherius, Firminus, Aulus, Eumachius, and Longinus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-white-fathers:
The White Fathers, Missionaries of Our Lady of Africa of Algeria, known in French as Pères Blancs, were founded in 1868 by Algiers's first archbishop, later Cardinal Lavigerie. The famine of 1867 left many Arab orphans, and educating and instructing those children occasioned the society's founding. From the start Lavigerie aimed at converting the Arabs and black peoples of Central Africa.

Mission posts arose in Kabylia and the Sahara, and in 1876 and 1881 two caravans from southern Algeria and Ghadames, seeking Sudan missions, were massacred by their guides. Upper Congo, with French Sudan founded in 1894 and Sahara missions grouped in a prefecture. In 1880, at the Holy See's request, the White Fathers opened a Greek Melkite seminary at Jerusalem. Though bound by oath to labour for Africa's conversion, they are not strictly a religious order and may retain personal property.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelm-wilme:
Wilhelm Wilmers was a Westphalian Jesuit who taught philosophy and theology across Europe and wrote widely used religion textbooks. Born at Boke in 1817, he died at Roermond in 1899. He joined the Jesuits in 1834, was driven from Switzerland with his order in 1847, and took orders in France in 1848. Teaching posts followed at Issenheim, Louvain, Cologne, Bonn, Aachen, and Maria-Laach.

Wilmers served as a theologian at the Cologne provincial council in 1860 and at the Vatican Council in 1870. Later he taught at Poitiers, Saint Helier, and Jersey, then gave himself wholly to writing in England and Holland. His textbooks on religion, first issued in the 1850s and 1870s, ran through many editions and several languages. His last works, on revealed religion and the Church, appeared in 1897, with a third volume finished after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-abbot:
William, Abbot of Marmoutiers, was a Breton monk who fought his archbishop over the terms of his blessing. Born in Brittany, he died at Marmoutiers on 23 May 1124. He had served as Archdeacon of Nantes, gave up that rank to enter the Benedictine house at Marmoutiers, and was chosen abbot in 1105 after Hilgotus died. Archbishop Rudolph II of Tours, who had often trampled the abbey's rights, refused him blessing unless he swore loyalty and pressed his right hand into the archbishop's.

William would swear but not yield his hand, and Saint Ivo of Chartres backed him in letters to Pope Paschal II. William went to Rome and took his blessing from the pope himself. Through Ivo and other bishops, abbot and archbishop made peace around 1115. William sat at the Poitiers synod in 1106 and gained the Abbey of Cellen-Brie from the Bishop of Meaux in 1107.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-po:
William of Poitiers was a Norman historian and chaplain to William the Conqueror, whose life of the king survives in a single battered manuscript. Born of a noted family at Préaux about 1020, he studied at Poitiers and fought as a knight in several battles. Then he took orders and became the Conqueror's chaplain, resolving to write his history. Hugh of Lisieux made him archdeacon, serving under Hugh and Gilbert Maminot in a circle debating astronomy and mathematics.

William knew Greek and Latin letters and taught verse to young students, earning praise from Ordericus Vitalis. His Gesta Guilelmi, offered to King William between 1071 and 1077, survives only in a Cottonian manuscript, its opening to 1047 and its close from 1068 lost. Drawing on Dudon, lost annals, witnesses, and his own memory, he gives a careful if panegyrical contemporary source, prized for Harold's stay in Normandy and the Conquest itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-weath:
William Weathers was titular Bishop of Amycla and the long-serving president of Saint Edmund's College, Old Hall. Born on 12 November 1814 to Welsh Protestant parents, he died at Isleworth in 1895. His mother and children converted after his father's death. Schooled by Franciscans at Baddesley and at Old Hall, he stayed forty years there, holding every office. He was master before ordination in 1838, prefect of discipline, vice-president, prefect of studies, and president from 1851 to 1868.

Weathers's presidency reshaped college rules and welcomed lay convert Ward as theology lecturer from 1852 to 1858. When Manning tried to hand the seminary to the Oblates of Saint Charles in 1855, the chapter appealed to Rome and the Oblates withdrew in 1861. In 1869 Manning moved the divines to Hammersmith and made Weathers rector until Vaughan closed it in 1892. Weathers, a bishop from 1872, then served as chaplain to the Sisters of Nazareth at Isleworth and wrote on electricity and magnetism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-xaverian-brot:
Xaverian Brothers are an institute founded by Theodore James Ryken at Bruges in 1839 under episcopal approval. Ryken crossed to America in 1837 seeking views, winning letters from seven bishops. Back in Europe, Bishop Boussens sanctioned his plan if Ryken first spent a novitiate with the Redemptorists at Saint-Trond. After it, Ryken set up his congregation at Bruges, where trials nearly killed it: recruits failed to stay, and bread came only through effort.

By June 1840 the brotherhood counted three members, but a banker's gift in 1841 bought Het Walletje, their home. A giver's mission fund helped too, and Sallust's motto, concord makes small things grow, became theirs. A boys' sodality, a school, catechism at Notre-Dame, deaf-mute training, and Bruges schools in 1844 followed, with members sent to Saint-Trond. England called them to Bury in 1846 and Manchester, and America to Louisville in 1854 under Spalding, then Baltimore Saint Mary's and Saint Xavier's.
certain-personal-matters:
H. G. Wells gathered some forty short essays and sketches into a volume published by T. Fisher Unwin in 1901. The first piece remembers his Aunt Charlotte, who hated cheap veneer, plated goods, and the word trashy, and who corrected a child for calling a penny a copper. Cheapness, in things and in people, is Wells's opening theme.

Later pieces take up the choice of a wife, conversation, schooling, house-hunting, chess, and staying at the seaside. A few are tales rather than essays, among them Dunstone's Dear Lady. Others look far ahead, to the extinction of man and life seen through a microscope. Wells writes lightly on small subjects and lets the large ones arrive unannounced.
christ-in-flanders:
Honore de Balzac dedicated Christ in Flanders, translated by Ellen Marriage, to Marcelline Desbordes-Valmore, a daughter of Flanders of whom modern days may be proud. The tale opens at a dimly remote period in Brabant, when a ferry boat crossed between Cadzand island and the Flemish coast. Ostend then was an obscure haven of a few hundred hearths.

A storm rises, the rich passengers crowd the safe end, and a quiet stranger in poor clothes calms the waters after the pattern of the Gospel. Balzac divides the boat into two ends of society, terror and wailing among the worldly, peace near the stranger. This short legend belongs to his Philosophical Studies, where faith gets gentler treatment than usual.
cinq-mars:
Alfred de Vigny published Cinq-Mars in 1826 as a founding novel of romantic fiction. This English edition carries prefaces by Charles de Mazade and Gaston Boissier of the French Academy. Essays trace De Vigny's rise, neglect, and revival as a genius. The novel retells the fall of Louis XIII's favorite in 1642.

Henri de Cinq-Mars climbs from gentleman to king's favorite while Richelieu rules France behind the throne. Love for Marie de Gonzague feeds an ambition that favor cannot satisfy. Plotting with the king's brother and Spain, he signs a treasonable treaty against the cardinal. His friend De Thou, a counsellor, follows him from loyalty rather than belief. Arrest, trial at Lyon, and scaffold close the story for both men. De Vigny mixes invented scenes with documents and speeches, in Walter Scott's manner. Readers rank the book as a study of ambition, and this file holds it whole.
clairvoyance-and-occult-powers:
Clairvoyance and Occult Powers is a set of lessons issued in 1916 under the name Swami Panchadasi, author of The Human Aura and The Astral World. Its synopsis lists the course lesson by lesson. Lesson I treats the astral senses, and Lesson II sets telepathy against clairvoyance as two distinct powers.

The introduction explains the book's method by contrast. Students in India, the author says, accept a teacher's statements without demanding proof. Western students ask for evidence, so the lessons proceed in the opposite way, with cases and instances. One case tells of a willed visit to a house at Kew: the writer willed himself into a front bedroom at midnight, and was seen there.
concerning-animals-and-other-matters:
Concerning Animals and Other Matters, by Edward Hamilton Aitken, collects natural history essays first printed in the Strand Magazine, the Pall Mall Magazine, and the Times of India. The contents run from bills of birds, tails, noses, and ears to the barn owl and domestic animals. Snakes take three chapters: snakes themselves, the Indian snake-charmer, and cures for snake-bite.

The cobra bungalow and the panther the author did not shoot keep the Indian setting. Coconut tree, betel nut, a Hindu festival, Indian poverty, and borrowed Indian words widen the book beyond zoology. Its illustration captions joke in the same voice: the rat, a near relation of the squirrel, is personally a gutter-snipe, known by the tail he drags like a dirty rope.
concerning-cats-my-own-and-some-others:
Concerning Cats: My Own and Some Others, by Helen M. Winslow, is a cat book in fourteen chapters, all titled with its own word. It begins with Concerning the Pretty Lady. She is the author's cat: gentle, dignified, and reserved as a duchess. She followed her mistress from boarding house to seashore cottage, to the mountains, and back. She was contented wherever her person went.

Other chapters take up her other cats, other people's cats, and historic cats. Cats in England, cat clubs and shows, and high-bred cats in America widen the survey; the Hon. Mrs. McLaren Morrison's cattery at Kepwick Park is visited with delight. Cats in poetry, cat artists, cat hospitals and refuges, the origin of cats, their varieties, and cat language close the circle.
creative-impulse-in-industry-a-propositi:
A plea to join schooling with the creative side of work fills Helen Marot's 1918 book, issued by the Bureau of Educational Experiments in New York. She calls it a proposition for educators. The book is inscribed to Caroline Pratt, who worked on play in child learning.

Four chapters make the case. First comes work and the creative impulse, then the American way of fitting people to industry, then the German way. Marot doubts the German system would thrive here, and says it is not the schooling America wants. The last chapter urges forms of industry that teach as they produce. The book speaks to the old fight over what job training should do to the worker.
days-of-the-discoverers:
Tales of the early voyages to America fill Louise Lamprey's book for young readers, issued by Frederick A. Stokes Company of New York under copyright of 1921. It stands in the Great Days in American History line. Florence Choate and Elizabeth Curtis drew the pictures.

Cortes in Mexico fills the sampled middle of the book. Envoys draw the strange beasts and the thunder birds, whose mouths breathed destruction, for the Emperor to see. The governor pledges goods till orders come, then takes his leave, and a game of diplomacy begins. Other chapters treat other discoverers in the same story form. Lamprey writes history as narrative, with speech and scene, for school-age readers.
de-quincey-s-revolt-of-the-tartars:
The flight of the Kalmuck Tartars fills De Quincey's essay, in a school edition made by William Edward Simonds of Knox College. Ginn and Company of Boston issued it in 1899 at the Athenæum Press. Simonds thanks the earlier editors, and Masson above all, in his preface.

De Quincey tells how the Kalmucks fled Russian rule for China. A strong Russian force hung on their rear, slowed only by its guns. New motives pressed the worn people on each day, he writes, while they were exhausted already. The Khan's advance reached its mark only on the second day of February. Notes and an introduction fit the tale for school use. The prose is De Quincey at his most rolling and grand.
deep-waters:
Short sea tales by W. W. Jacobs fill Deep Waters, dated 1919 on its title page. Twelve stories stand in the contents, among them Shareholders, Paying Off, Sam's Ghost, and The Winter Offensive. A night-watchman tells most of them in his own broad speech.

A sailorman, says the watchman, is like a fish: safest at sea. Ashore, one poor chap kept getting married, till six women stood in court at once to take away his character. Money, wives, ghosts, and skippers fill the rest of the set. One tale turns on a woman who thought the watchman was her lost husband. Jacobs writes dry, sly comedy of the docks, in tales short enough for one sitting.
dewey-and-other-naval-commanders:
Sea captains of the United States fill Edward S. Ellis's book for boys, issued by Hurst and Company of New York under a copyright of 1899. A portrait of Admiral George Dewey stands at the front. Ellis had written histories of the world, of the United States, and of New York.

Three chapters give Dewey's birth, boyhood, Civil War service, and war with Spain. Then the book runs back to the birth of the navy: privateers, Paul Jones, and the Ranger's fight with the Drake. The Barbary wars and Tripoli follow. Privateers of 1814, among them the Reindeer, Avon, and Blakely built near Boston, close the sampled text. Ellis writes stirring naval history for the young.
dickinson-life-and-letters:
Martha Dickinson Bianchi, Emily Dickinson's niece, published The Life and Letters of Emily Dickinson in 1924. Bianchi had known her aunt and guarded the family papers. Her book mixes biography with letters not printed before.

She describes the Amherst household, the poet's white dress, and her rare meetings with visitors. Family quarrels over the poems' editing hum in the background of the story. The letters show Dickinson's humor and devotion across her whole life. Though later scholars corrected some details, Bianchi's portrait fixed the myth of the recluse poet for a generation of readers. Photographs of the house and family accompany her text in this edition.
doe-osti-17133600-corrosion-tests-with-d:
E. Schneiderlochner, Ana Maria Popa, Yifeng Liao, and William Ebert of Argonne ran standard corrosion tests on eight TARS waste form materials from Pacific Northwest, in report ANL/CFCT-26/20 dated 30 September 2026. TARS materials are alkali borosilicate glass ceramics meant to lock up dehalogenated waste salt from fuel treatment. Locking cesium and strontium in a durable solid is the point.

Tests followed ASTM methods at 90 degrees Celsius and below, varying pH, temperature, and solution saturation. Crystal content rose from almost none in TARS-1 to dominant in TARS-8, and most crystals outlasted the glass phase, which carried the dose giving elements. Overall response looked like normal borosilicate glass. TARS-1 came out most durable and most promising, though its rate did not rise smoothly with temperature.
doe-osti-2589590-randomized-algorithms-f:
Faster ways to solve large linear systems close out a laboratory research project by Andrew Higgins, in Sandia report SAND2025-11831R. The method family is randomized sketching: shrinking a huge problem with a random map before solving it. Theory promised big savings, but how to sketch well in practice, and what sketching does to accuracy, had been little studied.

The team built fast graphics processor versions of three sketches: a dense Gaussian sketch, a sparse CountSketch, and a Hadamard-based method. Combining sketches captured the strengths of each. Their combined least squares solver beat the classic normal equations route by up to 77 percent on speed, while also improving stability. Code and results give solver writers hardware-tested options instead of paper promises.
doe-osti-2996972-water-sorption-study-of:
Emily Chavez and Dali Yang measure how polymers and their composites drink water from humid air, in Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-29643, issued 29 September 2025. Polymer binders hold many composites together, including Estane in the explosive PBX 9501 and a vinyl elastomer in filled composites. Both binders can break down with water, so uptake rates govern shelf life.

An automated vapor sorption instrument generated large data sets across humidity and temperature settings, replacing slow manual weighing. Python scripts processed the data and extracted the temperature laws for diffusion and sorption. Film samples of two Estane grades were run one-sided for short exposures as part of the set. The framework gives aging studies a faster, repeatable way to rank binder stability.
doe-osti-2998342-maintenance-of-advanced:
Argonne National Laboratory final report on the MARS project, led by Alexander Heifetz and covering October 2020 to March 2025, develops sensors that let advanced reactors maintain themselves. High-temperature reactors should undercut today's plants on cost, but upkeep is projected to be their largest operating expense. The test case is Kairos Power's fluoride salt-cooled reactor, a sealed design meant to run on its own with online refueling.

Few sensors survive that reactor's heat, radiation, and chemical hazards, so the project developed sensing for fluid properties and a monitoring plan around them. Analysis found the sensors under development compatible with Kairos's integral test facilities, and a detailed demonstration schedule was set. Early results suggest built-in sensing enables condition-based maintenance, fixing parts when data says so instead of on a calendar, stretching the time between shutdowns.
doe-osti-3008428-clean-water-production-:
Clean water production inside cooling towers is covered in the final report for DOE award DE-FE0032057 from Infinite Cooling of Malden, Massachusetts, led by principal investigator Karim Khalil. The grant period ran from July 2021 to September 2025, and the Fox Energy Center hosted project site work.

Power plants withdraw about 39 percent of United States freshwater, most of it for cooling, and cooling towers dominate that use. The technology ionizes the tower's exhaust plume with electric fields, charges the droplets, and pulls them onto collection electrodes where they merge and drain. Blowdown-grade water comes back as high-purity water fit for boiler feed, while plume abatement eases operating limits on the plant.
doe-osti-3010993-steel-creek-pen-branch-:
Four Savannah River Site streams gained new gauging stations in a report by J. R. Floyd of Savannah River National Laboratory, SRNL-STI-2025-00557. Stations on Steel Creek, Pen Branch, the D Area Discharge Canal, and the D006 Stream support groundwater modelling for the P Area Groundwater, CMP Pits, and D Area Watershed operable units. Each station pairs instruments for stage and flow measurement.

The installations use a MACE FloSeries3 FloPro logger with a MACE Doppler ultrasonic area velocity sensor, powered by a solar panel and a 12 volt battery. The sensor measures velocities from 0.08 to 26 feet per second, with one percent accuracy up to 10 feet per second.
doe-osti-3016054-advanced-characterizati:
University of Illinois final progress report for award DE-FE0032457, led by John W Scott of the Illinois Sustainable Technology Center, was submitted February 4, 2026. The grant ran from September 2024 to October 2025. Its subject is coal combustion residual wastewater, the effluent left from burning coal, and how to measure what is in it far more precisely.

The team built a One-Shot analysis system that separates and concentrates target elements, then reads them with plasma emission spectrometry in line. Ion chromatography methods covered anions in the wastewater. Fluorescence sensor arrays using reagents such as 8-hydroxyquinoline sulfate gave very low detection limits for several rare earth elements. Carbon dots made in the project also responded selectively to rare earths. The methods point toward pulling valuable rare earths out of waste streams, not just treating them.
doe-osti-3017354-cauer-prototype-for-but:
Sean K Lehman of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this report, LLNL-TR-2015493, dated December 10, 2025, on the Cauer prototype for Butterworth filters. It begins with a practical problem: he needed a real analog filter built from resistors, inductors, and capacitors, but knew only digital filter coefficients. Turning those coefficients into component values was the missing skill.

The report explains Cauer topologies as the bridge, then works the transformations in full: lowpass, highpass, bandpass, and bandstop. Worked examples carry analytic transfer functions and simulated chirp responses side by side. One example is a sixth-order bandpass design with one hertz bandwidth. Lehman is candid that an AI assistant helped and made errors he had to correct. Radio and instrumentation builders get the documentation he could not find when he needed it, with the math shown.
doe-osti-3019898-hector-v-3-5-0-equation:
Kalyn Dorheim and Steve Smith of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory documented the newest release of the Hector climate model in PNNL-38961, February 2026. Hector is a reduced-complexity model of Earth's energy balance and carbon cycle, kept up by the laboratory since 2015. The new release is the subject here. The document is narrow by design: an update, not a full manual. It records the equation and parameter changes made since the last release with a journal description. Methane and nitrous oxide sections lead the changes.

Radiative forcing formulas for nitrous oxide are written out in full. A calibration-to-observations section follows. Reduced-complexity models earn their keep by running fast enough for large ensembles and scenario sweeps. That speed is useful if the mathematics stays auditable. Dorheim and Smith's change log is that audit trail. Users reproducing a run can check every equation against this note.
doe-osti-3021047-high-field-quantum-diam:
Ronald Walsworth's final technical report for DOE Fusion Energy Sciences award DE-SC0021654 comes from the University of Maryland. It covers work from May 2021 to April 2025 on diamond-based magnetic field sensors for fusion devices. The sensors use nitrogen-vacancy centers, atomic defects in diamond whose light emission shifts with magnetic field. Fusion machines need magnetometers that survive strong fields and harsh conditions where conventional probes struggle.

The team studied how neighboring nitrogen-vacancy centers interact through cross-relaxation, which shapes the sensor's all-optical photoluminescence signal. Measurements on diamonds with about 0.3 and 3.8 parts per million of these centers matched simulations built on a coupled two-center model. Microwave-based resonance measurements resolved splittings of a few megahertz from hyperfine interactions. Sensitivities reached a few nanotesla per root hertz under the tested conditions. The results guide magnetometer designs for high-field fusion diagnostics.
doe-osti-3024504-robust-explanations-usi:
Rickard Ewetz of the University of Central Florida, with co-investigator Sumit Jha of Florida International University, reports project DE-SC0023494 on making artificial intelligence explain itself more robustly. The goal is trust: algorithms that produce clear explanations of their decisions, plus metrics for judging whether those explanations are valid and reliable. Three tools named in the title carry the approach: diverse adversarially trained ensembles, multi-modal contrastive learning, and attribution-based confidence scores.

Accomplishments include symbolic explanations for high-dimensional time series and a new algebra that tracks information flow through vision transformers. It turns their branching and merging paths into super-pixel heatmaps a person can read. The report is candid that not every objective was finished, because the principal investigator moved institutions; the remaining goals follow him to the new one.
doe-osti-3025421-a-community-guide-to-re:
Jason Ball and Peter A Cappers of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory wrote this community guide, published March 23, 2026, to the regulatory barriers that slow microgrids. It bundles three reports, the first covering foundational issues. A microgrid can island from the main grid during outages, but the rules it must satisfy were written for a centralized system. The authors quote analysis saying those rules tend to protect that system against the decentralized one.

One disconnect is standards drift. A project can install equipment meeting the current IEEE 1547-2018 standard while the local utility is legally bound to enforce rules based on the outdated 2003 version. A named section, the interconnection labyrinth, then walks through procedural and financial hurdles. The guide is written for communities, not lawyers, and it is peer reviewed.
doe-osti-3029214-where-should-we-put-flo:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-23071, by Christina Maria Brelsford and issued in April 2026, asks where flood sensors should be placed in Southeast Texas. Flooding there has grown worse with storms such as Hurricane Harvey and Tropical Storm Imelda. The network studied was built by the Southeast Texas Flood Control District, local counties, river authorities, and Lamar University, and it now runs more than 200 sensors.

Brelsford argues that past networks were sited to track the physical side of flooding, which gives a weak picture of risk to people. Because budgets are limited, each sensor should count. The report urges a broader design that weighs who is at risk, so better placement can help protect lives and homes and speed recovery after storms.
doe-osti-3029602-reliable-integration-of:
Sai Pushpak Nandanoori, Bowen Huang, Ramij Raja Hossain, and Veronica Adetola of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory study how giant computer loads behave, in an October 2025 technical report. Their aim is to help grid operators plan generation and keep supply steady as artificial intelligence data centers grow. The team works from two open datasets: the MIT Supercloud records and the SURF dataset. The MIT records carry the main weight of the study.

The MIT set spans about six months on the TX-Gaia cluster. It holds scheduler logs, per-job processor time series, node snapshots, file system activity, and building power and cooling sensor data. From such records the team infers job start and stop times, checks data quality, and builds synthetic load profiles. Those profiles let planners test grid plans without real center data.
doe-osti-3362659-roadmap-for-solar-photo:
Megan Jordan Culler, Jason Jack Forbush, and Megan Egan of Idaho National Laboratory draw a cyber roadmap for solar power. Sandia, Pacific Northwest, and Rockies lab co-authors join them. The report is INL/RPT-26-82339, dated April 2026. Solar farms now run on cloud links and smart inverters, which widens the attack surface for hackers. A break-in could cut output, wreck gear, or shake grid stability when many sites are hit at once.

The roadmap sorts attackers from nation states to lone script kiddies. One case study recalls a March 2019 denial-of-service hit on a Utah wind and solar operator, through a known firewall flaw, which cut site communications for short spells. The vision asks owners to build security in by design and raise cyber maturity across home and utility-scale solar alike.
doe-osti-3366491-radiological-safety-ana:
Idaho National Laboratory's users' manual for the Radiological Safety Analysis Computer, version 7.4, by Bradley J. Schrader and dated September 2025, documents the RSAC-7 code. Safety analysts use RSAC to calculate what happens if radioactive material escapes to the atmosphere at a nuclear facility: how much reaches people, and at what dose. The code builds its source term from reactor operating history or a criticality event.

Chapters cover atmospheric transport, filtration credits such as high-efficiency particulate air filters, and food chain pathways with element-by-element transfer factors for crops, milk, and meat. Appendix tables carry the parameter library, from soil buildup times to vegetable yields. The manual is the reference for analysts preparing the safety basis of DOE nuclear facilities. Export restrictions on the software are stated up front.
doe-osti-3376042-demand-response-roadmap:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory slide set by Sean Murphy and Josh Schellenberg, dated October 3, 2025, lays out a demand response roadmap for the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities. The board asked the lab to shape its demand response push for the Triennium 3 program cycle. Demand response pays users to trim load when the grid is tight. The board's sketch calls for third-party program runners, open talk protocols, and room for bulk and local grid needs.

The lab scored the state's standing with its Demand Flexibility Maturity Model. It then splits the build into three phases: lay the ground, stand the programs up, then scale until the grid feels the effect. Sample slides show the data a DER registry would hold: device type, serial and account IDs, charge rates, and dispatch logs. Such a registry is the spine that lets many small devices act as one resource.
doe-osti-3376419-multiplexed-inertial-co:
Argonne National Laboratory final CRADA report ANL/TAPS-C2023-00095, by Lorenzo Nocivelli with Rawand Rasheed of Helix Earth Technologies, covers computer models for a new kind of liquid-gas filter. The firm's MICRA filter pulls droplets out of fast gas streams by inertia and coalescence. Such filters serve high-rate chemistry, where amine sprays scrub gases. Stacked banks of the filters, the multiplexed layout of the title, raise the flow a plant can treat.

Three builds make up the work. First, a full spray model went into the open-source OpenFOAM code. It tracks amine spray birth, drift, and capture with coupled mass, motion, heat, and species terms. Second, the MICRA filter itself was modeled two ways: as a solid shape and as a porous block. Partner test data checked the model and it held. Third, a script now reshapes the filter geometry on its own for design sweeps.
doe-osti-3377121-beamline-device-designa:
Los Alamos National Laboratory memo LAMP-ENG-MOA-001, issued July 7, 2026 as LA-UR-26-25540, fixes how beamline devices get named at the LAMP project. R. Tyler Thornton of the Accelerator Operations and Technology division wrote it for LAMP and LANSCE management. Every magnet, gauge, and monitor needs a short code that control software can carry. Names that drift between crews cause real mix-ups. The memo sets one scheme and lists the codes in use.

Its ten-digit string descends from the old RICE system. The lab runs EPICS, which caps names at forty characters. Each LAMP beamline takes a two-letter code, or a letter and a digit. Injector A, code IA, handles the H-plus beam. Injector B, code IB, handles the H-minus beam and its short transport line. Injector C, for polarized protons, is marked not in use. Tables extend the list through the transport lines.
doe-osti-3409076-run-25-in-the-injectors:
Brookhaven note BNL-230024-2026-TECH, by K. Zeno and dated July 2026, reviews Run 25 in the injector chain that feeds the colliders. Injectors prepare particle beams before they enter the main rings. Small faults here limit every later experiment.

Pages track beam size, intensity, and transfer steps between machines. One pulse showed beam sizes of 5.5 and 4.6 millimeter-milliradians at a named monitor. Booster intensity reached about 5 billion particles for one cycle in the case shown. Operators can compare Run 25 with past runs, including 2021 EBIS work, and spot where tuning helped or hurt.
doe-osti-3943078-bioalcohol-chemistry-fo:
Sandia National Laboratories chemists Christian J. Devereux, Carles Martí, Pieterjan Robbe, Judit Zádor, and Habib N. Najm study how alcohols break down on the path from plant matter to fuel. Their report, SAND2026-26570R, was printed in September 2026. The key step is dehydration, where an alcohol loses water to form new compounds.

Computer models do the heavy lifting here. The team used a method called metadynamics, which pushes a simulated molecule along chosen measures so rare changes can be watched in full. Runs on ethanol show how the measures swing as the reaction nears. The authors also flag a flaw in how start and end points were set, which can shift the energy values, and they suggest a cleaner fix. Sharp reaction maps help engineers design better ways to turn biomass into fuel.
dream-psychology-psychoanalysis-for-begi:
Sigmund Freud lays out his dream theory for new readers in Dream Psychology, in the 1920 James A. McCann edition from New York, with M. D. Eder's translation and an introduction by André Tridon. The first chapter states the claim at once: dreams have a meaning, and that meaning is the dreamer's own mental act, not a message from gods or demons.

Nine chapters build the method. They cover the dream mechanism, why dreams disguise desires, dream analysis, sex in dreams, and the wish that Freud finds at the root of each dream. Case bits ground the talk, like the dreamer who that same evening heard a servant girl boast her child was made on the stairs. Later chapters take up the primary and secondary processes and the unconscious itself. Beginners get the full Freudian map in plain order.
edison-s-conquest-of-mars:
Garrett P. Serviss sends Thomas Edison against the Martians in Edison's Conquest of Mars, dated 1898, a sequel in spirit to Wells's War of the Worlds. The narrator takes up the record, he says, as a duty to posterity. The Martians died of disease on Earth, but their fleeing car fired an explosive that wrecked New York and shook down towns for miles.

Earth builds a fleet of airships and strikes back at Mars itself. Mid-voyage chapters show the Martian sky alive with craft of strange forms, gathering under the human squadron like hornets under a poked nest. Signals flash, and the crews rush to clear the range. Serviss writes big, earnest science romance: real astronomy of his day, huge guns, and Edison as the calm engineer of revenge. The book is a landmark of early American space fiction.
editorials-from-the-hearst-newspapers:
Arthur Brisbane wrote short, punchy editorials for the Hearst newspapers, and this volume gathers dozens of them. Brisbane, the most widely read American editorial writer of his day, took up whatever caught his mind. Titles here ask why all men are gamblers, whether animals have souls, and what nine hundred ninety-nine years will mean for the human race.

Other pieces treat God, immortality, microbes, automobiles, trusts, and unions in plain talk aimed at ordinary readers. Brisbane argues, jokes, and moralizes, often inside a single page. Read today, the pieces show mass journalism learning to sound like a neighbor: confident, curious, and sure the reader has five minutes, not an hour.
empire-builders:
Francis Lynde turns his railroad knowledge into a novel of finance and sabotage in Empire Builders, published by the Bobbs-Merrill Company in 1907. Stuart Ford, a young railroad builder, fights to push a Colorado line through against rivals who spike switches and steal payrolls. The first chapter opens on Engine Number 206, a narrow-gauge locomotive failing to push its snow plow through crusted drifts.

Ford needs thirty-five millions, the chapter title runs, and he finds it in Charles Edward and his money. Adair rides the line and watches Ford fret over the rotten commissary and the graft on the pay-rolls. Chapters like The Siege of the Nadia and The Star of Empire mix boardroom fights with mountain work. Jay Hambidge drew the illustrations.
england-under-the-tudors:
Arthur D. Innes's England Under the Tudors is a history of Tudor England, presented in a fourth edition for students and general readers. Innes writes at a moment when new material was piling up faster than historians could absorb it, and his general editor notes that standard histories of the last generation already needed revision.

The book retells the Tudor story from Henry the Seventh through Elizabeth, covering the break with Rome, the growth of royal power, and England's emergence as a sea power. Innes keeps the narrative clear and continuous, rather than burying it in monograph detail, while drawing on the newer research of his day. Students meeting the Tudors for the first time, and readers refreshing an old acquaintance, will find it a steady, readable guide.
esther-waters:
George Moore's novel Esther Waters appears here in an edition dated 1899. It opens with Esther, a strongly built girl of twenty, standing on a station platform with a heavy bundle and a roped box. She is on her way to a place called Woodview, up a lane past a lodge gate, to start work. The porter points out her road, and she walks into service with little more than what she carries.

Later scenes show Esther at work in other households, carrying jugs, clearing dishes, and facing questions from an employer who senses that something serious has happened. Moore gives her labor close attention: the lifting, the errands, the small shames and accidents of a servant's day. Readers get a plain, unsparing picture of a young working woman holding on to her dignity in a hard trade.
fairies-and-fusiliers:
Graves's Fairies and Fusiliers mixes war poems with whimsical verse in one slim volume. Robert Graves served with the Royal Welch Fusiliers, to whom he dedicates the book. The title page is dated 1918. Some poems came by leave of Harold Monro and the Nation's editor.

Two Fusiliers and Letter to S.S. from Mametz Wood face the war directly. A Dead Boche, The Last Post, and When I'm Killed share that ground. Goliath and David and Babylon retell old stories. I'd Love to Be a Fairy's Child and The Bough of Nonsense turn playful. A Child's Nightmare and The Spoilsport keep the fairy strain. Graves sets trench realism beside nursery fancy without a seam.
federalist-papers:
The Federalist Papers are 85 essays written in 1787 and 1788 to win support for the new United States Constitution. Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay wrote them under one pen name, Publius. The essays first ran in New York newspapers during the ratification fight.

The authors explain the Constitution piece by piece and answer the fears of its critics. Famous numbers defend an energetic union, a large republic that tames factions, and the separation of powers. Judges and scholars still cite the papers to read the founders' intent. They stand as the classic work of American political thought.
fighting-in-flanders:
Powell reports the first months of the Great War in Fighting in Flanders. E. Alexander Powell was a special correspondent of the New York World, sent with the Belgian forces in the field. Photographs by Donald Thompson fill the book. His chapters run from the war correspondents and the city of gloom to the fall of Antwerp. The preface is dated November 1, 1914.

The sampled pages catch a near disaster in Ghent. A Belgian in a crowd leapt onto a car and leveled a revolver at German soldiers inside it. Thompson knocked the man's hand up as Powell threw on the power and drove through the mob. Powell was told by General von Boehn himself that the shots would have doomed the city. The book is front-line reporting, written while the war was young.
five-of-maxwell-s-papers:
Five of Maxwell's Papers collects five scientific papers and addresses by James Clerk Maxwell. The first studies the Foramen Centrale, the yellow spot on the retina of the eye. Maxwell noticed an elongated dark spot in the blue of the spectrum, following his eye's motion. His 1856 report to the British Association explains the observation.

A theory of compound colours follows, presenting his experiments on mixing coloured lights. Poinsot's theory of rotating bodies receives a mathematical treatment. An address to a mathematical society and an introductory lecture on experimental physics complete the set. The papers show Maxwell before the electromagnetic fame, working on colour vision and mechanics. His method is characteristic: a simple observation, patiently varied, until it yields a law. Students of physics meet here the clearest experimental prose of the century.
flaubert-sand-letters:
A. L. McKenzie translated the Sand and Flaubert letters in 1921, with Stuart Sherman's opening essay. Sherman notes that the friendship ran twelve years, through the Franco-Prussian War and the Commune. Sand appears in her calm late years at Nohant, ringed by children and grandchildren.

Flaubert, the hermit of Croisset, writes from the opposite pole of life. The two giants argue over art, politics, and how a writer should live. Their exchange is funny, combative, and deeply fond by turns. Sherman calls it rich as biography alone, yet the letters also show two great minds at full stretch for any reader.
floor-games-a-companion-volume-to-little:
H. G. Wells wrote Floor Games after playing on nursery floors with his two young sons, and the book reads like a father thinking aloud. Wells, famous for scientific romances, treats toy soldiers and planks as tools for growing minds. A washable cork-carpet floor, he insists, starts the enterprise. Imagination, not expensive toys, does the heavy lifting.

Four toy groups anchor his system: soldiers and figures, bricks, boards and planks, and clockwork trains with rails. Boards become islands in a floor sea, hills on a plain, bridges, and station roofs. Chapters build the Wonderful Islands, raise cities, and rig funicular railways and marble towers up bookcase cliffs. War games get a brief nod despite the companion link to Little Wars. Wells keeps urging parents to buy simple, open-ended pieces and play along. Educators still cite the book as an early, joyful brief for learning through free play.
flowers-from-a-persian-garden-and-other-:
Clouston culls the literature of Persia in Flowers from a Persian Garden and Other Papers, dated 1890. W. A. Clouston takes his title from Sir William Ouseley's picture of that literature as a smiling garden. There the nightingale sings, fruit hangs thick, and wisdom is heard in moral sentences. Clouston, a folklorist, edited many Eastern romances, and this book gathers his papers.

The sampled pages give a taste of both halves of his work. One tale tells how the juice of the grape was sweetened. A mixture of the blood of a lion, a lamb, a pig, and a monkey was laid at the roots of the vines. Noah drank, and lay naked. Another paper takes up the luminous jewels of legend. Such gems, said to give light without the sun, fill the Arabian Nights, and Clouston weighs whether the Arabs took the notion from the rabbis.
four-american-leaders:
Eliot portrays four Americans in addresses written for public commemorations. Franklin was honored at Philadelphia on the two hundredth anniversary of his birth, and Washington before the Union League Club of Chicago. Channing's statue unveiling and a fourth commemoration complete the volume, published at Boston in 1906.

The Channing essay dwells on a paradox. His visions were far-reaching and his doctrines often radical, yet in habitual action he stayed surprisingly conservative. He broke with Boston's Second Church before thirty, with exquisite candor, yet attended church all his life. Charles William Eliot warns that each essay shows its man only in some of his aspects.
four-years:
William Butler Yeats's Four Years is a memoir of 1887 to 1891, the years when the Yeats family settled in Bedford Park after arriving from Dublin. Yeats remembers a red-brick house with wood mantlepieces copied from marble originals by the Adam brothers, with a balcony and a small garden under a tall chestnut tree.

The memoir recalls Bedford Park's crooked, picturesque streets, its tiled roofs and its co-operative stores, and the fading enthusiasm for the Pre-Raphaelite movement that had shaped the suburb. Yeats writes with the poet's eye for houses, streets and moods, and with hindsight about his own youth. Readers of Yeats will find Four Years an essential, beautifully written record of his formation.
friends-and-helpers:
Friends and Helpers, compiled by Sarah J Eddy and dated 1899, teaches children to treat animals with considerate kindness. Eddy states the aim in her preface without decoration: many homes neglect this teaching entirely, so the schoolteacher must arouse interest in the animals that depend on us. She quotes Sir Arthur Helps, who measured the world's advance by growing humanity and shrinking cruelty.

Three parts gather stories, verses, and short lessons about the services animals render to people. Horses, dogs, birds, and farm creatures appear as helpers to be understood, not merely used. Eddy argues that thoughtlessness, not malice, causes most cruelty, and that a child shown how animals suffer will grow into a less selfish adult. The book belongs to the humane education movement that put kindness lessons into American classrooms.
ghosts-i-have-met-and-some-others:
John Kendrick Bangs's Ghosts I Have Met and Some Others is a book of comic ghost stories, illustrated by Newell, Frost and Richards. Bangs dedicates it to choice spirits everywhere, and his contents promise ghosts that haunted him, a grandmother's hair sofa, and the mystery of Barney O'Rourke.

Other tales include an exorcism that failed, Thurlow's Christmas story, the Dampmere mystery, and Carleton Barker, first and second. Bangs tells his hauntings with a straight face and a wink, letting grotesque figures grin, flee through wainscoting, or discourse on Elysian silverware. Readers who like their ghosts funny rather than frightening will enjoy Bangs's genial spooks.
govdocs-archive_org-Volume3Appendix1TheP:
Appendix 1, titled The Programmers, is part of The Illuminati Formula Used to Create an Undetectable Total Mind Controlled Slave, a well-known work of mind-control conspiracy literature. The appendix stands apart from the main text as a reference section.

It profiles people the book's authors allege worked as mind-control programmers, naming figures they tie to secret programs. The claims are presented as fact by the authors but rest on the book's own conspiracy framework, not on official records. The library holds it as an archive item, without endorsement, for readers studying this literature and its influence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CarrollAudreyMr: nsia-CarrollAudreyMrs Carroll Audrey Mrs: the made public government document on Audrey Carroll, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, of the files. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DallasBirchers_:
United Press International reported from Dallas on a protest by local parents. Students at Bryan Adams High School had been required to watch Civil Riots, U.S.A., a film made by the John Birch Society. Parents objected to their children being made a captive audience for the group's message.

The dispute was about who controls what students see in a public school. The Birch Society used films to spread its view of unrest in America, and the school gave that film class time. The parents' protest, recorded in this short wire report, pushed back against both decisions at once.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDefectors_FB: Department of Justice Memorandum: Assassination of President John FKennedy - the garbled DOJ memo headed with the assassination. Damaged, but kept, complete, for researchers. A single memo. A US government document from the archive. Offers much to ponder.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JohnsonACMrs_Jo: Tom Bethell, a researcher on Jim Garrison's staff, sent the district attorney a memorandum on August 31, 1967. The memo reports an interview with Mrs. A. C. Johnson. Staff memos like this one carried witness talk from the field to Garrison's desk. The surviving record gives the writer, recipient, and date but not what Mrs. Johnson said, so it stands as a dated Garrison staff memo.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JoneMaryMrs_Jon: A copy survives of a letter sent to Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy concerning a man named W. M. Lutfey. The letter is filed under the name of Mrs. Mary Jone. Citizens wrote to the attorney general on every subject in his brother's administration, and their letters entered the files. The record gives the recipient and the man discussed, but no date or contents.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KoppelmanPMrs_K: Philomena E. Koppelman of Hartford, Connecticut, filed this United States patent application for a thimble fitted with a protective shield. The shield was meant to guard the finger during sewing. Patent applications describe an invention in formal language and state exactly what the inventor claims as new. The file preserves her application as filed, a small record of an ordinary inventor seeking protection for a household tool.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Lawyers_Lawyers: nsia-Lawyers Lawyers: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Smears_Smears:
Morton Mintz reported for the Washington Post on July 12, 1973, under the headline 'Weicker Says He Reported.' Senator Lowell P. Weicker Jr. of Connecticut had reported certain charges to investigators. The charges were attributed to unidentified 'Nixon reelection sources.' Weicker sat on the Senate's Watergate committee, where he had become one of the president's Republican critics.

Anonymous sourcing inside a scandal is itself a story: who is planting charges, and who carries them to the record. Mintz, the Post's careful investigative reporter, lays out what Weicker said he had done with the claims. The article preserves a senator's account of rumor handled through channels, at the summer's height, when the committee's hearings were remaking the scandal daily.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WeisbergFBIReco: The FBI released a set of cross-reference pages from its central records system under the Freedom of Information Act. The pages concern Harold Weisberg, the assassination researcher who sued the government many times for files. Cross-reference pages show how often a name appears across bureau records. For Weisberg, the release is both research material and a record of his long fight to open the files.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-cub:
After the Bay of Pigs invasion failed in April 1961, President John F. Kennedy turned on the agency that planned it. This briefing book, posted in April 2026 for the sixty-fifth anniversary, uses newly posted documents on that aftermath. The invasion itself had collapsed within days on a Cuban beach.

Kennedy considered reshaping the CIA and even dismantling it, the documents show. That reaction matters because the failed landing shaped his distrust during the missile crisis a year later. Readers get the paper trail of a president deciding what to do with an intelligence service that had failed him.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Bom: A Cuban airliner was bombed out of the sky in 1976, killing everyone aboard, in one of the worst terrorist attacks in the hemisphere's history. This briefing-book page revisits that bombing forty years later, drawing on the National Security Archive's records. The evidence here is the title alone, so no specific documents can be named. The page's value is its anniversary framing: the case, and the men long accused of planning it, remained unresolved four decades on.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
In the late 1980s a series of incidents slowly woke the Defense Department to attacks on computer networks. Michael Martelle edited this briefing book, posted in June 2019, twenty years after the response took shape. The military assembled the first joint task force built explicitly around cyber warfare.

That unit, Joint Task Force - Computer Network Defense, was a landmark in organization. Before it, network defense belonged to no one in particular. The records trace how scattered warnings became a standing command with a defined mission, a step every later American cyber unit descends from in some way.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_dnsa_US_:
Jimmy Carter's foreign policy, from 1977 to 1981, is documented here through papers written at the very top. Top-level memos to the president and National Security Council records anchor this publication. Many records were marked eyes only, and some carry Carter's own annotations.

The top secret memos show Carter handling arms control talks and the Iran hostage crisis. They also cover the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in his final year. His working relationships with Secretary of State Cyrus Vance and adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski come through in the paper. The set joined the Archive's award-winning digital series on American foreign policy.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_Rum:
Donald Rumsfeld, as secretary of defense, wrote short memos his staff called snowflakes. This posting draws on newly published snowflakes from the war in Afghanistan. Two years after the invasion, they show, Rumsfeld still lacked intelligence on who the enemies were.

That admission from the war's own manager is startling. The United States had toppled the Taliban quickly, then settled into a long fight against an enemy its leaders could not clearly name. A snowflake is a small document, but a run of them records a secretary's frustrations in his own terse style, day after day.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_guatemal: The Guatemala Genocide Ruling, Five Years Later: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In September 1979 an American Vela satellite recorded a double flash over the South Atlantic, the signature of a nuclear test. William Burr, Avner Cohen, and Richard Wolfson edited this briefing book, number 686, published forty years later in September 2019. Suspicion fell on Israel or South Africa.

A newly posted document shows the CIA saw the probability of a nuclear test as ninety percent or more. Yet White House science advisers dismissed that possibility, and the posting argues their dismissal looks weak against the added evidence. The Vela flash remains officially unexplained. These documents let readers judge the strongest case that a secret test lit up the ocean that night.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_peru_Per:
Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission delivered its final report in 2003, after years of internal conflict with the Shining Path and state forces. On the twentieth anniversary, in August 2023, the Archive posted a core collection of declassified American documents tied to that history.

Evidence here reaches only the anniversary and the collection's existence, so claims stay modest. American documents matter in Peru's reckoning because Washington supported Peruvian governments through the conflict years. A core collection lets readers and researchers test the commission's findings against what United States officials reported at the time. Anniversaries of truth reports are when archives can restart a national conversation.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Perestroika was Mikhail Gorbachev's program to rebuild Soviet life in the late 1980s. Thirty years on, the National Security Archive issued Briefing Book number 504 on that effort. Edited by Svetlana Savranskaya and Anna Melyakova and published in March 2015, it gathers newly released records on what reform achieved and where it fell short.

Newly published material includes a report on the Chernobyl disaster and records of Gorbachev's meetings with French leader Francois Mitterrand and President George H. W. Bush. One record holds Gorbachev's 1991 appeal for help from abroad as the Soviet Union came apart. The Archive sums up the record as great gains beside large missed chances, and the papers let readers judge both for themselves.

In December 1988, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev came to New York and met President Ronald Reagan and Vice President George H. W. Bush at Governors Island. Thirty years later, in December 2018, the National Security Archive published declassified documents on that meeting and on the famous United Nations speech Gorbachev gave on the same trip.

In that speech, Gorbachev offered deep cuts in Soviet forces, a move the Archive calls an arms race in reverse. The released papers show the United States and its NATO allies worrying about losing control of the public story of the Cold War. Readers can watch a superpower rivalry turn, in real time, into something closer to partnership, and see how hard that shift was to manage.

George H. W. Bush hosted Mikhail Gorbachev in Washington and at Camp David in the spring of 1990, months after the Berlin Wall fell. Briefing Book number 707, compiled and edited by Thomas Blanton and Svetlana Savranskaya and published in June 2020, presents Soviet and American documents from that summit, thirty years after it happened.

Germany's future dominates the talks, along with the shape of Europe, regional trouble spots, and Moscow's deepening money crisis. Gorbachev leaves with ceremony and a symbolic trade deal, but not the aid or arms cuts he wanted. The papers show a Soviet leader running out of time, and they connect to the editors' award-winning book on the last superpower summits, then due out in paperback.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Reading_Barr: When Attorney General William Barr released the Mueller report in 2019, he released it with redactions: black bars hiding grand jury material, ongoing cases, and intelligence methods. A National Security Archive briefing book page takes up the sport of reading those redactions. It studies what the blacked-out text's length, placement, and context reveal. The subject is what Special Counsel Robert Mueller found. His investigation covered Russian election interference and the Trump campaign. Only the page capture is preserved here, marking the Archive's entry in a national pastime of that spring.
government-by-the-brewers:
Adolph Keitel spent thirty years inside the brewing trade, and then wrote this attack on it. Government by the Brewers? asks whether the beer interest rules American politics. His contents list the charges: prohibition banishes crime, beer is a habit-forming drug, and beer is not a temperance drink. One chapter calls non-alcoholic beer a mysterious compound of drugs.

Keitel argues that lower alcohol in beer will raise, not lower, drunkenness, and that brewers attack distillers to hide their own crimes. Crime, he says, is planned in saloons, and the beer traffic does not respect the home. The book is a polemic, written with an insider's zeal on the dry side. It shows the temperance fight at full heat, when the brewers were cast as a hidden government.
grant-personal-memoirs:
Ulysses Grant wrote his Personal Memoirs in 1885 while dying of throat cancer, racing to finish. Mark Twain published the book and championed it. Grant completed it days before his death, and it secured his family's future.

The memoirs cover his West Point years, the Mexican War, and his Civil War commands in plain, clear prose. Shiloh, Vicksburg, Chattanooga, and Appomattox receive his calm, exact judgment. He praises and blames without bitterness, even toward old foes. Critics rank the book among the finest memoirs ever written by a soldier or a president. Twain's firm sold the set door to door with striking success.
great-astronomers:
Sir Robert S. Ball, Cambridge professor of astronomy, wrote Great Astronomers as a gallery of lives from Ptolemy to John Couch Adams. Ball explains each man's discoveries while trying, as his preface says, to make the character and surroundings real. Copernicus, Tycho Brahe with his island observatory, Galileo, Kepler, and Newton anchor the early chapters.

Flamsteed, Halley, Bradley, the Herschels, father and son, Laplace, Airy, Hamilton, Le Verrier, and Adams carry the story to Ball's own century. Some sketches began as magazine pieces, including work for Good Words and the Quarterly Review. Ball writes as an insider who knew the later men's world. The book suits any reader who wants the history of astronomy told through its makers.
great-italian-and-french-composers:
George T. Ferris set himself a hard task in 1878: to compress the famous Italian and French composers into one small volume. His note owns the embarrassment of the choice. The bulk of the space goes to composers of the higher rank, while lesser names get brief mention to fix their place. He wrote, he says, for the music-loving public, not merely for critics and scholars. His sources include Hullah's history and Fétis's great dictionary of musicians.

Italian opera masters and French stage composers fill the sketches. Lives, works, and critical verdicts are packed tight. Ferris writes in the warm, popular style of his Great Singers books. Such volumes brought concert-room knowledge to the parlor in an age before recordings. This one still gives a brisk map of two schools that shaped opera for the whole world.
great-pictures-as-seen-and-described-by-:
Esther Singleton edited and translated Great Pictures in 1899, gathering famous writers on famous paintings, with many illustrations. The plan is in the title: each picture is seen and described by a writer of note. The first piece treats Bordone's Fisherman Presenting the Ring to the Doge Gradenigo, by Théophile Gautier. Walter Pater writes on Botticelli's Birth of Venus.
